• His saying: ﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and He revives the earth after its death. And thus you will be brought out.﴾ (Ar-Rum: 19). That is: from your graves, living after death.

• His saying: ﴿And We sent down blessed water from the sky and caused gardens and grain to grow, and We revived a dead land with it. Thus will be the emergence.﴾ (Qaf: 9-11). That is: your emergence from graves alive after death.

• His saying: ﴿Until, when they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land, and send down water upon it, and bring out with it all kinds of fruits. Thus do We bring out the dead, that perhaps you may remember.﴾ (Al-A'raf: 57).

• His saying: ﴿So look at the traces of God's mercy, how He revives the earth after its death. Indeed, that is the Reviver of the dead, and He is over all things Powerful.﴾ (Ar-Rum: 50).

• His saying: ﴿So We revived the earth thereby after its death. Thus is the resurrection.﴾ (Fatir: 9). (p-280)

• His saying: ﴿Then We revived with it a dead land. Thus you will be brought out.﴾ (Az-Zukhruf: 11). Among that is His saying here: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells﴾ (Al-Hajj: 5), with the proof of His saying after it: ﴿That is because God is the Truth, and it is He who gives life to the dead, and because He is over all things Powerful, and because the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and because God will resurrect those in the graves﴾ (Al-Hajj: 6-7).

﴿And among people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating Book﴾. ﴿Turning aside his side [in arrogance], to lead others astray from the way of Allah. For him in this world is disgrace, and We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the Burning﴾.

Some scholars said: The first verse, which is ﴿And among people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge, and follows every rebellious devil﴾ [al-Hajj: 3], was revealed concerning the ignorant followers who dispute without knowledge, following their leaders from among the devils of mankind and jinn. This last verse, however, concerns the leaders, the callers to misguidance who are followed in that. What indicates this is that He said in the first verse: ﴿and follows every devil﴾ [al-Hajj: 3], and said in this one: ﴿Turning aside his side to lead others astray from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 9]. Thus it becomes clear that he is one who misguides others and is followed in disbelief and misguidance. This is according to the recitation of the majority (al-Jumhur), with the *ya'* of *yudill* pronounced with a *damma* (*yuḍillu*, "he leads astray"). As for the recitation (qira'a) of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, which has a *fatha* on the *ya'* (*yaḍilla*, "he goes astray"), there is no proof in the verse for this meaning. We have already explained the meaning of the disbelievers' disputing about Allah without knowledge, so there is no need to repeat it here.

Some scholars said regarding His words in this noble verse: ﴿without knowledge﴾ [al-Hajj: 8], meaning without necessary knowledge (*'ilm ḍarūrī*) that they have regarding what they dispute about. ﴿Nor guidance﴾ means reasoning and rational reflection by which the intellect is guided to what is correct. ﴿Nor an illuminating Book﴾ means clear, luminous revelation by which one knows what he disputes about. So he has no necessary knowledge, no acquired knowledge through sound rational reflection, and no knowledge from revelation. Thus he is utterly ignorant in every respect.

His words ﴿turning aside his side﴾ [al-Hajj: 9] (*thāniya 'iṭfihi*) are a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to the implied subject pronoun in *yujādilu* ("disputes"). The meaning is: he argues falsely while being one who turns his side, i.e., who twists his neck away from accepting the truth out of arrogance and aversion. The word *thāniya* is the active participle of *thana al-shay'* ("he bent the thing") when he twisted it. The root *'aṭf* means the side, and the two *'iṭfā* of a man are his two sides from his head down to his hips. The Arabs say: *thanā fulānun 'anka 'iṭfahu*, meaning "so-and-so turned his side away from you," i.e., he turned away from you. The scholars chose to express this here with "neck," saying *thāniya 'iṭfihi* means "twisting his neck," even though *'iṭf* includes the neck and other parts, because the first sign of aversion appears in the neck of a person, who twists it and turns his face away from a thing by bending it.

The exegetes say that the *lām* in His words ﴿to lead others astray from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 9] and similar verses, where the final cause (*'illa ghā'iyya*) does not clearly appear, as in His words ﴿So the people of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], is the *lām* of consequence (*lām al-'āqiba*). The rhetoricians claim that this involves a subsidiary metaphor (*isti'āra tab'iyya*) in the meaning of the particle. We promised to clarify this in Surat al-Qasas.

We say here: The apparent view is that the correct position on this is other than what they mentioned, and that the *lām* in all of these is the *lām* of causation (*lām al-ta'līl*). The meaning is clear, without difficulty, as the Hafiz Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed out in several places in his tafsir.

The explanation of this: Allah is the One who decreed for the disbeliever, from eternity, that he should dispute about Allah without knowledge while twisting his neck in aversion from the truth and in arrogance. He decreed this for him so that He would make him one who goes astray and leads others astray. He has perfect wisdom in that,

- like His words: ﴿We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it﴾ [al-An'am: 25]; meaning, lest they understand it. Likewise ﴿So the people of Pharaoh picked him up﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], meaning Allah decreed that they would pick him up, in order that He might make him for them an enemy and a grief. This is clear and without difficulty, as you see. What He, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse about some disbelievers turning away from the truth and being arrogant, He clarified in other verses of the Book of Allah,

- like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away arrogantly, as if he had not heard them﴾ [Luqman: 7],

- and His words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," they turn their heads aside, and you see them turning away while they are arrogant﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 5],

- and His words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾ [al-Nisa': 61],

- and His words, concerning Luqman in his advice to his son: ﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people in contempt﴾ [Luqman: 18]; meaning, do not turn your face away from them in arrogance toward them.

- and His words concerning Pharaoh: ﴿And [there is a sign] in Moses, when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority. But [Pharaoh] turned away with his army﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 38-39]. His words ﴿turned away with his army﴾ (*fa-tawalla bi-rukniht*) mean: he twisted his side.

- and His words: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and distances himself by his side﴾ [al-Isra': 83],

and other verses besides these.

His words in this noble verse: ﴿For him in this world is disgrace﴾ [al-Hajj: 9], meaning humiliation and contempt. Allah has humbled those who disputed about Allah without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating Book, such as Abu Jahl ibn Hisham and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, by killing them on the day of Badr.

It is understood from this noble verse that whoever twists his side in arrogance toward the truth and aversion from it, Allah treats him in the opposite manner of his intention, so He humbles and humiliates him. That humiliation and abasement is the opposite of what he was hoping for in pride and greatness.

This concept from this verse is also indicated by other verses,

- like His words: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but pride, which they will never attain﴾ [Ghafir: 56],

- and His words to Iblis when he became arrogant: ﴿So descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein. So get out; indeed, you are of the debased﴾ [al-A'raf: 13]. *Al-saghar* means lowliness and humiliation, we seek refuge with Allah from that, as we have already explained.

- and His words: ﴿And We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the Burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 9]; meaning, We will burn him with the Fire, and make him taste the pain of its heat on the Day of Resurrection. It was called the Day of Resurrection because people will stand (*yaqumūna*) on that day before the Lord of the worlds, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected for a tremendous Day, the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 4-6].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth, and that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ The meaning: when the disbeliever is made to taste the torment of the Blaze on the Day of Resurrection, it will be said to him, "That," i.e., this torment which We cause you to taste, is "for what your hands have sent forth," i.e., what you sent forth in the world of disbelief and sins. ﴿And that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [al-Hajj: 10], so He does not wrong anyone even to the extent of an atom's weight. ﴿And if there is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward﴾ [al-Nisa': 40]. The apparent view is that the verbal noun formed from "anna" (that) and its complement in His saying, ﴿and that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [al-Hajj: 10], is in the genitive position, in coordination with "ma" (what), which is governed by the preposition "bi" (for).

The meaning is: this torment which Allah causes you to taste has come to you for two reasons: what your hands sent forth of evil deeds, namely disbelief and sins, and the justice of the One who recompenses you with that just recompense, and His not being unjust. We have already clarified earlier the well-known problem concerning the negation of the intensive form (ṣīghat al-mubālaghah) in His saying, ﴿is not ever unjust﴾, so that suffices here and there is no need to repeat it.

In this noble verse there are three questions:

The first: it is what we mentioned just now, that we have already explained its answer earlier, namely: the well-known principle in Arabic grammar (ʿilm al-ʿarabiyyah) is that when negation enters upon the intensive form, it does not necessitate the negation of the basic act itself.

So if you say, "Zayd is not a great oppressor of people (laysa Zaydun bi-ẓallāmin lil-nās)," its well-known meaning is that he is not excessive in wrongdoing, and this does not preclude that some wrongdoing at all may come from him. We have already put forward the clarification of this.

(p-283) The second question: He attributed everything that he sent forth to his hands in His saying, ﴿for what your hands have sent forth﴾, yet his disbelief, which is his greatest sin, is not an act of the hand but of the heart and the tongue. Although some kinds of striking with the hand indicate disbelief, it is more evident in the tongue and the heart than in the hand. And his fornication was not done by his hand but by his private part, and similar sins that are committed without the hand.

The answer to this is clear: among the methods of the Arabic language, in which the Qur'an was revealed, is the attribution of all actions to the hand, since it is the limb with which most actions are performed, so it predominates over others, and there is no problem with that.

The third question: it may be asked, what is the reason for the use of the demonstrative of distance in His saying, ﴿That (dhālika) is for what your hands have sent forth﴾, although the torment referred to is near and present?

The answer to this: among the methods of the Arabic language is placing the demonstrative of distance in the position of the demonstrative of nearness. We have clarified this matter in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" in discussing His saying, may He be exalted, at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1-2]; i.e., this Book.

Among the evidences for this in the Arabic language is the saying of Khifaf ibn Nudbah al-Sulami:

*If my horses have been struck at their core, then deliberately, before my eyes, I aimed at Malik.*

*I said to him while the spear was bending its shaft: "Look at Khifaf, indeed I am that (dhalika)."*

He means: "I am this."

What He, may He be exalted and high, mentioned in this noble verse, that it will be said to the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ and so on, is clearly a rebuke, reproach and humiliation for him. Similar statements in the Qur'an are numerous, such as His saying, ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire. Then pour over his head the torment of boiling water. Taste it! Indeed you were the mighty, the noble. This is what you used to doubt﴾ [al-Dukhan: 47-50], and His saying, ﴿The Day they are pushed into the fire of Hell with a shove. "This is the Fire which you used to deny. Is this magic, or do you not see? Burn therein, so be patient or be not patient; it is all the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do"﴾ [al-Tur: 13-16]. Verses of this kind are very numerous.

(p-284) The subject pronoun in His saying, ﴿He calls upon, besides Allah, that which can neither harm him nor benefit him﴾ [al-Hajj: 12], refers to the disbeliever mentioned in His saying: ﴿And if trial strikes him, he turns back on his face. He has lost the world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss﴾ [al-Hajj: 11]. That is, that disbeliever calls upon, besides Allah, that which cannot harm him if he abandons its worship and disbelieves in it, and cannot benefit him if he worships it and claims that it will intercede for him.

What Allah, exalted is He, mentions in this noble verse, that idols cannot harm those who disbelieve in them and cannot benefit those who worship them, He explains elsewhere, as in His saying: ﴿And they worship, besides Allah, that which can neither harm them nor benefit them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah." Say, "Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth? Exalted is He above what they associate with Him."﴾ [Yunus: 18], and His saying about His Prophet Ibrahim: ﴿He said, "Do they hear you when you call, or do they benefit you or harm you?" They said, "Rather, we found our fathers doing thus."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 72–74].

The meaning is that they acknowledged that they do not hear, do not benefit, and do not harm, but they worshipped them out of imitation of their fathers. Verses of this kind are many.

* *

Tanbih (a note of caution or clarification)

If it is said: what is the reconciliation between His negating both benefit and harm from that deity worshipped besides Allah in His saying, ﴿that which can neither harm him nor benefit him﴾ [al-Hajj: 12], and affirming both in His saying, ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ [al-Hajj: 13]? For the comparative form in His saying "nearer" (aqrab) indicates that there is benefit and harm, but the harm is nearer than the benefit.

The answer: the scholars have several responses to this.

Among them is what al-Zamakhshari mentioned. He said: If you say: harm and benefit are negated of the idols in one verse and affirmed for them in the other, and this is a contradiction.

I say: When the meaning is understood, this misconception disappears. Allah, exalted is He, has made the disbeliever foolish, in that he worships an inanimate object that possesses neither harm nor benefit, and yet he believes in it, in his ignorance and error, that he will gain benefit from it when he seeks its intercession. Then He said on the Day of Resurrection: this disbeliever will say, with calling and shouting, when he sees his harm through the idols and his entry into the Fire because of worshipping them, and does not see any effect of the intercession he claimed for them: ﴿Surely one whose harm is nearer than his benefit—wretched is the protector, and wretched is the companion﴾ [al-Hajj: 13]. (p-285) He repeated "calls upon" as if He had said: he calls upon, besides Allah, that which cannot harm him and cannot benefit him. Then He said: for one whose harm, by his being worshipped, is nearer than his benefit, by his being an intercessor: wretched is the protector and wretched is the companion. End of his quotation.

It is not hidden that this answer of al-Zamakhshari is unconvincing, because what is worshipped besides Allah has no benefit whatsoever, so that it could be said that its harm is nearer than its benefit. Abu Hayyan has explained that his answer does not hold.

Among them is what Abu Hayyan gave in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit).

Its summary is: the first verse concerns those who worship idols. Idols neither benefit those who worship them nor harm those who disbelieve in them; therefore He said of them: ﴿that which can neither harm him nor benefit him﴾. The indication that what is meant by this is idols is the use of the word *ma* (what) in His saying, ﴿that which can neither harm him nor benefit him﴾ [al-Hajj: 12], because the word *ma* is used for that which does not reason, and idols do not reason.

As for the other verse, it concerns one who worshipped some of the tyrants who were worshipped besides Allah, such as Pharaoh, who said: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38], ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 29], ﴿I am your most exalted lord﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24]. Indeed Pharaoh and his like among the tyrants who were worshipped may lavish the blessings of this world upon their worshippers. That is why the people who were sorcerers said to him: ﴿Indeed, will there be a reward for us if we are the victors?' He said, 'Yes, and indeed you will be, then, among those brought near﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 41–42]. This worldly benefit, in comparison with what they will encounter of punishment and eternal abiding in the Fire, is as nothing. So the harm of this worshipped one, through the eternal abiding of his worshipper in the Fire, is nearer than his benefit, which is a passing, small, worldly gain. The indication that the one worshipped in this last verse is some of the tyrants who are of the class of rational beings is the use of *man* (who), which is used for one who reasons, in His saying: ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ [al-Hajj: 13]. This is the essence of Abu Hayyan's answer, and it has a valid direction. And Allah knows best.

Know that the *lam* in ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ [al-Hajj: 13] presents a well-known difficulty, and the scholars have several answers to it.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned three of them:

The first: that the *lam* is displaced from its original position, and that this is one of the stylistic features of the Arabic language in which the Qur'an was revealed. The original is: "He calls upon the one whose harm is nearer than his benefit." Accordingly, *man* (the relative pronoun) is in the position of a direct object of *yad'u* (he calls upon), and the *lam* is a preparatory particle for an oath (*muwatti'a li-l-qasam*), entering upon the subject (*mubtada'*), which together with its predicate forms the relative clause. Emphasis of the subject within the relative clause with the *lam* or otherwise presents no difficulty.

Ibn Jarir said: and it is related from the Arabs by report: "Minha 'indi lama ghayruhu khayrun minhu" (from me is what, for another, is better than it); that is: "with me is what, for another, is better than it." And: "A'taytuka lama ghayruhu khayrun minhu" (I gave you what, for another, is better than it); that is: "what for another is better than it."

The second: that His saying *yad'u* (he calls upon) is an emphasis of *yad'u* in the verse before it. Accordingly, His saying *liman darruhu* (for one whose harm...) is in the position of the nominative by inception (*mubtada'*), the clause *darruhu aqrabu min naf'ihi* (whose harm is nearer than his benefit) is the relative clause of the relative pronoun *man*, and the predicate is the clause: ﴿Wretched is the protector﴾. This meaning is like the saying of the Arabs: "*Lama fa'altaa lahuwa khayrun laka*" (what you did, indeed it is better for you).

Ibn Jarir said, when he mentioned this view: The second *lam* in ﴿Wretched is the protector﴾ is the answer to the first *lam*. He said: this view is more correct according to the school of the grammarians, and the first is closer to the school of the exegetes. End of quotation.

The third: that *man* is in the position of an object of *yad'u*, and that the *lam* entered upon the direct object. He attributed this to some of the Basran grammarians, while quoting those who attributed it to them as saying it is anomalous (shadh). And the closest of them to me is the first.

Al-Qurtubi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He did not see any benefit from it at all, but He said ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ [al-Hajj: 13] as an elevation of speech, like His saying: ﴿And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. We have left aside the remaining opinions regarding the aforementioned *lam*, because they do not appear to us to be sound, and knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Wretched is the protector﴾. Al-mawla (the protector, patron, or ally) is everything between which and you a bond has been established, by which it allies with you and you ally with it. Al-ashir (the companion) is al-mu'ashir, meaning the associate, the friend, and the intimate.

The verified position is that what is meant by "the protector" and "the companion" in this noble verse, the blameworthy ones, is the object of worship that they used to call upon besides Allah, as is the apparent and immediate meaning from the context.

As for His saying: ﴿That is the far-off error﴾ [al-Hajj: 12]; that is, far removed from the truth and from what is correct.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the sky, then cut it off, and let him see whether his scheme removes what enrages him.﴾ There are well-known interpretations of this noble verse among the scholars, and some of them are witnessed by other Qur'anic verses.

The first: the meaning is: whoever among the disbelieving envious ones, toward him (ﷺ), thinks that Allah will not help him; that is, that Allah will not help His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿Let him stretch a rope⁠﴾ [al-Hajj: 15]; that is, with a rope to the sky, meaning the sky of his house, and what is meant by it is the ceiling, because the Arabs call everything that is above you a sky, as the poet said:

"And every elevated thing is sometimes called a sky, but the excellence lies where the sun and the moon are."

As we have explained in the surah of al-Hijr.

The meaning is: let him tie the end of the rope to the beam of the ceiling. ﴿Then let him cut⁠﴾ [al-Hajj: 15]; that is, let him strangle himself with the rope, tying it around his neck, and hang with the rope fastened to the ceiling until he dies. The word "cutting" is applied to strangulation because strangulation cuts off breath by blocking its passages; and for this reason, panting, which is the successive interruption of breath, is called "qat'" (cutting). ﴿Then let him see, when he has been strangled, whether his scheme removes⁠﴾ — that is, whether his act removes what enrages him of the victory of Allah for His Prophet (ﷺ) in this world and the Hereafter.

The meaning is: that act of this disbelieving envious man does not remove what enrages and angers him of Allah's victory for His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Zamakhshari said: His act was called a "scheme" because he placed it in the position of a scheme, since he could not do anything else, or as a form of mockery, because he did not scheme against the one he envied; he only schemed against himself. What is meant is: he has in his hand nothing but what does not remove what enrages him. End of quotation.

The summary of this view is that Allah says to His envious opponents (ﷺ), who wait for misfortunes to befall him and think that his Lord will not help him: "Die of your rage." He will surely be His helper, in spite of your noses. Among those who held this view are Mujahid, Qatadah, Ikrimah, 'Ata', Abu al-Jawza', and others, as Ibn Kathir transmitted from them. This is, in my view, the most apparent of them.

Among what witnesses to this meaning in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿And when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage. Say: Die in your rage.﴾

The second: the meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah will not help His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) in this world and the Hereafter, while in fact the victory comes to him (ﷺ) from the sky, let him stretch a rope to the sky and ascend by that means until he reaches the sky and cuts off the descent of revelation from the sky, thereby preventing victory from reaching him (ﷺ).

The meaning is that, even if the victory of Allah for His Prophet enrages him, he has no stratagem and no ability to prevent the victory, because he cannot ascend to the sky and prevent victory from descending upon him (ﷺ) from it. According to this view, the imperative form in His saying "then let him stretch" and His saying "then let him cut" is for incapacitation (taʿjīz). Then let that envious man, who is unable to cut off victory from him (ﷺ), see whether his scheme, when it reaches the utmost of his effort against the Prophet (ﷺ), removes what enrages him of Allah's victory for His Prophet (ﷺ).

The meaning is that if he exerts every ounce of his strength in scheming against the Prophet (ﷺ) to prevent Allah's victory from him, he is not able to do so, and his scheme does not remove what enrages him of Allah's victory for His Prophet (ﷺ).

Among what witnesses to this view from the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? Then let them ascend by means. [They are] a defeated host of the factions there.﴾ [Sad: 10–11] We have explained the meaning of this verse in the surah of al-Hijr.

Some scholars have a third view regarding the meaning of this noble verse: that the pronoun in ﴿will not help him⁠﴾ refers to "whoever" in His saying ﴿Whoever thinks⁠﴾ [al-Hajj: 15], and that "victory" here means "provision," so the meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah will not help him, that is, will not provide for him, let him strangle himself and kill himself, since there is no good in a life in which there is no provision and help from Allah; or let him strangle himself and die of rage and grief, for that will change nothing of what Allah has decreed and determined. Those who held this view said that the Arabs call provision "victory." Abu 'Ubayda said: A beggar from Banu Bakr stood before us and said: "Whoever gives me, may Allah give him," meaning: whoever gives me, may Allah give to him. They said: from this is the Arab saying "a victorious land" (ardun manṣūrah), that is, one that has been rained upon. And from it is the saying of a man from Banu Fa'qas:

"Indeed you do not give a man beyond his right, and you do not possess the side which the rain has helped (nāṣiruh)."

That is, giving him.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon and forgive him, says: This last view is clearly untenable, as you see. Those who said that the pronoun in His saying ﴿that Allah will not help him⁠﴾ refers to the religion or the Book do not contradict those who said the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), because the victory of the religion and the Book is his victory (ﷺ), as is not hidden. And Allah's victory for him (ﷺ) in this world is by elevating his word, subduing his enemies, and making his religion manifest, and in the Hereafter by elevating his rank and avenging against those who denied him, and similar things, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed We shall help Our messengers and those who believe in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses stand.﴾ [Ghafir: 51]. If it is said: you have established that the pronoun in "help him" refers to him (ﷺ), though he has not been mentioned, how do you establish the return of the pronoun to something not mentioned? The answer is what more than one has said: that he (ﷺ), although he has not been mentioned, the speech indicates him, because faith in His saying in the verse before it, ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens⁠﴾ [al-Hajj: 14], is faith in Allah and in Muhammad (ﷺ), and the turning away from the religion mentioned in His saying ﴿turns over on his face⁠﴾ [al-Hajj: 11] is a turning away from what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought.

As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿then let him cut⁠﴾, it was recited by Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Warsh from Nafi' with a kasra on the lam, according to the original form of the lam of command, and the rest recited it with a sukun on the lam, for lightness.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾. We have already presented the verses that clarify this in several places in this blessed Book, so that makes repeating it here unnecessary.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them; there will be poured over their heads boiling water,﴾ ﴿by which will be melted what is in their bellies and [their] skins.﴾ ﴿And for them are maces of iron.﴾

What Allah, exalted and high, has mentioned in this noble verse of the kinds of punishment of the people of the Fire (may Allah protect us and our Muslim brothers from it, and from everything that brings us closer to it, in word and deed) has been explained in other verses of the Book of Allah. His saying here, ﴿garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], means: Allah cuts out for them garments of fire, and clothes them in them, which are cut to fit them, as His saying concerning them: ﴿Their garments will be of tar﴾ [Ibrahim: 50]. The sarabil (garments) are the clothes which are shirts, as we have already explained. And like His saying: ﴿They will have beds of Hell and over them coverings [of Hell]﴾ [al-A'raf: 41]. The ghawashi (coverings) are the plural of ghashiyah, which is a covering like a quilt. That is the meaning of His saying here: ﴿garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. His saying here, exalted is He: ﴿there will be poured over their heads boiling water﴾ He also mentioned in other than this place, like His saying: ﴿Then pour over his head the torment of boiling water. Taste! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble﴾ [ad-Dukhan: 48-49]. The hamim (boiling water) is water that has reached extreme heat. And like His exalted saying: ﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal, which scalds the faces﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. His saying here, ﴿by which will be melted what is in their bellies﴾ [al-Hajj: 20], means: it will be melted by that boiling water when they are made to drink it, and it reaches their bellies, melting everything in their bellies of fat, intestines and other things, as His saying exalted is He: ﴿and they will be given boiling water which cuts their intestines to pieces﴾ [Muhammad: 15]. The Arabs say: "I melted (sahhartu) the thing, and it melted (infasahara)," so it is sahir; that is, I melted it and it melted. From this is the saying of Ibn Ahmar describing a sandgrouse feeding its young in a desert wasteland:

"It is fed a morsel cast onto a barren plain, which the sun melts, yet it does not melt."

That is, the sun melts it, yet it endures this and does not melt.

His saying: "and the skins." The apparent meaning is that it is conjoined to "what" in His saying: ﴿by which will be melted what is in their bellies﴾ [al-Hajj: 20], which is the deputy subject of "will be melted." According to this apparent and immediate meaning of the verse, that boiling water melts their skins just as it melts what is in their bellies, because of its intense heat.

The meaning is: "by which will be melted what is in their bellies, and by which will be melted the skins," that is, their skins; so the alif and lam stand in place of the possessive. Some scholars said: "and the skins" is in the nominative by a deleted verb conjoined to "will be melted," and its estimate is: "and the skins will be burned by it." A parallel to the deletion of the governing verb, where its object remains in the nominative after the waw, is the saying of Labid in his Mu'allaqa:

"The branches of the al-ayhaqan grew tall, and their gazelles and ostriches gave birth in both of the two sides."

He means: "and their ostriches laid eggs," because the ostrich does not bear a young one but lays eggs, unlike the gazelle, which bears a young one. An example of this in the accusative is the saying of another:

"When the women appear on a day and darken their eyebrows and eyes..."

"We see the penises of us, when they see them, standing, bowing and prostrating."

He means: "and they darkened the eyebrows, and they applied kohl to the eyes."

And his saying:

"I saw your husband in battle, girding a sword and a spear."

That is: "and carrying a spear," because a spear is not girded.

And the saying of another:

"You see him as if Allah slits his nose and his eyes, if his master returns to him the reward."

He means: "and gouges out his eyes."

Among its well-known witnesses is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"I fed her straw and cold water, until her eyes ran with tears."

He means: "and I gave her cold water to drink." Among examples of this in the Qur'an is His saying exalted is He: ﴿And those who had settled the abode and the faith﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], that is: "and they held firmly to the faith" or "they were attached to the faith." An example of this in the genitive is the saying: "Not every white thing is fat, nor every black thing a date"; that is: "nor every black thing is a date." To this issue he pointed in the Khulasa with his saying:

"It stands alone in conjoining a governing particle that has been removed, while its governed word remains, to avert a suspicion you should guard against."

His saying exalted is He in this noble verse: ﴿And for them are maces of iron﴾ [al-Hajj: 21]. The maqami' (maces) is the plural of miqma'ah, with a kasra on the first mim and a fatha on the last mim; it is also said miqma' without the ha'. In the language it is an iron rod like a hook with which the head of an elephant is struck. In the verse they are great iron clubs with which the guardians of the Fire strike the heads of the people of the Fire. Some scholars said: the maqami' are whips of fire. There is no doubt that the maces mentioned in the verse are of iron, because He, exalted is He, explicitly stated this.

His saying exalted is He: ﴿These are two adversaries who dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ [al-Hajj: 19] was revealed concerning the duellists at the Battle of Badr. They were: Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Ubaydah ibn al-Harith ibn al-Muttalib; and among their opposing duellists from the disbelievers were: Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, his son al-Walid ibn Utbah, and his brother Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, as is established in the two Sahihs and others.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whenever they wish to get out of it, from distress, they will be returned into it, and [it will be said], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾

What He, majestic and exalted, mentions in this noble verse is that the people of the Fire, whenever they wish to leave it because of the distress that afflicts them therein (we seek refuge in Allah from it), will be returned into it and prevented from leaving it. He has made this clear in other places, such as His saying in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, even if they had whatever is on the earth entirely and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them, and they will have a painful punishment. They will wish to leave the Fire, but they will not be ones who leave it, and for them is an enduring punishment.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 36–37]. And His saying in al-Sajdah: (p-292) ﴿Whenever they wish to leave it, they will be returned into it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. As for His saying in this verse of al-Hajj, ﴿and taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 22], the saying is omitted from it (ḥudhifa fīhi al-qawl).

The meaning is: they will be returned into it, and it will be said to them, "Taste the punishment of the burning." This omitted saying in al-Hajj is made explicit in al-Sajdah, in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whenever they wish to leave it, they will be returned into it, and it will be said to them, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. The exegetes say: the flame of the Fire lifts them up until it nearly throws them out of it, then the keepers of the Fire strike them with iron maces and return them to its depths. We seek refuge in Allah from it, and from everything that brings one near to it of speech and action.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah and the Sacred Mosque, which We made [a place] for all people, equal for the resident therein and the visitor; and whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing – We will make him taste of a painful punishment.﴾ Know that the predicate of "inna" (indeed) in His saying here: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Hajj: 25] is omitted, as you see.

What the verse indicates is that the implied sense is: Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah – We will make them taste of a painful punishment. This is also shown by His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing – We will make him taste of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 25], and the best way to interpret the Qur'an is by the Qur'an.

If it is asked: what is the reason for conjoining the present-tense verb to the past-tense verb in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and [they] bar﴾?

The answer comes in four aspects, one of which is clearly untenable:

The first: it is what some of the scholars of Arabic grammar (ʿarabiyya) have mentioned, that the present tense may not be tied to a specific time, whether present or future, and so it then indicates continuity. Among its instances is: ﴿and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 25], and His saying: ﴿those who believe and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28]. This was said by Abu Hayyan and others.

The second: that "yasuddūna" (they bar) is the predicate of an omitted subject, the sense being: "Indeed, those who disbelieve, and they bar..." On this reading the conjoined clause is a nominal, not a verbal, clause. This view was favoured by al-Qurtubi.

The third: that "yasuddūna" is a present-tense verb used to denote the past, i.e., "they disbelieved and barred." This is not evident.

The fourth: that the wāw is superfluous and the clause "yasuddūna" is the predicate of "inna," i.e., "Indeed, those who disbelieve bar..." (p-293) the verse. This is the one we previously stated to be clearly untenable, and it is as you see. What He, may He be exalted, mentions in this verse, that among the deeds of the disbelievers is barring from the way of Allah and from the Sacred Mosque, He has clarified in other places,

such as His saying: ﴿And barring from the way of Allah and disbelief in Him and the Sacred Mosque and expelling its people from it is greater in the sight of Allah﴾ (the verse) [al-Baqarah: 217];

and His saying: ﴿They are those who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and the sacrificial animals detained from reaching their place of sacrifice﴾ [al-Fath: 25];

and His saying: ﴿And let not the hatred of a people – that they barred you from the Sacred Mosque – lead you to transgress﴾ (the verse) [al-Ma'idah: 2], among other verses. And His saying in this noble verse: ﴿equal for the resident therein and the visitor﴾ [al-Hajj: 25].

It was read by the majority of the seven readers, other than Hafs from ʿAsim, as "sawāʾun" with a ḍammah on the hamzah. In its i'rab according to this majority reading, "sawāʾun" is in the nominative, and there are two views:

The first: that "al-ʿākif" is the subject (mubtada'), "al-bādī" is conjoined to it, and "sawāʾun" is the fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam). It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used in the sense of a descriptive adjective.

The meaning: "The resident and the visitor are equal therein," i.e., they are equal in it. This i'rab is the more evident of the two.

The second: that "sawāʾun" is the subject (mubtada') and "al-ʿākif" is the agent (fā'il) that stands in place of the predicate. The apparent justification for beginning with the indefinite "sawāʾun" in this view is that it governs the prepositional phrase in which it stands, since the meaning is: "equal therein are the resident and the visitor." The subject and predicate clause is in the position of the second object of "jaʿalnā" (We made).

Ḥafs from ʿAsim read "sawāʾan" with the fatḥah, which is the second object of "jaʿalnā," used in the sense of "ṣayyarnā" (We rendered). "Al-ʿākif" is the agent of "sawāʾ," meaning: "the resident therein and the visitor being equal." From the speech of the Arabs: "I passed by a man, equal are he and the nonexistent (ʿadam)." And whoever holds that "jaʿala" in the verse is transitive to one object says that "sawāʾan" is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the pronoun in "jaʿalnāhu," i.e., We placed it for the people in the state of being equal for the resident therein and the visitor, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for the people﴾ (the verse) [Ali 'Imran: 96].

Some people of knowledge said: the intended "Sacred Mosque" in this noble verse includes the entire Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram). For this reason some scholars derived from this verse that the dwellings of Makkah (ribaʿ Makkah) may not be owned. We have previously presented the discussion of this question fully, along with the views of the scholars and the examination of their evidences, in the commentary on Surat al-Anfal, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here. "Al-ʿākif" is one who resides in the Ḥaram, and "al-bādī" is one who comes to it from the desert, and likewise others from the regions of the world.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: "wal-bādī" was read by Abu ʿAmr and Warsh from Nafiʿ with the yā' after the dāl in continuous recitation (waṣl) and its omission in pausal recitation (waqf). It was read by Ibn Kathir with the yā' both in continuous recitation and pausal recitation, (p-294) and the rest of the seven read it without the yā', both in continuous recitation and pausal recitation.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing – We will make him taste of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 25]. We have already clarified the removal of the difficulty concerning the entry of the particle "bi-" (bi) upon the object in His saying "bi-ilḥādin" (by deviation), and its like in the Qur'an, and we multiplied the Arabic evidences for that in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾ [Maryam: 25], so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here.

Ilḥād linguistically originally means inclination (al-mayl). The meaning of ilḥād in the verse is: to incline and deviate from the religion of Allah which He legislated. This includes every inclination and deviation from the religion, and it primarily includes disbelief in Allah, associating partners with Him within the Sacred Precinct, doing something of what He has forbidden, and abandoning something of what He has made obligatory. Among the greatest of these is violating the sanctities of the Ḥaram. Some people of knowledge said: this includes monopolizing food in Makkah. Some said: this includes a man's saying: "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah." It is related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he had two tents: one at the edge of the Ḥaram and the other at the edge of the Ḥill (outside the Sacred Precinct). When he wished to rebuke his family or his servant, he would do so in the tent that was not in the Ḥaram, considering that such conduct falls under deviating therein by wrongdoing.

The author of this commentary – may Allah pardon him and forgive him – says: What appears on this question is that every transgression by abandoning an obligation or committing a prohibited act falls under the wrongdoing mentioned. As for permissible matters, such as a man rebuking his wife or his servant, these are neither deviation nor wrongdoing.

* *

Question

Some people of knowledge said: whoever intends to commit an evil deed in Makkah, Allah makes him taste a painful punishment because of his intention to do so, even if he does not commit it, unlike other places outside the Meccan Sacred Precinct, where one is not punished for mere intention. It is related from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him: "If a man intended deviation therein by wrongdoing while he was in ʿAden Abyan, Allah would make him taste of the painful punishment." This is established from Ibn Masʿud, and his attribution to him as a statement (waqf) is more authentic than its attribution to the Prophet (raf'). Those who held this view cited as evidence the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing – We will make him taste of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 25], because He, may He be exalted, linked the tasting of the painful punishment to the intention of deviation by wrongdoing therein, as the linking of a consequence to its condition. This is supported by the statement of some people of knowledge that the particle "bi-" in His saying "bi-ilḥādin" is because the intention is implicitly the meaning of resolve (hamm); i.e., "whoever resolves therein upon deviation." This is what Ibn Masʿud and others said.

(p-295) This noble verse therefore specifies the generality of the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Whoever resolves upon an evil deed and does not do it, a good deed is recorded for him," the hadith. Accordingly, this specification is due to the severity of the violation within the Meccan Sacred Precinct, and the reason for this is evident.

The author of this commentary – may Allah pardon him and forgive him – says: It is possible that the meaning of "intends" (yurid) in His saying: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation﴾ [al-Hajj: 25] is the determined resolve to commit the sin therein. A determined resolve to commit a sin is itself a sin for which one is punished in all of Allah's lands, Makkah and others.

The evidence that intending a sin, when it is a determined resolve, is like committing it is the authentic hadith of Abu Bakrah in the Sahih: "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we understand the killer, but what about the killed?" He said: "Indeed, he was eager to kill his companion." Their saying "what about the killed?" is a question seeking to identify the specific sin for which he entered the Fire, although he did not commit the killing. The Prophet ﷺ clarified by his saying "Indeed, he was eager to kill his companion" that his sin which brought him into the Fire was his determined resolve and his eagerness to kill his Muslim companion. We have previously stated many times that "inna" with kasrah and tashdid indicates causation, as established in the method of implication and alerting (maslak al-iy'a' wal-tanbih).

An example of punishment for a determined resolve to commit a forbidden act therein is what befell the People of the Elephant of total destruction, by means of the birds in flocks, "striking them with stones of baked clay" [al-Fil: 4], because of their resolve to commit abominations in the Ḥaram. Allah destroyed them for that resolve before they did what they had resolved upon. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in His saying "fihi" refers to the Sacred Mosque, but the ruling concerning the whole Ḥaram in aggravating the mentioned sin is likewise. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We settled for Abraham the place of the House, [saying], "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circle it, stand [in prayer], and bow and prostrate."﴾ Meaning: remember when We settled [him]. The Arabs say: "bawwa'tu lahu manzilan" (I prepared a dwelling for him), "bawwa'tuhu manzilan" (I settled him in a dwelling), and "bawwa'tuhu fi manzilin" (I settled him in a dwelling), all with one meaning: I prepared it for him, enabled him in it, and lodged him in it. So "tabawwa'ahu" means he dwelt in it (nazalahu), and "tabawwa'tu lahu manzilan" also means I prepared a dwelling for him and lodged him in it. Thus "bawwa'ahu," which is transitive by itself, is like His saying: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds - We will surely settle them in lofty chambers of Paradise﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 58], and His saying: ﴿And those who emigrated for the cause of Allah after they had been wronged - We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾ [al-Nahl: 41]. From the same usage is the verse of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib al-Zubaydi:

How many a noble brother of mine, I settled him with my own hands in a grave (lahd),

meaning: I prepared it for him and lodged him in it.

"Bawwa'tu lahu" is like His saying here: ﴿And when We settled for Abraham﴾ [al-Hajj: 26].

"Bawwa'tuhu fihi" is like the words of the poet:

And she was settled in the core of her people, and her settler was completed among her folk.

Meaning: she descended in nobility into the core of lineage. "Tabawwa'at lahu manzilan" is like His saying: ﴿And We inspired to Moses and his brother: "Settle your people in Egypt in houses"﴾ [Yunus: 87].

"Tabawwa'ahu":
- like His saying: ﴿And He has caused us to inherit the land, to settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [al-Zumar: 74];
- and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed﴾ [Yusuf: 56];
- and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who were settled in the home [i.e., Medina] and in faith﴾ [al-Hashr: 9].

The root of "tabawwu'" is from "mabā'ah," which is the dwelling place of a people in any location. So His saying: ﴿We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾ [al-Hajj: 26] means: We prepared it for him and made him aware of it, so that he would build it by Our command upon its original foundations which had been effaced, when We commanded him to build it, just as a place is prepared for one who wishes to descend into it.

The exegetes say: He settled it for him and showed it to him by means of a wind called al-Khajuj, which swept away what was above the foundation until the first foundation, which had been effaced, became visible, and Abraham and Isma'il built upon it. It is also said: He sent a cloud which settled over it, and its shadow was the size of the area of the House, so they dug down to the foundation, it appeared to them, and they built upon it. They also say that it had been effaced since the time of the flood of Noah, and that its site had been a sheepfold for a man of Jurhum. And Allah knows best.

What the Qur'an indicates is only this: that Allah settled its place for Abraham, prepared it for him, and made him aware of it so that he might build it on its site. A group of the people of knowledge held that the first to build it was Abraham, and that it had not been built before him. The apparent meaning of his saying, when he left Isma'il and Hajar in Mecca: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in an uncultivated valley near Your Sacred House﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], indicates that it had been built and had been effaced, just as His saying here, ﴿the place of the House﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], indicates, because it implies that it had a previous, known place. And Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿that you do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House﴾, and so on, is connected to an omitted element. The omitted element is indicated by the verse in al-Baqarah, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We charged Abraham and Isma'il: "Purify My House for those who circle it"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125]. So the mentioned verse of al-Baqarah shows that the meaning of this verse of al-Hajj, ﴿And when We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], is "and We charged him," i.e., We enjoined him, "that you do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circle it." The verse of al-Baqarah adds that Isma'il was also commanded with this together with his father Abraham. Once you know that the meaning is "We charged Abraham that he not associate anything with Me, and [that he] purify My House," and so on.

Know that "an" (that) has two possibilities:

The first: it is the explanatory "an" (mufassirah), and according to this, the purification of the House from polytheism and other things is the explanation of the charge to Abraham; i.e., the charge is his being enjoined with the mentioned purification.

The second: it is the verbal-source "an" (masdariyyah), based on the entry of the verbal-source "an" upon imperative verbs.

If it is said: How can it be explanatory of the charge to Abraham, when it is not mentioned here?

The answer: It is mentioned in surah al-Baqarah on this very matter, and the Qur'an explains part of itself by another part. What is mentioned there is as if it were mentioned here, because the speech of Allah confirms its parts one another. The purification here, in His saying, ﴿purify My House﴾, encompasses both spiritual and physical purification: it is purified physically from filth and spiritually from polytheism and sins. Therefore He said, ﴿do not associate anything with Me﴾ [al-Hajj: 26]. The tribe of Jurhum used to place idols beside it, worshipping them besides Allah. We have previously discussed in detail in surah al-Isra' what was at the Ka'bah of idols on the year of the Conquest, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) purified it from the impurities and filth of idols, just as Allah commanded Abraham here, and He said to our Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the creed of Abraham﴾ [al-Nahl: 123]. By "those who circle" in this verse is meant those who circumambulate the House, and by "those who stand and those who bow and prostrate" is meant those who pray; i.e., purify My House for those who worship by circumambulation or prayer. "Ruka'" is the plural of "raki'" (one who bows), and "sujud" is the plural of "saajid" (one who prostrates).

His saying, may He be exalted, in this verse: ﴿do not associate anything with Me﴾: the word "shay'an" (anything) is the object of "do not associate"; i.e., do not associate with Me any partner, whatever it may be. It is also possible that it is a substitute for the absolute object of "do not associate"; i.e., do not associate anything with Me of association, neither little nor much.

The meaning according to this is: do not associate with Me any association, little or much. Nafi' and 'Asim (in the narration of Hafs) and Ibn 'Amir (in the narration of Hisham) read "baytiya" with a fatha on the ya'; the rest of the seven read it with sukun.

Know that the historians have much discussion about the story of Abraham and Isma'il building the House, and among what they claim is that Allah raised the Sacred House to the heavens at the time of the Flood, and that it was of red ruby. The compiler of the genealogical poem followed this, saying:

A cloud guided Abraham to it, and it is by the measure of the area, showing him it.
It is also said that a Khajuj guided him, sweeping around it until what it had founded appeared.
Before the angels, of the building, before its being raised to the heavens.

It is well known that this and similar material resembles the Isra'iliyyat, and from it only what is confirmed by evidence from the Book or the Sunnah is accepted as true; for this reason we generally minimize the mention of such things.

* *

Issue

It is derived from this noble verse that it is not permissible to leave any filth at the Sacred House of Allah, nor any impurity, whether spiritual or physical. Therefore no one who commits what does not please Allah is to be left in it, nor anyone who defiles it with any impurity of najasah.

There is no doubt that the entry of photographers into the Masjid al-Haram around the House of Allah with cameras, photographing those who circle, stand, and bow and prostrate, is contrary to what Allah commanded of the purification of His Sacred House for those who circle, stand, and bow and prostrate. Violating the sanctity of the House of Allah by committing the prohibited act of photography there is not permissible; for the sound hadiths indicate that photographing a human being is prohibited, and their apparent meaning is general to all types of photography. And there is no doubt that committing anything the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prohibited is among the spiritual filth and impurities from which the House of Allah must be purified. Likewise, speech that is harmful to the religion and to monotheism which occurs in the mosque is not permissible to be approved or left.

We ask Allah for ourselves, for those whom Allah has placed in charge of our affairs, and for our Muslim brothers, success in what pleases Him in His sanctuary and throughout His lands; indeed He is Near, Responsive.

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 27 (part 1 of 7):

﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep mountain pass.﴾

The *adhan* (proclamation) in the language means informing. From it is the saying of Allah, ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater pilgrimage﴾, and the saying of al-Harith ibn Hilliza:

*"Asma' has announced to us her parting, and many a sojourner tires of his stay."*

The *hajj* in the language means intending and frequently coming and going. The Arabs say: "The clan of so-and-so *hajja* so-and-so," when they intend him and make frequent coming and going to him. From it is the saying of al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di:

*"Do you not know, O Umm Asma', that the vicissitudes of fate have struck me in my prime?*
*And I witness from 'Awf many gatherings, who visit (yahujjuna) the abuse (sibb) of al-Zibriqan, the saffron-dyed."*

His saying *yahujjuna* means they frequently intend him, come and go to him, and make repeated visits to him. *Sibb*, with a kasra, means the turban. By their visiting his turban he means that they visit him, so he referred to him by the turban.

*Rijal* in the verse is the plural of *rajil*, which is one who walks on his feet. *Dhamir* is the camel or the like, the emaciated one whom the journey has exhausted. His saying *ya'tina* means the lean camels, which are expressed by the wording *kulli dhamir* (every lean camel), because it has the meaning: "and upon lean camels they will come from every deep mountain pass." The word *kull* is a form of generality which includes many lean camels. *Fajj* is a path, and its plural is *fijaj*. From it is the saying of Allah, ﴿And We made in it wide roads as paths, that they might be guided﴾ [al-Anbiya': 31]. *'Amiq* means distant. From it is the saying of the poet:

*"When horses come from deep distant passes, drawn in their course by a dishevelled, pale-faced rider."*

The word *'umq* is most often used for distance downward, as one says: "a deep well" (bi'r 'amiqa), meaning far in its depth.

The address in His saying ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage﴾ [al-Hajj: 27] is to Ibrahim, as is evident from the context. This is the view of the majority, in contrast to those who claim that the address is to our Prophet, may Allah bless him and Ibrahim and grant them peace. Among those who said so was al-Hasan, and al-Qurtubi inclined to it. So the saying of Allah ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage﴾ means: "And We commanded Ibrahim to proclaim to the people the pilgrimage," i.e., inform them, call out to them concerning the pilgrimage, i.e., that Allah has made the pilgrimage to His Sacred House obligatory upon them.

The exegetes mentioned that when his Lord commanded him to proclaim to the people the pilgrimage, he said: "O Lord, how can I convey it to the people when my voice does not reach them?" He said: "Call out, and upon Us is the conveyance." So he stood at his station. It was said: on the stone. It was said: on al-Safa. It was said: on Abu Qubays, and he said: "O people, your Lord has taken a House, so make pilgrimage to it." It is said that the mountains humbled themselves, until the voice reached the ends of the earth and made heard whoever was in the wombs and the loins. Everything that heard him responded, of stone, clay and tree, and whoever Allah had decreed would perform pilgrimage until the Day of Resurrection said: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am."

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said after mentioning this account: "This is the substance of what has been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and others of the early generations, and Allah knows best. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted it at length." End of his words.

His saying ﴿they will come to you on foot﴾ is in the jussive mood as the answer to a command. According to the grammarians of Arabic, it is jussive by a conditional understood to be implied by the command, according to the more correct view; i.e., "If you proclaim to the people the pilgrimage, they will come to you." He said *ya'tukum* (they will come to you) because the one called turns toward the caller, even though their coming is in reality for the pilgrimage, since Ibrahim's proclamation was for the pilgrimage; i.e., they will come to you answering your call, performing pilgrimage to the Sacred House of Allah, as you called them to that.

According to the view of al-Hasan, mentioned from him, that the address is to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, there is in this verse evidence for the obligation of the pilgrimage. According to the view of the majority, the obligation of the pilgrimage upon this Ummah from it is based on the premise that the law of those before us is law for us, as we have clarified in surah al-Ma'ida. Moreover, other verses indicate that the obligation mentioned on the tongue of Ibrahim was likewise established on the tongue of our Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

- such as His saying: ﴿And for Allah is the pilgrimage to the House, incumbent upon the people who are able to make their way thereto. And whoever disbelieves - indeed, Allah is free from need of the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97];
- and His saying: ﴿And complete the pilgrimage and the umrah for Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 196];
- and His saying: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever makes pilgrimage to the House or performs umrah, there is no blame upon him for going between them. And whoever volunteers good, indeed, Allah is Appreciative and Knowing﴾ [al-Baqara: 158].

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse, and His saying ﴿They will come to you on foot and on every lean camel﴾, the verse: "Those scholars who hold that performing pilgrimage on foot is better than performing it riding, for those able to do so, may take evidence from this verse, because He mentioned them first, which indicates concern for them and the strength of their resolve." Waki' said, from Abu al-'Umays, from Abu Halhala, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I have no regret over anything except that I wish I had performed the pilgrimage on foot, because Allah says ﴿they will come to you on foot﴾."

What most of the scholars hold is that performing pilgrimage riding is better, following the example of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for he performed pilgrimage riding despite his complete strength, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. End of his words.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: Know that it has been established in the *usul* (the principles of jurisprudence) that the source of disagreement in this question, namely whether riding in pilgrimage is better than walking, and its like, is the classification of the actions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with respect to natural disposition (*jibilla*) and legislation (*tashri'*), into three categories:

The first category: purely natural action, meaning an action which human nature requires by its disposition, such as standing, sitting, eating and drinking. This is not done for legislation and emulation, so no one says: "I sit and stand seeking nearness to Allah and following the example of His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, because he used to stand and sit," because he did not do that for legislation and emulation. Some say: his natural action indicates permissibility, and some (p-301) say: it indicates recommendation. The apparent view is what we have mentioned, that it was not done for legislation, but it indicates permissibility.

The second category: purely legislative action. This is what was done for the sake of emulation and legislation, like the actions of prayer and the actions of pilgrimage, together with his saying: "Pray as you have seen me pray," and his saying: "Take from me your rites."

The third category, which is the one intended here, is the action which admits of being natural or legislative. Its criterion is that human nature requires it by its disposition, but it occurred in connection with an act of worship, by being performed within it or in its means, such as riding in pilgrimage. His riding, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in his pilgrimage admits of being natural, because human nature requires riding, just as he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to ride on his journeys without being bound in worship by that riding, but rather because human nature required it. And it admits of being legislative, because he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did it while he was engaged in pilgrimage, and he said: "Take from me your rites." Among the branches of this question are: the resting sitting in prayer; returning from the 'Id prayer by a route other than the one by which he went to the 'Id prayer; lying down on the right side between the two rak'as of dawn and the dawn prayer; entering Makkah from Kada', with a fatha and a long vowel; leaving from Kudа', with a damma and a short vowel; and staying at al-Muhassab after departing from Mina; and the like.

In all these matters there is disagreement among the scholars, because they admit of being natural or legislative. Al-Shanqiti's reference to this question is found in *Maraqi al-Su'ud* in his words:

*"And an action rooted in natural disposition, like eating and drinking, is not a religious law.*
*Other than the attribute recognized and what admits of being legislative, in it, say, there is some hesitation.*
*So riding in pilgrimage follows that rule, like lying down after the dawn prayer."*

The well-known position of the school of Malik is that riding in pilgrimage is better, except in the circumambulation and the sa'y; walking in these two is obligatory.

Sanad and al-Lakhmi from the Malikis said: walking is better because of the hardship, and his riding, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was natural, not legislative.

What we have mentioned from Malik, that riding in pilgrimage is better than walking, is the view of most scholars, and Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and others held it.

Al-Nawawi said in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*: "We have mentioned that the sound position in our school is that riding is better." Al-'Abdari said: "Most jurists hold this." Dawud said: "Walking is better," and he argued with the hadith of 'A'isha: "The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to 'A'isha: 'But it is according to the measure of your expense, or your fatigue.'" Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim. In a sound narration: "according to the measure of your hardship and your fatigue." Al-Bayhaqi narrated with his chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I have no regret over anything as I regret not performing pilgrimage on foot." And from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Ibn 'Abbas said: "I have not regretted anything that escaped me in my youth except that I did not perform pilgrimage on foot. Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali performed twenty-five pilgrimages on foot, while the noble camels were led with him. He divided his wealth with Allah three times, until he would give the shoe and keep the sandal." End of the point of relevance from it. The raised (marfu') hadith from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the virtue of pilgrimage on foot is weak. The hadith of 'A'isha which is agreed upon, to which al-Nawawi referred, strengthens the argument of those who say that walking in pilgrimage is better than riding, because it involves more fatigue and hardship. The wording of al-Bukhari: "But it is according to the measure of your expense or your fatigue," and the wording of Muslim: "But it is according to the measure of your fatigue," or he said: "your expense." *Nasab* means weariness and hardship.

* *

Issues related to this noble verse:

The first issue: The Book, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslims have established the obligation of the pilgrimage once in a lifetime, and it is one of the five pillars upon which Islam is built, by consensus.

As for the evidence for its obligation from the Book of Allah, it is the saying of Allah: ﴿And for Allah is the pilgrimage to the House, incumbent upon the people who are able to make their way thereto. And whoever disbelieves - indeed, Allah is free from need of the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97].

As for the Sunnah, the hadiths on this are numerous. Among them is what Muslim narrated in his Sahih from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: He said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, addressed us and said: 'O people, Allah has enjoined upon you the pilgrimage, so make pilgrimage.' A man said: 'Every year, O Messenger of Allah?' He remained silent until he said it three times. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and you would not have been able to do it. Then he said: Leave me as I have left you, for those before you were destroyed by their excessive questioning and their disagreement with their prophets. So when I command you to do something, do of it what you are able, and when I forbid you from something, leave it.'" End of his words.

The point of evidence from this hadith is his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "O people, Allah has enjoined upon you the pilgrimage, so make pilgrimage." A similar one was recorded by Imam Ahmad and al-Nasa'i. It has been cited from this hadith that a bare command, devoid of indicators, does not require repetition, as is established in the *usul*.

The evidence that it is one of the five pillars upon which Islam is built is the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, agreed upon, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer, giving the zakat, the pilgrimage, and fasting in Ramadan." This is the wording of al-Bukhari.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 27 (part 2 of 7):

Many ḥadīths have been transmitted on the virtue of the ḥajj (the pilgrimage to the House) and on encouragement to perform it. Among them is the ḥadīth of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked, 'Which deed is the best?' He said, 'Faith in Allah and His Messenger.' It was said, 'Then what?' He said, 'Jihad in the way of Allah.' It was said, 'Then what?' He said, 'A mabrūr ḥajj (an accepted, sincere pilgrimage).'" Agreed upon (by al-Bukhārī and Muslim). And from him, may Allah be pleased with him, also: he said, "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Whoever performs ḥajj and does not engage in obscenity or wickedness returns as on the day his mother bore him.'" Also agreed upon. And from him, may Allah be pleased with him, also: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "'Umrah to 'umrah is an expiation for what lies between them, and the mabrūr ḥajj has no reward but Paradise." Agreed upon. And from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, we see jihad as the best deed; should we not fight (in jihad)?' He said, 'But the best jihad is the mabrūr ḥajj.'" Narrated by al-Bukhārī. And also from her, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no day on which Allah frees more servants from the Fire than the day of ʿArafah. He draws near, then boasts of them to the angels, saying, 'What do these seek?'" Recorded by Muslim with this wording. The ḥadīths on this subject are numerous. The virtue of ḥajj, and that it is one of the five pillars, is well known.

* *

Know that the obligation of the aforementioned ḥajj is conditioned upon several conditions, namely: sanity, puberty, Islam, freedom, and capability (istiṭāʿah). There is no disagreement among the scholars on this. As for sanity, its being a condition for the obligation of every legal duty (taklīf) is clear, because one who is not sane cannot be obligated in any way. As for puberty being a condition, it is also clear, because the child is exempt from the pen until he reaches maturity (ḥtilām). So puberty and sanity are both conditions of obligation. As for Islam: the apparent position, on the view that disbelievers are addressed by the subsidiary rulings of the Sharīʿah (furūʿ al-sharīʿah), is that it is a condition of validity (shart ṣiḥḥah) and not a condition of obligation. On the view that they are not addressed by them, it is a condition of obligation. The sounder view is that disbelievers are addressed by the subsidiary rulings of the Sharīʿah, as we have clarified its evidence elsewhere. Thus Islam is a condition of validity with respect to them. It is known that even if it is a condition of obligation, it is also a condition of validity, because some conditions of obligation are also conditions of validity, such as the time for prayer, which is a condition both of its obligation and of its validity. And a condition of obligation may not be a condition of validity, such as puberty and freedom, for a child is not obligated to perform ḥajj, although it is valid if he does it, and likewise a slave. However, it does not suffice as the obligatory pilgrimage of Islam (ḥajjat al-Islām) [p. 304], except if it is performed after puberty and after freedom. As for freedom, it is a condition of obligation, so ḥajj is not obligatory upon a slave. The scholars based the non-obligation of ḥajj upon a slave on two matters:

The first: the consensus of the scholars on this. However, if he performs ḥajj, his ḥajj is valid, but it does not suffice for the obligatory pilgrimage of Islam. If he is freed after that, the obligatory pilgrimage of Islam is incumbent upon him.

Al-Nawawī said in Sharḥ al-Muhadhdhab: "The ummah has agreed that a slave is not obligated to perform ḥajj, because his usufruct is owed to his master, so he is not capable (mustaṭīʿ). His ḥajj is valid with his master's permission and without it, with no disagreement among us." Al-Qāḍī Abu al-Ṭayyib said: "This is also the view of all the jurists." Daʾūd said: "It is not valid without his master's permission." End of the relevant point from him.

The second matter: a ḥadīth from the Prophet ﷺ that indicates this. It was reported from him ﷺ through the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "Whatever child performs ḥajj and then reaches puberty, upon him is the obligatory pilgrimage of Islam; and whatever slave performs ḥajj and then is freed, upon him is the obligatory pilgrimage of Islam." Ibn Ḥajar said in al-Talkhīṣ concerning this ḥadīth: "It was narrated by Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Ismāʿīlī in the Musnad of al-Aʿmash, al-Ḥākim, al-Bayhaqī, and Ibn Ḥazm, who authenticated it, and al-Khaṭīb in al-Tārīkh, through the ḥadīth of Muḥammad ibn al-Minhāl, from Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ, from Shuʿbah, from al-Aʿmash, from Abū Ṭabyān, from him (Ibn ʿAbbās)." Ibn Khuzaymah said: "The sound (version) is mawqūf (ending with the Companion)." Indeed, he narrated it in that way from the transmission of Ibn Abī ʿAdī from Shuʿbah. Al-Bayhaqī said: "Muḥammad ibn al-Minhāl alone transmitted it in marfūʿ form, while al-Thawrī narrated it from Shuʿbah as mawqūf."

I say: But it is in al-Ismāʿīlī and al-Khaṭīb from al-Ḥārith ibn Surayj from Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ, as a corroborating narration (mutābaʿah) for Muḥammad ibn al-Minhāl. What supports the authenticity of its marfūʿ form is what Ibn Abī Shaybah narrated in his Muṣannaf: Abū Muʿāwiyah informed us, from Abū Ṭabyān, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Memorize from me and do not say, 'Ibn ʿAbbās said,'" then he mentioned it. This clearly indicates that he meant it to be marfūʿ, which is why he forbade them from attributing it to him. On this subject, from Jābir, Ibn ʿAdī recorded it with the wording: "If a child performed a single ḥajj, it would be incumbent upon him a (second) ḥajj when he reaches puberty," the ḥadīth. Its chain is weak. Abū Dāwūd recorded in al-Marāsīl from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī a ḥadīth similar to the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbās, as a mursal report, and in it there is an unidentified narrator (rāwī mubham). End of (the quotation) from al-Talkhīṣ.

Al-Bayhaqī said in his Sunan: "Abū al-Ḥasan al-Muqrī informed us: al-Ḥasan ibn Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq narrated to us: Yūsuf ibn Yaʿqūb narrated to us: Muḥammad ibn al-Minhāl narrated to us: Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us: Shuʿbah narrated to us from Sulaymān al-Aʿmash, from Abū Ṭabyān, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Whatever child performs ḥajj and then reaches the age of ḥinth (legal maturity), upon him is to perform another ḥajj.
