Whatever bedouin performs ḥajj and then emigrates, upon him is another ḥajj. Whatever slave performs ḥajj and then is freed, upon him is another ḥajj.'" Then he related the ḥadīth through another chain as mawqūf upon [p. 305] Ibn ʿAbbās, and remained silent without clarifying whether the mawqūf or the marfūʿ is more authentic. Al-Nawawī said in Sharḥ al-Muhadhdhab concerning this ḥadīth:

"Al-Bayhaqī recorded it in the first chapter of the Book of Ḥajj with a good chain. He also recorded it as mawqūf, and that does not harm it. The marfūʿ narration is strong, and the fact that Muḥammad ibn al-Minhāl alone transmitted it in this form does no harm, for he is trustworthy, acceptable, and precise. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim narrated from him in their Ṣaḥīḥs." End of quotation.

You have learned from the words of Ibn Ḥajar that Ibn al-Minhāl was followed in raising the aforementioned ḥadīth by al-Ḥārith ibn Surayj, so the sole transmission (tafarrud) has ceased. The apparent view is that this al-Ḥārith is Ibn Surayj al-Naqqāl, who is not used as evidence because of his weakness. From what we have mentioned, you know that the aforementioned ḥadīth is not below the level of being used as evidence. The point of evidence from it, that freedom is a condition for the obligation of ḥajj, is that if one performs ḥajj while a slave, and then is freed after that, the obligatory pilgrimage of Islam becomes binding upon him. Had it been obligatory upon him while he was a slave, his ḥajj would have sufficed for the obligatory pilgrimage of Islam, as is apparent. And Allah knows best.

Abū ʿĪsā al-Tirmidhī, may Allah have mercy on him, said, and his exact words are:

"The scholars have agreed that if a child performs ḥajj before reaching maturity, then upon him is ḥajj when he reaches it, and that pilgrimage does not suffice for him as the obligatory pilgrimage of Islam. Likewise, if a slave performs ḥajj while in bondage and then is freed, upon him is ḥajj when he finds a way to it, and what he performed while in bondage does not suffice for him. This is the view of al-Thawrī, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, and Isḥāq."

* *

As for capability (istiṭāʿah): Allah, exalted is He, has stated its condition in His saying: ﴿And for Allah, upon the people, is the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 97]. The meaning of istiṭāʿah in the Arabic language is well known, but the interpretation of istiṭāʿah in the verse has been disputed among the scholars.

Capability, according to the well-known position of the school of Mālik, on which the fatwā is based, is the possibility of reaching (the Ḥaram) without great hardship beyond the ordinary hardship of travel, together with security for one's self and property. They do not require provisions and a mount (rāḥilah). Rather, ḥajj is obligatory according to them upon one who is able to walk, if he has a craft by which he earns his sustenance on the road, such as a camel driver, a leather worker, a carpenter, and those similar to them.

Al-Shaykh al-Ḥaṭṭāb said, in his commentary on the words of Khalīl in his Mukhtaṣar (concise abridgment): "Ḥajj became obligatory by capability, meaning the possibility of reaching (the Ḥaram) without great hardship, and security for one's self and property," and his exact words are: "Mālik said in the Kitāb of Muḥammad, and in the Samāʿ of Ashhab, when he was asked concerning the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 97]: 'Is that the provisions and the mount?' He said: 'No, by Allah. That is not but the capacity of people: a man finds provisions and a mount but cannot manage the journey, and another is able to walk on his feet. There is no description clearer in this than what Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 97].'" He added in the Kitāb of Muḥammad: "Many a child is stronger than an adult." He quoted the words of Mālik in al-Muqaddimāt, then said after it: "Whoever is able to reach Makkah, either on foot without great hardship, or riding by purchase or hire, then ḥajj is obligatory upon him." He quoted it in al-Tawḍīḥ. End of quotation from al-Ḥaṭṭāb.

Know that some of the Mālikīs stipulate for the aforementioned craft that it not be degrading to him.

Know that the Mālikīs differed concerning the poor man whose habit is begging from people in his town, and whose custom is that people give to him, and that begging is his livelihood, if he knows that if he goes out for ḥajj and begs, people will give him what he lives on as they used to give him in his town. Is his begging and their giving to him a cause by which he becomes capable, because by it he is able to obtain provisions, so that ḥajj becomes obligatory upon him for this reason, or is it not obligatory upon him for this reason?

Some held that ḥajj is not obligatory upon him by this, and it is not counted as capability. Khalīl ibn Isḥāq, may Allah have mercy on him, decided this view in his Mukhtaṣar, in which he stated, in his chapter that sets out what the fatwā is based upon, concerning what does not establish capability: "Not by debt, nor by gift, nor by begging absolutely."

The meaning of his words is that whoever cannot reach Makkah except by incurring a debt for that, or by accepting a gift from one who gives him money, or by begging from people absolutely, is not counted as capable by that, and ḥajj is not obligatory upon him. His words "or by begging absolutely" mean, in the unrestricted sense, whether begging was his habit in his town or not, and whether it was people's custom to give to him or not. As for when people's custom is not to give to him, then ḥajj is forbidden for him, because it is casting oneself into ruin (tahlukah), whether begging was his habit in his town or not. As for when people's custom is to give to him, and begging was not his habit in his town, then there is no disagreement that he is not counted as capable and ḥajj is not obligatory upon him. As for when begging is his habit in his town, and it is his livelihood, and people's custom is to give to him, this is the point of disagreement. We have just mentioned Khalīl's statement in his Mukhtaṣar that ḥajj is not obligatory upon him, and he is not counted as capable by begging from people, in his words "or by begging absolutely." Al-Shaykh al-Mawwāq said, in his commentary on Khalīl's words "and begging absolutely": Khalīl said in his Manāsik: "The apparent position of the school is that ḥajj is not obligatory upon one whose habit is begging, when the custom is to give to him, and it is disliked for him to set out. If his habit is not begging, or the custom is not to give to him, ḥajj is dropped by unanimous agreement." Al-Shaykh al-Ḥaṭṭāb said in his commentary on Khalīl's words "or by begging absolutely," and his exact words are: "As for the fourth case, which is when his habit in his town is begging and it is his livelihood, and the custom is to give to him, the author said in his Tawḍīḥ and Manāsik: 'The apparent position of the school is that ḥajj is not obligatory upon him, and it is disliked for him to go out,' and he decided this here. He said in al-Shāmil: 'It is the well-known view.' He let stand in its commentaries the author's words in their unrestricted form, and so did al-Basāṭī and al-Shaykh Zarrūq, and Ibn Ghāzī did not point it out." End of the relevant point from him. Al-Ḥaṭṭāb also said: "Ibn al-Ḥājib mentioned the two views without preference. Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām, the author in al-Tawḍīḥ, Ibn Farḥūn, the author of al-Shāmil, and those after them accepted both, and they preferred the view of its dropping, and some of them declared it the well-known view, and so did the commentators of the Mukhtaṣar." End of the relevant point from him.

The meaning of his words "they preferred the view of its dropping" is: the dropping of the obligation of ḥajj for one whose habit is begging and receiving.

The second of the two Maliki positions: that a poor man whose habit is to beg in his own town, and whose people are accustomed to giving him, if their custom is to give him on the journey of Hajj just as they gave him in his town, is thereby considered capable (mustati'an), and that his acquiring provision through that begging is considered capability (istita'ah). Most of the Malikis hold this view.

Al-Hattab, in his commentary on Khalil's statement in his Mukhtasar, "or begging in general," after mentioning the view that such begging and giving do not count as capability, and that Hajj is not obligatory thereby, but that setting out in that state is disliked, said the following:

I say: the texts of the people of the school that I have come across explicitly state otherwise, and that Hajj is obligatory upon one whose habit is begging, if the custom is to give him. Then he cited many transmissions from the scholars of the Malikis explicitly stating that Hajj is obligatory for him. The adherents of this view among the Maliki scholars, who are the majority, explained it as applying to the poor man for whom begging is permitted because he cannot earn his living, and that since that begging is permissible for him, and his livelihood comes from it while at home, he is thereby able to reach Makkah through that begging and giving. They said: whoever is able to do so by a permissible means is obligated to perform Hajj.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears to me to be preponderant by evidence among the two Maliki positions on this issue is the first view: that Hajj is not obligatory upon one who lives on his way by the charity of people, and that the begging of people does not count as capability.

Among the evidences indicating this is the generality of the words of Him, Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And there is no blame upon those who find nothing to spend﴾ [at-Tawbah: 91], and we have mentioned in this blessed book repeatedly that what matters is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion, and we have shown the evidences for this from the authentic Sunnah. He, Exalted, has explicitly stated in this noble verse the lifting of blame from those who find nothing to spend. There is no doubt that one who begs people because of his severe poverty falls within the generality of "those who find nothing to spend," and He, Exalted, has explicitly negated blame from them, so it follows that blame is negated from him regarding the obligation of Hajj, which is clear. The Shaykh Ibn al-Qasim, may Allah have mercy on him, cited this verse mentioned above in support of what we have stated.

However, many of the later Maliki scholars applied Ibn al-Qasim's view, for which he argued with the aforementioned verse, to one whose habit is not begging in his own town. They said: thus his statement does not address the point of dispute.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The apparent meaning of the noble verse is generality over all those who find nothing to spend, so restricting it to one whose habit is not begging without evidence from the Book or the Sunnah is neither valid nor reliable. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that a general term cannot be specified except by evidence that must be relied upon, whether it is a connected or a disconnected specifier.

Among what supports this in general is what is established in Sahih al-Bukhari: Yahya ibn Bukayr narrated to us, Shababah narrated to us, from Warqa', from Amr ibn Dinar, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The people of Yemen used to perform Hajj without taking provisions, and they would say: "We are the reliant upon Allah (al-mutawakkilun)." When they arrived at Madinah, they would ask people (for food). So Allah, Exalted, revealed: ﴿And take provision, for the best provision is piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197]. Ibn Uyaynah also narrated it from Ikrimah as a mursal report. End of quotation from Sahih al-Bukhari.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari in his discussion of this hadith: al-Muhallab said: In this hadith there is jurisprudence that abandoning begging is part of piety, and this is supported by the fact that Allah praised those who do not beg people importunately, for His statement: ﴿for the best provision is piety﴾ means: take provision, and be wary of harming people by asking them and of the sin in that. End of the relevant portion of his statement.

In it there is clear evidence for the prohibition of a person setting out for Hajj without provision in order to beg people, and its apparent meaning is general to every pilgrim who begs people, whether poor or rich, and whether his habit was begging in his own town or not. Interpreting the texts according to their apparent meanings is obligatory unless there is evidence that must be relied upon. Among what supports this is that those whom Allah praised in His Book for refraining from begging people were among the most destitute of the poor, as is well known, and Allah, Exalted, explicitly stated that they were poor, and indicated the severity of their poverty, in His statement: ﴿For the poor who have been restricted in the cause of Allah, unable to move about in the land. The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their modesty; you will recognize them by their mark. They do not ask people persistently﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273]. So He explicitly stated that they are poor, and praised them for modesty and not asking.

The way the verse indicates the severity of their poverty is what some scholars explained: the meaning of His statement ﴿you will recognize them by their mark﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273] is: by the manifest effects of poverty and need upon them.

Ibn Jarir said in his tafsir, after mentioning the view that what is meant by "their mark" is the sign of their poverty through the visible effects of hunger and destitution upon them, and the other view that what is meant by "their mark" is their sign, which is humility and lowliness, the following:

The most correct of these views is to say: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed His Prophet ﷺ that he would recognize them by their signs and the effects of need upon them. End of the relevant portion of his statement.

The author of ad-Durr al-Manthur fi at-Tafsir bi al-Ma'thur said: Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from ar-Rabi': ﴿you will recognize them by their mark﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273], he says: you recognize in their faces the exertion of need. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Zayd: ﴿you will recognize them by their mark﴾, he said: the shabbiness of their clothing. End of quotation. Similar to this is abundant in the statements of the exegetes.

So the noble verse, by its explicit wording, indicates praise for the poor who are patient and abstain from asking people, and by its implicit meaning indicates the censure of asking people. The hadiths reported concerning the censure of begging in general are very numerous. From all of this you know that asking people is not capability for a pillar of Islam, and that the statement of some Malikis, that it does not count as capability, is the correct view, and it is the view of the majority of scholars. Among those who held it are ash-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Hanifah. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted it from al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ahmad and Ishaq. Some of the companions of Malik also held it. Al-Baghawi said: and this is the view of the scholars. End of quotation.

Said by an-Nawawi.

Capability according to Abu Hanifah is provision and mount. So if one is able to walk and his habit is asking people, Hajj is not obligatory upon him according to him, as we mentioned shortly before.

Capability in the school of ash-Shafi'i is provision and mount, on condition that he finds them at the market price. If he finds them only at more than the market price, the obligation of Hajj falls from him. The Shafi'is also stipulate: the availability of water at the places of stopping, and this is a condition about which there should be no disagreement, because if he does not find water he will perish. The Shafi'is also stipulate: that he be healthy, not sick, and there should be no disagreement that a severe illness which makes travel an extreme hardship invalidates the obligation of Hajj.

Al-Shafi'i also stipulates that the road be safe without a tax (khifarah). Khifarah, with a triptote of the kha', is the money taken from the pilgrim. The Shafi'is also stipulate that he have enough time in which he can travel and perform the rites. These conditions apply to one who is capable in his own person, not to what they call the one capable through another. If the distance between him and Makkah is one in which prayer is shortened, and he is able to walk on his feet, but does not find a mount, or finds one at more than the market price or the market rate for hire, the obligation of Hajj is not incumbent upon him according to them, and his ability to walk does not count as capability according to them, based on the hadith of provision and mount in explaining capability. And if he does not find what he can spend on provisions and water, but he is a earner, a craftsman who earns by his craft what suffices him, then according to ash-Shafi'i there is a detail related by Imam al-Haramayn from the Iraqi Shafi'is: if he earns in a day only the sufficiency of one day, Hajj is not obligatory upon him, because he would be cut off from earning during the days of Hajj; and if he earns in a day the sufficiency of several days, Hajj is obligatory upon him. The Imam said: there is a possibility in this, for ability to earn on the day of Eid is not treated like possession of a sa' in the obligation of zakat al-fitr. Thus the Imam mentioned it, and ar-Rafi'i transmitted it and remained silent on it. End of quotation from an-Nawawi. By "the Imam" he means Imam al-Haramayn.

His statement "there is a possibility in this" means that it is possible that Hajj is not obligatory by that in any case.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What he mentioned is based on the well-known disputed principle, namely whether the ability to acquire is equivalent to acquisition or not. The more apparent view is that the ability to acquire is equivalent to actual acquisition. And Allah knows best.

According to Ahmad and his companions, capability is provision and mount. Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: The required capability is possession of provision and mount, and this is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, ash-Shafi'i and Ishaq. At-Tirmidhi said: and this is what the scholars act upon. And Ikrimah said: it is health. End of the relevant portion of his statement.

* *

Having learned the views of the scholars on the meaning of capability mentioned in His statement ﴿whoever is able to make his way to it﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 97], these are their evidences.

As for the majority who explained capability as provision and mount, their proof is the hadiths reported from the Prophet ﷺ explaining capability in the verse as provision and mount. This has been reported from him through the hadith of Ibn Umar, the hadith of Ibn Abbas, the hadith of Anas, the hadith of Aisha, the hadith of Jabir, the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, and the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. End of quotation.

As for the hadith of Ibn Umar, at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah narrated it through Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Khuzi, from Muhammad ibn Abbad ibn Ja'far al-Makhzumi, from Ibn Umar. At-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: This is a hasan hadith, and the practice of the scholars is upon it: that when a man possesses provision and a mount, Hajj becomes obligatory upon him. Ibrahim ibn Yazid is al-Khuzi al-Makki, and some scholars have criticized him because of his memory. End of quotation from at-Tirmidhi.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: At-Tirmidhi's grading of this hadith as hasan has no basis, because the Ibrahim al-Khuzi mentioned is abandoned (matruk), and his hadith is not used as evidence, as many have definitively stated. Az-Zayla'i in Nasb ar-Rayah transmitted from at-Tirmidhi that when he narrated the aforementioned hadith, he said in it: it is a gharib hadith that we only know from the hadith of Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Khuzi, and some scholars have criticized him because of his memory. End of quotation.

What az-Zayla'i transmitted from him implies that he did not grade it as hasan, but described it as gharib. What az-Zayla'i mentioned, at-Tirmidhi mentioned in another place. And you know that Ibrahim al-Khuzi is not used as evidence. Therefore no hadith whose chain includes him can be hasan.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 27 (part 4 of 7):

The author of *Nasb al-Raya* (al-Zayla'i) said: It has another route in the *Sunan* of al-Daraqutni, related by Muhammad ibn al-Hajjaj al-Musaffar: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Abbad ibn Ja'far, from Ibn Umar, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ). Muhammad ibn al-Hajjaj al-Musaffar is weak. [End of quote.] And as al-Zayla'i said, it is weak. He said in *al-Mizan* about him: Abbas related from Yahya that he is not trustworthy. Ahmad said: We have abandoned his hadith. Al-Bukhari said, from Shu'bah: They were silent about him. Al-Nasa'i said: He is abandoned (matruk). Then he mentioned some of his strange reports. In any case, he is not to be used as evidence.

Know that Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Khuzi, whom Jarir ibn Hazim followed in this report through the route of Muhammad ibn al-Hajjaj al-Musaffar mentioned just now, is not to be used as evidence. Others among the weak narrators also followed him in it.

Al-Zayla'i said in *Nasb al-Raya*, after mentioning the hadith of Ibrahim al-Khuzi mentioned above, which is found in al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah: al-Daraqutni narrated it, then al-Bayhaqi in their *Sunan*s.

Al-Daraqutni said: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr al-Laythi has followed Ibrahim ibn Yazid in it. (p. 312) He narrated it from Muhammad ibn Abbad, from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the same way. [End quote.]

This which he pointed to was narrated by Ibn Adi in *al-Kamil*, and he gave it a defect (i'lal) through Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Laythi, and he attributed to al-Nasa'i and Ibn Ma'in its weakening. Then he said: The hadith is known through Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Khuzi, and through this route it is gharib (a single-route report). Then he related from al-Bayhaqi the weakening of the said Ibrahim. He said: It was narrated through other routes, all of them weak. It was also narrated from Ibn Abbas as his own statement. And we have narrated it through sound routes from al-Hasan from the Prophet (ﷺ) as a mursal (a report in which the Successor omits the Companion), and in it there is strength for this chain. [End quote.] Then al-Zayla'i said after this statement we quoted from him: The Shaykh (i.e., Ibn al-Turkmani? — as cited) said regarding his words "in it there is strength": there is room for scrutiny. Because it is known among them that when a route is single, and trustworthy narrators related it as a mursal while a weak narrator alone raised it, they consider the musnad (connected) report defective by the mursal, and attribute the error to the weak narrator's version. If that is what causes the musnad to be weak, how can it strengthen it? [End quote.] And he is right, as is known in the principles and the science of hadith.

Then al-Zayla'i said: He (i.e., the Shaykh in *al-Imam*) said: What he pointed to from the statement of Ibn Abbas, Abu Bakr ibn al-Mundhir related it: Ilan ibn al-Mughirah narrated to us, Abu Salih Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, Mu'awiyah ibn Salih told me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas, his statement. The mursal was related by Sa'id ibn Mansur in his *Sunan*: Hisham narrated to us, Yunus narrated to us, from al-Hasan, who said: "When the verse was revealed: ﴿And for Allah, upon the people, is a pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], a man said: O Messenger of Allah, what is the way? He (ﷺ) said: 'Provision and a mount.'" [End quote.]

Al-Haytham narrated to us, Mansur narrated to us, from al-Hasan, the like of it.

Khalid ibn Abd Allah narrated to us, from Yunus, from al-Hasan, the like of it. He said: These chains are sound, except that they are mursal. Ibn al-Mundhir said: The hadith in which the mention of provision and mount occurs does not establish as musnad. The correct report is al-Hasan's from the Prophet (ﷺ) as a mursal. As for the musnad, it was related only by Ibrahim ibn Yazid, who is abandoned (matruk); Ibn Ma'in and others weakened him. [End quote.] From *Nasb al-Raya*.

By this you know that the hadith of Ibn Umar mentioned was not established as musnad through any sound route, and it was not confirmed, because Ibrahim al-Khuzi is abandoned, and Muhammad ibn al-Hajjaj al-Musaffar, whom we mentioned Ibrahim followed in it through Jarir ibn Hazim's route, is not to be used as evidence, as we have shown. And we have shown that the following of Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr al-Laythi does not strengthen it, because he is weak; al-Nasa'i weakened him, and Ibn Adi gave the hadith a defect through him in *al-Kamil*. Al-Dhahabi said in *al-Mizan*: Ibn Ma'in weakened him, and al-Bukhari said: munkar al-hadith (rejected in hadith). Al-Nasa'i said: He is abandoned. [End quote.] From him.

(p. 313) As for the mursal of al-Hasan al-Basri mentioned, although its chain to al-Hasan is sound, it is not to be used as evidence, because the mursal reports of al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, are not to be used as evidence.

Ibn Hajar said in *Tahdhib al-Tahdhib*: Al-Daraqutni said: The mursal reports of al-Hasan contain weakness. He also said in *Tahdhib al-Tahdhib*: Muhammad ibn Sa'd said: Al-Hasan was a comprehensive scholar, lofty, a jurist, trustworthy, trustworthy in what he related, an ascetic, a devout worshipper, abundant in knowledge, eloquent, handsome and of fine appearance. What he transmitted with a chain (musnad) and narrated from those he heard from is evidence, and what he related as mursal is not evidence.

The author of *Tadrib al-Rawi* in the commentary on al-Nawawi's *Taqrib* said: Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: The mursal reports of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab are the most sound of mursal reports, and the mursal reports of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i are acceptable, and there is none weaker among mursal reports than the mursal reports of al-Hasan and Ata', for they used to take from anyone. [End quote.] Then after this statement he said: Al-Iraqi said: The mursal reports of al-Hasan are, in their view, like the wind (i.e., unreliable), and not being used as evidence for al-Hasan's mursal reports is the well-known position among the hadith scholars. Some people of knowledge said: They are sound when trustworthy narrators relate them from him. Ibn Hajar said in *Tahdhib al-Tahdhib*: Ibn al-Madini said: The mursal reports of al-Hasan, when trustworthy narrators relate them from him, are sound; how little falls from them. Abu Zur'ah said: Everything that al-Hasan says, "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said," I found it to have a firm origin, except for four hadiths. [End quote.]

This, then, is the sum of the discussion regarding the hadith of Ibn Umar from him (ﷺ), that he explained "the way" as provision and mount. You have learned that it was not established through any sound route, according to the discipline of hadith science.

As for the hadith of Ibn Abbas, Ibn Majah related it in his *Sunan*: Suwayd ibn Sa'id narrated to us, Hisham ibn Sulayman al-Qurashi narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "And he also informed me of it, from Ibn Ata', from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The provision and the mount,' meaning his words: ﴿whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]." In this chain is Hisham ibn Sulayman ibn Ikrimah ibn Khalid ibn al-As al-Qurashi al-Makhzumi, of whom Abu Hatim said: His hadith is unstable (mudtarib al-hadith), but his standing is truthfulness; I see no harm in him. Al-Uqayli said: In his hadith from other than Ibn Jurayj there is error. Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: Acceptable (maqbul). [End quote.]

Muslim has taken narrations from him, and al-Bukhari in his *Sahih*, in the chapter on sales, said: Ibrahim ibn al-Mundhir told me: Hisham narrated to us, Ibn Jurayj informed us, I heard Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Nafi', client of Ibn Umar, who said: "Whichever fruit is sold and then pollinated..." and he mentioned the hadith from his statement. This indicates that he is also among al-Bukhari's narrators. Ibn Hajar said in *Tahdhib al-Tahdhib*, after mentioning this statement we mentioned: As for the earlier scholars not mentioning him among al-Bukhari's narrators, that is because al-Bukhari did not take from him except in this place in the supporting narrations (mutaba'at), and he cited it with the wordings of corroborating evidence (shawahid). [End quote.] From him.

By what we have mentioned you know that this hadith of Ibn Abbas, in Ibn Majah, is not below the level of hasan, together with the fact that it is supported by what preceded and what will come, God willing.

Al-Zayla'i said in *Nasb al-Raya*: Al-Daraqutni also related the hadith of Ibn Abbas mentioned in his *Sunan*, from Dawud ibn al-Zibriqan, from Abd al-Malik, from Ata', from Ibn Abbas. He also related from Husayn ibn al-Mukhariq, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Simak ibn Harb, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, is Hajj every year? He said: 'No, rather once.' It was said: 'What is the way to it?' He said: 'The provision and the mount.'" [End quote.]

Then he said: Dawud and Husayn are both weak. [End quote.] As for Dawud ibn al-Zibriqan mentioned, Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: Abandoned (matruk), and al-Azdi called him a liar. As for Husayn ibn al-Mukhariq mentioned, al-Dhahabi said of him in *al-Mizan*: Al-Daraqutni said: He fabricates hadith. Ibn al-Jawzi related that Ibn Hibban said: It is not permissible to use him as evidence. [End quote.]

This is the essence of what is in the hadith of Ibn Abbas mentioned.

As for the hadith of Anas, al-Hakim related it in *al-Mustadrak*: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Hazim, the hafiz, in Kufa, and Abu Sa'id Isma'il ibn Ahmad the merchant, narrated to us, both saying: Ali ibn Abbas ibn al-Walid al-Bajali narrated to us, Ali ibn Sa'id ibn Masruq al-Kindi narrated to us, Ibn Abi Za'idah narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah, from Qatadah, from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, "from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His words, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And for Allah, upon the people, is a pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. He said: It was said: O Messenger of Allah, what is the way? He said: 'The provision and the mount.'" Then he said: This is a hadith sound according to the criteria of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), but they did not relate it. Hammad ibn Salamah followed Sa'id in his narration from Qatadah. Abu Nasr Ahmad ibn Sahl ibn Hamdawayh, the jurist, in Bukhara, narrated it to us; Salih ibn Muhammad ibn Habib, the hafiz, narrated to us; Abu Umayyah Amr ibn Hisham al-Harrani narrated to us; Abu Qatadah narrated to us; Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: "That the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the saying of Allah: ﴿whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], and it was said: What is the way? He said: 'The provision and the mount.'" Then he said: This is a hadith sound according to the criteria of Muslim, but they did not relate it. [End quote from *al-Mustadrak*.] Al-Dhahabi, the hafiz, confirmed the authenticity of the two mentioned routes. So the hadith of Anas is sound, as you see. The author of *Nasb al-Raya* said: Al-Daraqutni related it in his *Sunan* through both chains. [End quote.]

As for the hadith of Aishah, the author of *Nasb al-Raya* said: Al-Daraqutni related it in his *Sunan* from Attab ibn A'yan, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from Yunus ibn Ubayd, from al-Hasan, from his mother, from Aishah, who said: "A man asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And for Allah, upon the people, is a pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾, and he said: 'The way: the provision and the mount.'" [End quote.] Al-Uqayli narrated it in *Kitab al-Du'afa'* and gave it a defect through Attab, and said: In his hadith there is error. [End quote.]

Al-Bayhaqi said in *Kitab al-Ma'rifah*: It is not preserved (laysa bi-mahfuz). Then al-Bayhaqi related it from Abu Dawud al-Hafari, from Sufyan, from Yunus, from al-Hasan, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the way? He said: 'The provision and the mount.'" [End quote.]

You have known from what we mentioned that the hadith of Aishah mentioned was given a defect by al-Uqayli through Attab ibn A'yan, and he said that in his hadith there is error, and that al-Bayhaqi said it is not preserved. Al-Dhahabi said in *al-Mizan* about the said Attab: Al-Uqayli said: In his hadith there is error. Hisham ibn Ubayd Allah related from him a hadith that was contradicted in its chain. [End quote.] From him.

As for the mursal of al-Hasan that he pointed to, we have already discussed it fully shortly before.

As for the hadith of Jabir, the author of *Nasb al-Raya* said: Al-Daraqutni related it from Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr, from Abu al-Zubayr or Amr ibn Dinar, from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both, with the wording of the hadith of Aishah. Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Ubayd Allah al-Laythi, they abandoned him, and they agreed on his weakness, as has passed. We have already mentioned that the said Muhammad is not to be used as evidence. By this you know that the mentioned hadith of Jabir is not fit for use as evidence.

As for the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, the author of *Nasb al-Raya* said: Al-Daraqutni related it from Bahlul ibn Ubayd, from Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, from Ibrahim, from Alqamah, from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, in similar wording. Bahlul ibn Ubayd, Abu Hatim said: He is one who has gone off in hadith (dhahib al-hadith). [End quote.]

Al-Dhahabi said in al-Mizan regarding the aforementioned Bahlul: Abu Hatim said, "Weak in hadith, perishing (dhahib)." Abu Zur'ah said, "He is nothing." Ibn Hibban said, "He steals hadith." End of quotation from him.

From what has been mentioned, you know that the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud mentioned is not fit to serve as evidence. As for the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-'As (p-316), the author of Nasb al-Raya also said: al-Daraqutni narrated it too through Ibn Lahi'ah and Muhammad ibn Ubayd Allah al-'Arzami, from his father, from his grandfather, with similar wording. Ibn Lahi'ah and al-'Arzami are both weak. The Shaykh said in al-Imam: al-Daraqutni narrated this hadith from Jabir, Anas, Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-'As, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Aisha, and there is in none of them a chain that can be used as evidence. End of quotation from him.

This is the summary of the narrations of the hadiths that come concerning the interpretation of "the way" (al-sabil) in the verse as provision and mount. Several scholars said: this hadith is not established with a connected chain, and it has no sound route except the route transmitted by al-Hasan as a mursal.

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears to me, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that the hadith of provision and mount is established and is not below the level of being used as evidence. This is because the two routes that al-Hakim brought out in al-Mustadrak from Anas, he said: "Both of them have a sound chain," and the hafiz al-Dhahabi affirmed their authentication and did not object to it at all. The claim against Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah and Hammad ibn Salamah in their narrating the hadith from Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ, that it is an error, and that the correct version is from Qatadah from al-Hasan as a mursal, is a claim without any basis; rather, it is an accusation of error and wahm against reliable, well-known narrators without any supporting proof.

The correct view among the verifying scholars of usul and hadith is that when a hadith comes through one sound route and also through other routes that are not sound, those other routes do not constitute a defect in the sound route, provided their transmitters did not oppose all the memorizers. Rather, the sole narration of a trustworthy, upright transmitter in what no one else contradicts him in is accepted by the verifying scholars.

So the narration of Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah and Hammad ibn Salamah of the aforementioned hadith from Qatadah from Anas, raised to the Prophet, they did not oppose others in it; rather, they memorized what others did not memorize, and whoever memorizes is a proof against whoever does not. Claiming error against them without proof is itself an error. The statement of al-Nawawi in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: "al-Hakim narrated the hadith of Anas and said: it is sound; but al-Hakim is lenient, as has been explained many times before. And Allah knows best." 

It is answered: even if we grant that al-Hakim is lenient in authentication, it does not follow that his authentication is never accepted at all. Many of al-Hakim's authentications correspond to the reality of the matter, and his authentication of the hadith of Anas mentioned was not lenient; therefore al-Nawawi did not point to any reason for his leniency in it, and he did not speak against any of its narrators. Rather, it is a correct authentication.

If it is said: Hammad ibn Salamah's follow-up mentioned, its narrator from Hammad is Abu Qatadah Abdullah ibn Waqid al-Harrani, who is matruk (abandoned), whose hadith is not used as evidence, as many scholars of the men (rijal) firmly stated. Ibn Hajar said of him in al-Taqrib: matruk. So al-Hakim was lenient in saying that this route is according to the condition of Muslim, although its chain includes this Abu Qatadah.

The answer: Abu Qatadah mentioned, although most scholars declared him weak, was declared trustworthy by Imam Ahmad, who praised him, and the trustworthiness and praise of Imam Ahmad is sufficient. Ibn Hajar and al-Dhahabi mentioned that Abdullah ibn Ahmad said to his father: Ya'qub ibn Isma'il ibn Subayh mentioned that Abu Qatadah mentioned used to lie, and this was very grave to him, and he praised him and said: he seeks truthfulness. He said: "I saw him resembling the people of hadith." Ahmad said in another place: "There is nothing wrong with him, a righteous man, resembling the people of devotion, who sometimes erred." In one of the two narrations from Ibn Ma'in he said: "Abu Qatadah al-Harrani is trustworthy." Ibn Hajar and al-Dhahabi both recorded this from him. The statement of one who said, "Perhaps he grew old and became confused," is conjecture and assumption, and confusion is not established by it. It is well known that the established principle in usul and the sciences of hadith is that the correct view is that ta'dil (praise) is accepted in general terms, while tajrih (criticism) is accepted only in detail. Moreover, in the narration of Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah from Anas, there is no criticism of any of its narrators.

Among what supports this is the agreement of the hafiz and critic al-Dhahabi with al-Hakim in authenticating the follow-up of Hammad. Moreover, the sound hadith of Anas mentioned is strengthened by the mursal of al-Hasan, especially according to the view of those who say his mursal narrations are sound when reliable transmitters such as Ibn al-Madini and others narrate them from him, as we have previously mentioned.

What also supports this is that the well-known position of Malik, Abu Hanifa and Ahmad is to use mursal reports as evidence, as we have mentioned several times. It is also supported by the numerous hadiths we mentioned, even if they are weak, because they strengthen one another, especially the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, for we have mentioned its chain and shown that it is not below the level of being used as evidence.

Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar: "It is not hidden that these routes strengthen one another, so they are fit to be used as evidence."

What also supports the mentioned hadith is that most people of knowledge act upon it, as we previously quoted from Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi that he said regarding the hadith of "provision and mount": "and the practice of the people of knowledge is in accordance with it." We have shown that this is the view of the majority, including the three Imams: Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad.

So the conclusion is: the hadith of provision and mount, with the totality of its routes, is not below the level of acceptance and being used as evidence.

What appears to me as the stronger of the two opinions of the people of knowledge is that what is considered in this matter is what enables one to reach (the sanctuary) going and returning.

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears to me, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that the hadith of provision and mount, although fit to be used as evidence, does not imply that one who is able to walk on his feet without grave hardship is exempt from Hajj if he is unable to obtain a mount. Rather, Hajj is obligatory upon him, because he is able to reach it by a way (istita'a ilayhi sabilan). Just as the craftsman who earns his sustenance from his trade during the journey of Hajj is obligated to perform Hajj, since his ability to obtain provision along the way is like obtaining it in fact.

* *

If it is said: how do you say it is obligatory upon one who is able to walk on his feet, and not upon one who lacks a mount, while you acknowledge the acceptance of the Prophet's ﷺ interpretation of "the way" as provision and mount? That indicates that walking on foot is not part of the way mentioned in the verse.

The answer has two aspects:

The first: the apparent and immediate meaning is that the Prophet ﷺ interpreted the verse according to the most common circumstances of ability, because most pilgrims are from distant lands, coming from far countries, and it is common for a person to be unable to walk on foot over long distances and for his journey to be impossible without provision. So he ﷺ interpreted the verse according to what is most common. The established principle in usul is that when a text is describing the usual matter, it has no implication of contrast (mafhum mukhalafa). For this reason, the majority of scholars prohibited a man from marrying his stepdaughter (rabiba) who was not in his guardianship, saying that the verse "those in your guardianship" (al-lati fi hujurikum) [al-Nisa': 23] follows the usual case, so it has no implication of contrast, as we have mentioned many times. Since the most common circumstance of ability is provision and mount, and the hadith follows that, it has no implication of contrast. Therefore Hajj is obligatory upon one who is able to walk on his feet, either because the distance is not long, or because that person is strong enough to walk. Likewise it is obligatory upon the craftsman whose trade supplies his sustenance during the journey, because he is in the same meaning as one who possesses provision. And Allah knows best.

The second aspect: Allah, the Exalted, in His Book, placed the pilgrim who rides and the pilgrim who walks on foot on equal footing, and He mentioned the walker before the rider, in His saying: (p-319) ﴿And proclaim to the people the Hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep mountain pass﴾ [al-Hajj: 27].

We have already discussed this noble verse in full. This is the summary of what relates to the one who is able by himself.

* *

As for what they call the one who is able by means of another, there are two types:

The first of them: one who cannot perform Hajj by himself, due to being chronically ill, or elderly, or the like, but he has wealth with which he can pay someone to perform Hajj on his behalf. Is Hajj obligatory upon him, considering that he is able by means of another, and thus he enters under the general meaning of "whoever is able to make his way to it" [Al 'Imran: 97]? Or is Hajj not obligatory upon him, because he is incapable and not able by his own self, so he does not enter under the general meaning of the verse?

Al-Shafi'i and his companions held the first view; so, according to them, he must pay the wage of a hired person who performs Hajj on his behalf, on condition that this is available at the going rate (ujrat al-mithl). Al-Nawawi said: this is also the view of the majority of scholars, among them 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, Ahmad, Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Dawud. Malik said: it is not obligatory upon him, and it is not obligatory except that he is able to perform Hajj by himself. Malik argued with the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that man has nothing but what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39] and with the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿whoever is able to make his way to it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], and this person is not able by himself, so the name "one who is not able" applies to him; and because it is an act of worship in which substitution is not valid when one is able, so likewise when one is incapable, like prayer. The majority who hold that Hajj is obligatory upon him argued with hadiths narrated by the group.

Among them: what al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn Shihab, from Sulayman ibn Yasar, from Ibn 'Abbas, from al-Fadl ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them: that a woman (ḥ) Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us, 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salamah narrated to us, Ibn Shihab narrated to us from Sulayman ibn Yasar, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "A woman from Khath'am came in the year of the Farewell Hajj and said: O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the obligation of Allah to perform Hajj has come upon my father, an elderly man who cannot sit steadily on a mount; may I perform Hajj on his behalf? He said: 'Yes.'" In another narration in Sahih al-Bukhari from Ibn 'Abbas, she said: "The obligation of Allah has come upon my father, an elderly man who cannot remain steady on the mount; should I perform Hajj on his behalf?" He said: "Yes," and that was during the Farewell Hajj.

In a wording in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Abbas: "The obligation of Allah upon His servants concerning Hajj has come upon my father, an elderly man who cannot remain steady on the mount; should I perform Hajj on his behalf?" He said: "Yes," and that was during the Farewell Hajj. End quote.

Muslim said in his Sahih: Yahya ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: I read to Malik, from Ibn Shihab, from Sulayman ibn Yasar, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: "That al-Fadl was riding behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when a woman from Khath'am came asking him for a ruling. Al-Fadl began looking at her and she was looking at him, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned al-Fadl's face to the other side. She said: O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the obligation of Allah upon His servants concerning Hajj has come upon my father, an elderly man who cannot remain steady on the back of his camel; should I perform Hajj on his behalf? He said: 'Yes.'" And that was during the Farewell Hajj.

In a wording of Muslim: "She said: O Messenger of Allah, my father is an elderly man upon whom is the obligation of Allah concerning Hajj, and he cannot remain steady on the back of his camel. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Then perform Hajj on his behalf.'" End quote.

This hadith, on which the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) agreed, was narrated by the rest of the group, except that some of them narrate it from Ibn 'Abbas, namely 'Abd Allah, and some narrate it from his brother al-Fadl ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 27 (part 6 of 7):

Abu Dawud said in his Sunan: Hafs ibn Umar and Muslim ibn Ibrahim told us, with its meaning, both saying: Shu'bah told us, from al-Nu'man ibn Salim, from Amr ibn Aws, from Abu Razin, (Hafs said in his narration: "a man from the Banu Amir") that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, my father is a very old man who cannot perform Hajj, nor 'Umrah, nor travel." He (ﷺ) said: "Perform Hajj on your father's behalf and perform 'Umrah."

Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi said: Yusuf ibn 'Isa told us: Waki' told us, from Shu'bah, from al-Nu'man ibn Salim, from Amr ibn Aws, from Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, that he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my father is a very old man..." up to the end of the hadith, like the wording of Abu Dawud which we mentioned. Then he said: Abu 'Isa said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith. The 'Umrah is mentioned from the Prophet (ﷺ) in this hadith only in the sense that a man performs 'Umrah on behalf of another. Abu Razin al-'Uqayli's name is Laqit ibn Amir." End of quotation from him.

The hadith of Abu Razin was also narrated by Ibn Majah, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, and from 'Ali ibn Muhammad, who said: Waki' told us, from Shu'bah, with it, roughly as above. Al-Hakim also narrated it in al-Mustadrak and said: "This is a sahih hadith according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not record it."

Al-Tirmidhi, after mentioning the hadith agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim) concerning the story of the woman of Khath'am who asked the Prophet (ﷺ), said the following: "Other than this hadith, several hadiths have been authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) on this topic. The practice on this among the scholars, from the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and others (p. 321), is in accordance with it. Al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq say this, holding that Hajj may be performed on behalf of the deceased."

Malik said: "If he bequeaths that Hajj be performed on his behalf, it is performed on his behalf." Some have permitted that Hajj be performed on behalf of a living person who is elderly or in a condition in which he cannot perform Hajj, and this is the view of Ibn al-Mubarak and al-Shafi'i. End of quotation from the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi.

Al-Nasa'i said in his Sunan: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim informed us, saying: Waki' informed us, saying: Shu'bah told us, from al-Nu'man ibn Salim, to the end of the chain and text, as we mentioned just above from al-Tirmidhi. End.

And from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "A young woman from Khath'am came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'My father is old, he has become senile (afnada), and the obligation of Allah regarding Hajj has reached him, and he cannot perform it. Would it be sufficient if I perform it on his behalf?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Yes.'" Narrated by Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sahih. End of quotations from both, through the transmission of al-Mujid in al-Muntaqa and al-Nawawi in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab.

Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar: "The hadith of 'Ali was also narrated by al-Bayhaqi." End. His statement in this hadith "and he has become senile (afnada)" means: he has become confused and his mind has weakened due to old age.

Al-Nasa'i said in his Sunan: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim informed us, saying: Jarir informed us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Yusuf ibn al-Zubayr, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "A man from Khath'am came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'My father is a very old man who cannot sit on a mount, and the obligation of Allah regarding Hajj has reached him. Is it sufficient that I perform Hajj on his behalf?' He said: 'Are you the eldest of his sons?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you see, if he had a debt, would you pay it?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then perform Hajj on his behalf.'"

In another wording of al-Nasa'i, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), my father died without performing Hajj. Shall I perform Hajj on his behalf?' He said: 'Do you see, if your father had a debt, would you pay it?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then the debt of Allah has more right (to be paid).'"

In another wording in al-Nasa'i, from Ibn 'Abbas: "A man asked the Prophet (ﷺ): 'My father has reached the time of Hajj while he is a very old man who cannot stay firm on his mount. If I tie him down, I fear he will die. Shall I perform Hajj on his behalf?' He said: 'Do you see, if he had a debt which you paid, would it be sufficient?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then perform Hajj on your father's behalf.'" End of quotation from the Sunan of al-Nasa'i.

The hadith of Ibn al-Zubayr which we mentioned just above in al-Nasa'i: al-Mujid said in al-Muntaqa: "It was narrated by Imam Ahmad and al-Nasa'i, with its meaning."

Al-Shawkani said: "The Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) said: its chain is acceptable (salih)." End of quotation. Hadiths similar to this are numerous.

(p. 322) As for the second of the two types of one who is able by means of another: it is one who cannot perform Hajj himself, and has no wealth to pay to someone who would perform Hajj on his behalf, but he has a son who obeys him if he orders him to perform Hajj, and the son is able (to perform it). Is Hajj obligatory upon the father, and is the son obliged to perform Hajj on his behalf because (the father) is able by means of another? On this there is a difference of opinion among the scholars.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: "A branch on their (the schools') positions concerning the disabled (ma'dub) who does not find anyone to send for Hajj on his behalf, but finds someone who obeys him: we have mentioned that our school holds that Hajj is obligatory upon him. Malik, Abu Hanifah and Ahmad said: it is not obligatory upon him. You know that Malik argued, concerning the case of the incapable person who has wealth, with the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And that there is not for man except what he strives for﴾ (al-Najm 39), and with the fact that he is incapable by himself, so he is not able to reach the House by way (sabil)..., to the end of what preceded. And (he argued) that Sa'id ibn Mansur and others narrated from Ibn 'Umar, with a sahih chain, that no one performs Hajj on behalf of anyone, and similar from al-Layth and Malik. And that those who opposed him argued with the hadiths we mentioned, which contain wording whose apparent meaning is obligation, such as likening it to a debt owed to a person, and the questioner's saying: 'Would it be sufficient for him that I perform Hajj on his behalf?' Sufficiency (ijza') indicates a demand (for payment). In some of its narrations the questioner says: 'Indeed, upon him is the obligation of Hajj,' and he asks the Prophet's permission to perform Hajj on his behalf; and he (ﷺ) did not explain to him that Hajj had fallen from him because of his old age and his inability to stay firm on the mount; and by his saying to the son: 'You are the eldest of his sons,' and his ordering him to perform Hajj on his behalf."

As for those who distinguished between the disabled person having wealth, for whom they made Hajj obligatory, and his having a son who obeys him, for whom they did not make it obligatory: this is because the wealth is his own property, so he must hire (someone) with it, whereas the son is another accountable person, not obliged by an obligation upon another person. And because, even if he has a son, he is not able by body, nor by provision and mount. If he were to find a person other than the son who obeys him in performing Hajj on his behalf, would his ruling be the ruling of the son? On this there is a well-known difference of opinion. In the branches of the Shafi'is there is an explanation of the reasoning for each view, so consult it in al-Nawawi's Sharh al-Muhadhdhab. The most apparent of them is that it is like (the case of) the son."

* *

Note (tanbih)

If a person dies without performing Hajj, while Hajj had become obligatory upon him because of his ability, either by himself or by means of another according to those who hold that view, and he has left wealth, is it obligatory that Hajj and 'Umrah be performed on his behalf from his wealth? On this there is a difference of opinion among the scholars. Some said: it is obligatory that Hajj be performed on his behalf, and 'Umrah on his behalf from his estate, whether he died having neglected it or not neglecting it, because death overtook him before performing Hajj immediately. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad.

(p. 323) Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: "This is the view of al-Hasan, Tawus and al-Shafi'i." Abu Hanifah and Malik said: it lapses with death, and if he bequeathed it, it is from one-third (of the estate). This is the view of al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i, because it is a bodily act of worship, so it lapses with death, like prayer. They also argued that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And that there is not for man except what he strives for﴾ (al-Najm 39), takes precedence over the apparent meaning of the hadiths, indeed over their explicit meaning, because it is more authentic than them. The opponents answered that the hadiths specify the general meaning of the Qur'an, and that the disabled person was obligated to perform Hajj through his own striving, by advancing wealth and the wage of the one who performs Hajj on his behalf; so this is from his striving. And they answered their analogy with prayer by saying that proxy (niyabah) does not enter prayer, unlike Hajj. Those who said that Hajj must be performed on his behalf from the principal of his wealth relied on hadiths which came concerning this, indicating that whoever dies after Hajj had become obligatory upon him before his death, Hajj is performed on his behalf.

Among them: what al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih: Musa ibn Isma'il told us, Abu 'Awanah told us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "A woman from Juhaynah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'My mother vowed to perform Hajj but she did not perform it until she died. Shall I perform Hajj on her behalf?' He said: 'Yes, perform Hajj on her behalf. Do you see, if your mother had a debt, would you pay it? Pay Allah's (debt), for Allah has more right to be fulfilled.'" End.

Although the Hajj in this hadith was a vow, Allah's obligation of it upon His servants in His Book is stronger than its obligation by vow. Some scholars used the aforementioned hadith as evidence for the validity of a vow to perform Hajj by one who has not performed it.

Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: "If (the one who performs it on behalf) performs it, it suffices him for the Hajj of Islam according to the majority, and he is obliged to perform the Hajj of the vow. It was said: it suffices for the vow, then he performs the Hajj of Islam. It was said: it suffices for both."

Al-Bukhari also said in the Book of Oaths and Vows: Adam told us, Shu'bah told us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: 'My sister vowed to perform Hajj, and she died?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'If she had a debt, would you pay it?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then pay Allah's (debt), for He has more right to be paid.'" End.

Al-Mujid said in al-Muntaqa, after indicating this hadith of al-Bukhari: "It indicates the validity of Hajj performed on behalf of the deceased, by an heir or other than an heir, since he (ﷺ) did not ask him whether he was an heir or not, and he likened it to a debt."

(p. 324) It has been established in the principles of jurisprudence that the Prophet's (ﷺ) not asking for detail, i.e., not seeking clarification of the circumstances of the incident, is treated as general wording in statements. This is indicated by the poet in Maraqi al-Su'ud with his words:

"Treat the omission of inquiry as equivalent to general wording in statements."

Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, disagreed with this principle, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence, along with the explanation of the disagreement in the legal questions, following the disagreement on this principle mentioned.

Among them: what al-Nasa'i narrated in his Sunan: Muhammad ibn Bashshar informed us, saying: Muhammad told us, saying: Shu'bah told us, from Abu Bishr, who said: "I heard Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrating from Ibn 'Abbas: 'A woman vowed to perform Hajj and died, so her brother came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about it. He said: "Do you see, if your sister had a debt, would you pay it?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then pay Allah's (debt), for He has more right to be fulfilled."'" End.

These hadiths we mentioned concerning the vow of Hajj: we have explained that Allah's obligation of the Hajj obligation is greater than its obligation by vow, and yet the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered its fulfilment and likened it to a debt owed to a human being. We will also mention, if Allah wills, hadiths in which there is no vow of Hajj.

Al-Nasa'i said in his Sunan: Abu 'Asim Khushaysh ibn Asram al-Nasa'i informed us, from 'Abd al-Razzaq, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my father died without performing Hajj. Shall I perform Hajj on his behalf?' He said: 'Do you see, if your father had a debt, would you pay it?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then Allah's debt has more right.'" End.

The men of this chain are well-known reliable narrators, and there is no objection regarding any of them except al-Hakam ibn Aban al-'Adani. Ibn Ma'in and al-Nasa'i said of him: "reliable (thiqah)." Abu Zur'ah said: "sound (salih)." Al-'Ijli said: "reliable, a proponent of the Sunnah." Ibn 'Uyaynah said: "I came to Aden and did not see anyone like al-Hakam ibn Aban." Ibn Hibban counted him among the reliable narrators and said: "He may have erred at times. The munkar reports in his narrations came from his son Ibrahim's narrating from him, and Ibrahim is weak." Ibn Khalfun related his authentication from Ibn Numayr, Ibn al-Madini and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. End. Ibn 'Adi said: "There is weakness in him." Ibn Khuzaymah said in his Sahih: "The people of knowledge of hadith have spoken regarding the argument from his report." From what has been mentioned, you know the soundness of arguing with the aforementioned hadith, and there is no mention of a vow of Hajj in it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 27 (part 7 of 7):

(p-٣٢٥) Al-Nasa'i also said in his Sunan: Imran ibn Musa informed us, saying: Abd al-Warith narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Tayyah narrated to us, saying: Musa ibn Salamah al-Hudhali narrated to me, that Ibn Abbas said: "The wife of Sinan ibn Salamah al-Juhani ordered that he ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): that her mother had died without performing Hajj, so would it suffice for her to perform Hajj on her mother's behalf? He said: 'Yes. If her mother had a debt and she paid it on her behalf, would it not have sufficed for her? So let her perform Hajj on her mother's behalf.'" This chain is sahih (authentic). In another wording in al-Nasa'i, also from Ibn Abbas, by another chain: "A woman asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about her father, who died without performing Hajj. He said: 'Perform Hajj on behalf of your father.'" Its chain is also sahih. Ibn Majah narrated something similar from the hadith of Ibn Abbas by another sahih chain.

Al-Mujidd said in al-Muntaqa: And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: My father died, and Hajj al-Islam was obligatory upon him. Shall I perform Hajj on his behalf? He said: 'Tell me, if your father had left a debt upon him, would you have paid it on his behalf?' He said: Yes. He said: 'Then perform Hajj on your father's behalf.'" Narrated by al-Daraqutni. End of quotation from al-Muntaqa.

Al-Tirmidhi said in his Sunan: Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from Abd Allah ibn Ata', from Abd Allah ibn Buraydah, from his father, who said: "A woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: My mother died without performing Hajj; shall I perform Hajj on her behalf? He said: 'Yes, perform Hajj on her behalf.'" End quote. Then he said: Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a hasan sahih hadith. End quote. Al-Bayhaqi narrated something similar by a sahih chain.

Al-Shafi'i said in his Musnad: Sa'id ibn Salim informed us, from Hanzalah, who said: I heard Tawus say: "A woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: My mother died, and Hajj was obligatory upon her. He said: 'Perform Hajj on behalf of your mother.'" It is not hidden that this hadith of al-Shafi'i is mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain), but it is strengthened by the hadiths previously mentioned and by what will come, if Allah wills.

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: Ali ibn Hajar al-Sa'di narrated to me, Ali ibn Musahhir Abu al-Hasan narrated to us, from Abd Allah ibn Ata', from Abd Allah ibn Buraydah, from his father, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "While I was sitting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a woman came to him and said: I gave a slave-girl in charity to my mother, and she has died. He said: 'Your reward is due, and the inheritance has returned her to you.' She said: O Messenger of Allah, she had an obligation to fast for a month; shall I fast on her behalf? He said: 'Fast on her behalf.' She said: She never performed Hajj at all; shall I perform Hajj on her behalf? He said: 'Perform Hajj on her behalf.'" End quote from Sahih Muslim.

These hadiths and others like them are the proof of those who said: whoever was obligated to perform Hajj during his life, and left wealth, must have Hajj performed on his behalf. However, not all of them are explicit in this, but some of them are explicit in it, such as the comparison to a human debt and what has been mentioned before. The opponents replied that Hajj consists of physical acts, even though it requires wealth, and physical acts lapse with death, so there is no obligation for an act after death; the one who performs Hajj on his behalf is a volunteer doing a good deed. They said: The basis of the comparison to a debt is that both benefit from that act: the debtor benefits from the payment of his debt on his behalf, and the dead person benefits from Hajj performed on his behalf. Paying a debt on behalf of someone does not necessarily mean that paying it on his behalf is obligatory; it may be that paying it on his behalf is not obligatory upon him.

They also argued that all the hadiths concerning Hajj on behalf of the dead came after seeking permission for Hajj on his behalf. They said: An imperative after seeking permission is like an imperative after a prohibition; it indicates permissibility, because both the seeking of permission and the earlier prohibition are indicators that turn the imperative away from obligation toward permissibility.

Ibn al-Subki said in Jam' al-Jawami' in the section on the imperative: "If it comes after a prohibition — the Imam (al-Razi) said: or after seeking permission — then it indicates permissibility. Abu al-Tayyib, al-Shirazi, al-Sam'ani and the Imam (al-Ghazali) said: it indicates obligation, and Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) suspended judgment." End of quotation from him. So you see that he began by stating that an imperative after seeking permission indicates permissibility, while the disagreement on this question is well known. We have mentioned the opinions of the scholars on it in the verses of Maraqi al-Su'ud at the beginning of Surat al-Ma'idah.

Among the examples of an imperative after seeking permission indicating permissibility: when the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about what they had caught with trained hunting animals, and asked his permission to eat it, the words of Allah, the Exalted, were revealed concerning this: ﴿So eat of what they catch for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4]. This command to eat became permissibility, because it came after a question and a request for permission.

Among its examples from the Sunnah is the hadith of Muslim: "Shall I pray in the sheepfolds? He said: 'Yes'" — the hadith (in full). The meaning of "Yes" here is: pray in them. This command to pray in them indicates permissibility, because it came after seeking permission. The disagreement of the scholars of usul (legal theory) on the question of the imperative after a prohibition or after seeking permission is well known.

This is the essence of their statements regarding one who is able only through another, and the obligation of Hajj on behalf of one who was obligated during his life, died before performing Hajj, and left wealth. You have learned their evidences and their discussion of them.

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The hadiths we have mentioned clearly indicate the legitimacy of Hajj on behalf of one who is incapacitated (al-ma'dub, one disabled by an illness that prevents travel) and of the dead.

We have already stated that the more apparent view in our opinion is that Hajj is obligatory immediately. Accordingly, if one neglected it while able to perform it, until he died in a state of neglect despite having the ability, then Hajj is performed on his behalf from his estate, if he left wealth, because the obligation of Hajj became established upon his responsibility, and so it became a debt upon him. The Prophet (ﷺ), in the hadiths mentioned, explicitly stated the priority of paying the debt owed to Allah when he said: "The debt of Allah is more deserving to be paid."

As for one whom death overtook before he was able to perform it, and who died without neglect, the apparent view for us is that there is no sin upon him and no debt to Allah upon him, because he was not able to carry out the act so that it would become established upon his responsibility. Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. The hadiths mentioned indicate the permissibility of a man performing Hajj on behalf of a woman and the reverse, and this is the position of the majority of scholars. Only al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy disagreed on this.

The hadiths mentioned are a proof against him. We have already stated that Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and those who agreed with him did not act upon the apparent meaning of these hadiths, though they are numerous and authentic, because according to them they contradict the apparent meaning of the Qur'an in His words: ﴿And that man will have nothing but what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], and His words: ﴿Whoever is able to make his way there﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. The one incapacitated and the dead are neither of them able, since it is true to say that he is not able by himself.

Know that what is well known about Malik, that he said: "No one performs Hajj on behalf of anyone," means in his view: the Hajj of a healthy person who is able is not valid on his behalf for an obligatory Hajj. The incapacitated one, in his view, is not able, and even less so the dead. So performing Hajj on their behalf from their own wealth is not obligatory in his view except by a bequest. If he bequeaths it, it is valid from one-third of the estate, and a volunteer Hajj performed on his behalf by his guardian is, in his view, contrary to what is preferable, rather it is disliked.

The preferable course in his view is that the wealth with which Hajj would be performed on his behalf be spent on something other than Hajj, such as giving it as charity on his behalf, or freeing a slave on his behalf, and similar things. If someone enters the state of ihram for Hajj on his behalf, his ihram is valid and his Hajj on his behalf is valid.

The summary: proxy performance on behalf of a healthy person for an obligatory Hajj is prohibited in his view, and for a non-obligatory Hajj it is disliked. The one who is incapable has, in his view, no obligation of Hajj at all.

Khalil ibn Ishaq said in his Mukhtasar: "Proxy performance by a healthy person in an obligatory Hajj is prohibited, otherwise it is disliked." End of quotation.

His commentator al-Khattab said: "What enters into the author's words 'otherwise it is disliked,' apparently, are three cases: a healthy person appointing a proxy for a voluntary Hajj, an incapable person appointing a proxy for an obligatory Hajj, and an incapable person appointing a proxy for a voluntary Hajj. But in reality there are only two cases here, because the incapable person has no obligation." End of quotation.

Know that some Malikis interpreted the mentioned disliking as prohibition. The hadiths we have mentioned are a proof against Malik and those who agreed with him. And Allah knows best.
