Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 28 (part 1 of 6):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves﴾. The lam in His saying "li-yashhadu" [al-Hajj: 28] is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), and it is connected to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And proclaim to mankind the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel﴾ [al-Hajj: 27]. That is: if you proclaim it among them, they will come to you on foot and riding, in order that they may witness, i.e., attend, benefits for themselves; and what is meant by their attending the benefits is that the benefits be obtained by them.

His saying "manafi'a" (benefits) is the plural of "manfa'a" (benefit), and here He did not specify what these benefits are. Some of them have been explained in other Qur'anic verses, and that among them are worldly benefits and otherworldly benefits. As for the worldly ones, they are like the profits of trade: when the pilgrim sets out with trade goods, he generally obtains profit, and that is a worldly benefit.

The scholars of tafsir have unanimously agreed that the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198] is that there is no sin or hardship upon the pilgrim if he seeks profit through trade during the days of the Hajj, provided that this does not distract him from anything of the performance of his rites, as we have already explained.

So His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ contains an explanation of some of the benefits mentioned in this verse of "al-Hajj," and this is a worldly benefit.

Among the worldly benefits is what they obtain from the camels (budn) and the sacrificial animals, as its detail will come shortly, God willing; such as His saying regarding the camels: ﴿For you therein are benefits until a specified term﴾, according to one of the two interpretations. And His saying: ﴿So eat from them﴾ in both places. All of this is a worldly benefit, and in it there is also an explanation of some of the benefits mentioned in this verse of "al-Hajj."

The verse of "al-Baqarah," according to how a group of the Companions and those after them explained it, has clarified it. Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir al-Tabari chose this in his tafsir, and he justified his choice by the abundance of ahadith indicating it: that among the benefits mentioned in the verse of "al-Hajj" is the forgiveness of the pilgrim's sins, so that no sin remains upon him if he is mindful of his Lord in his Hajj by carrying out what he was commanded and avoiding what he was forbidden.

That is because he said: the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203] is that the pilgrim returns forgiven, and no sin remains upon him, whether he hastens in two days or delays until the third; but this forgiveness of his sins is conditional upon his being mindful of his Lord in his Hajj, as He stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿for him who fears Allah﴾ (liman ittaqa), i.e., this forgiveness of sins and the removal of wrongs is only for those specifically who are mindful.

It is known that this noble verse has other aspects of interpretation besides this.

Among those from whom Ibn Jarir transmitted that its meaning is that He forgives the pilgrim all his sins, whether he hastens in (p-112) two days or delays, are: Ali, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Mujahid, Ibrahim, Amir, and Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah.

When he had mentioned the sayings of the scholars concerning it, he said: The most correct of these sayings is the saying of the one who said: its interpretation is that whoever hastens from the three days of Mina, leaving on the second day, there is no sin upon him; God erases his sins if he was mindful in his Hajj, avoiding in it what God commanded him to avoid, and doing in it what God commanded him to do, obeying Him by performing it according to the limits He set for him. And whoever delays until the third day of them, not departing until the second departure, until he leaves on the day after the first departure, there is no sin upon him, for God's expiation of what preceded of his sins and crimes, if he feared God in his Hajj by performing it within its limits.

We only said that this is the most correct of its interpretations because of the widespread reports from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he said: "Whoever performs this House's Hajj and does not indulge in obscenity or wickedness returns as on the day his mother bore him." And that he said: "Follow up between Hajj and 'Umrah, for they remove poverty and sins as the bellows removes the impurity of iron, gold and silver." Ibn Jarir, may Allah have mercy on him, cited with his chains of transmission hadiths indicating this. In one wording of his, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Follow up between Hajj and 'Umrah, for they remove poverty and sins as the bellows removes the impurity of iron, gold and silver, and the accepted Hajj has no reward but Paradise." In another wording of his, from Umar, reaching the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Follow up between Hajj and 'Umrah, for following them up removes poverty and sins as the bellows removes impurity, or the impurity of iron." In another wording of his, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "When you have completed your Hajj, you are like the day your mother bore you." And other similar reports, the mention of all of which would make the book too long, which indicate that whoever performs Hajj and completes it within its limits as Allah commanded, comes out of his sins, as His majestic praise said: ﴿there is no sin upon him for whoever fears Allah﴾ in his Hajj. Thus in the words of the Messenger of God ﷺ there is what clarifies that the meaning of His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾ is that he comes out of his sins, his wrongs are removed, and his offenses forgiven, up to the end of his lengthy discourse on the subject.

In it he explained that there is no basis for the saying of the one who said: the meaning is no sin upon him in hastening, and no sin upon him in delaying; because delaying until the third day cannot involve sin such that it would be said of it, "there is no sin upon him." And the saying of the one who said that the occasion of revelation was that some of them used to say: hastening is not permissible, and some of them said: delaying is not permissible.

(p-113) So the meaning of the verse is a prohibition against condemning the one who delays by the one who hastens, and the reverse: i.e., let neither of them accuse the other of sin; this saying is erroneous because it contradicts the saying of all the people of interpretation.

The conclusion: he, i.e., al-Tabari, demonstrated with many proofs that the meaning of the verse is what he mentioned, namely that the pilgrim departs forgiven, as on the day his mother bore him, with no sin upon him, whether he hastens in two days or delays. It may appear to the observer that linking the negation of sin in His saying ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾ to hastening and delaying in the verse, like linking the consequence to its condition, suggests that the negation of sin applies only to hastening and delaying. But the proofs that Abu Ja'far al-Tabari advanced for the meaning he chose are persuasive, and many ahadith support them, and the best way to explain the Qur'an by the Qur'an is the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ.

So His saying in this verse of "al-Baqarah": ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾ is the meaning of his ﷺ saying: "He returns as on the day his mother bore him." And His saying: ﴿for him who fears Allah﴾ is the meaning of his ﷺ saying: "Whoever performs this House's Hajj and does not indulge in obscenity or wickedness," because whoever does not indulge in obscenity and does not commit wickedness is the one who fears God.

From the lengthy discourse of Ibn Jarir to which we referred, he said the following text: If someone says: what brings the lam into His saying "liman ittaqa" and what is its meaning? It is said: what brings it is the meaning of His saying "fa-la ithma 'alayhi," because in His saying "fa-la ithma 'alayhi" there is the sense of: We removed his sins and expiated his wrongs; so in that there is the sense of: We made the expiation of sins for the one who feared God in his Hajj; and "We made the expiation of sins" is omitted, being sufficiently indicated by His saying "fa-la ithma 'alayhi." Some grammarians of Basra claimed that it is as if, when he mentions this concession, he has informed of a matter, saying "liman ittaqa," i.e., this is for the one who feared God. Some of them denied this from his saying; he claimed that the attribute must have something to which it is attached, because it does not stand by itself; but it is, as he claimed, connected to an omitted saying.

So the meaning of the discourse for him is what we said: that whoever delays, there is no sin upon him for the one who fears God, and His saying "wa-man ta'akhkhara fa-la ithma 'alayhi" takes the place of the saying. End of the relevant point from Ibn Jarir's discourse.

Upon interpreting this noble verse such that the meaning of "fa-la ithma 'alayhi" in both places is that the pilgrim is forgiven all his sins, so that no sin remains upon him, then the forgiveness of all his sins, which this interpretation indicates, is among the greatest of the benefits mentioned in His saying: ﴿that they may witness benefits for themselves﴾. Accordingly, this verse of "al-Baqarah" has explained part of what the verse of "al-Hajj" indicates, and the Sunnah has clarified this explanation with the authentic ahadith we have mentioned, such as the hadith: "Whoever performs this House's Hajj and does not indulge in obscenity or wickedness returns as on the day his mother bore him." And the hadith: "The accepted Hajj has no reward but Paradise." Among those benefits which the Qur'an did not specify is the hadith: "Allah boasts of the people of 'Arafah to the people of the heavens," the hadith in full, as previously mentioned. Among those benefits which the Qur'an did not specify is the facilitation of the gathering of Muslims from the regions of the earth at specific times and specific places, so that they feel Islamic unity, and so that some of them may benefit from others in matters that concern all of them, of this world and the religion; and without the obligation of Hajj, this could not be achieved for them. So it is a great legislation from the All-Wise, All-Aware. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and that they may mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the livestock animals﴾.

His saying "wa-yadhkurū" is in the accusative by the deletion of the nun, because it is conjoined to the accusative governed by the hidden "an" after the lam of causation, namely His saying: ﴿that they may witness benefits for themselves﴾.

The explanation of the meaning: And proclaim to mankind the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, in order that they may witness benefits for themselves, and in order that they may draw near to Him by shedding the blood of what He has provided for them of the livestock animals, while mentioning the name of Allah over them at the time of slaughter and sacrifice. The apparent sense of the Qur'an indicates that this drawing near by sacrifice on these known days is only the offerings (hadaya), not the sacrifices (dahaya); because sacrifices do not require proclaiming the Hajj so that those who sacrifice come on foot and riding; rather that applies to offerings, as appears. From here Malik and his companions held that the pilgrim at Mina is not obligated to offer a sacrifice nor is it recommended for him, and whatever is slaughtered in that place and at that time, he makes it an offering (hady), not a sacrifice.

His saying: ﴿and that they may mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them﴾, i.e., over the sacrificing and slaughtering of what He has provided for them ﴿of the livestock animals﴾, in order that they may draw near to Him with their blood, because that is piety from them; it reaches their Lord, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Their meat does not reach Allah, nor their blood, but piety from you reaches Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 37]. In some places He has stated that it is not permissible to eat from what the name of Allah was not mentioned over, as in His saying: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾, and His saying: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 119]. In this noble verse, He, may He be majestic and exalted, has made clear that He made the Sacred Precinct of Makkah a place of sacrifice where blood is shed as a drawing near to Allah, and the name of Allah is mentioned over them at their slaughter. This verse does not specify whether the like of this occurred for every nation or not; but He has specified in another place that He made the like of this for every nation among the nations, in His saying, may He be exalted: (p-115) ﴿And for every nation We have appointed a rite, that they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them of the livestock animals﴾ [al-Hajj: 34].

And since you know that among the wisdoms of proclaiming the Hajj to mankind, so that they come on foot and riding, is their drawing near to their Lord by the blood of livestock, mentioning the name of Allah over them at their slaughter, and that the verse is closer to intending the hady than the udhiyah, then here is the detailed explanation of the rulings concerning the offerings for which they were called to mention the name of Allah over what He has provided of them.

Know first that the hadyu (the animal offering, al-hadi) is of two kinds: an obligatory hadi, and a non-obligatory hadi, which its owner offers voluntarily seeking nearness to Allah, the Exalted. As for "the known days" (al-ayyam al-ma'lumat) on which Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned that the animals are slaughtered and the name of Allah is mentioned over them, the scholars have many opinions concerning them. The verified view, if Allah wills, is that all but two of those many opinions are invalid and not to be relied upon, and that the two relied upon are these: the Qur'an indicates that the known days are the days of sacrifice (al-nahr), by His saying: ﴿And mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the livestock animals﴾. Their mention of Allah over them means the invocation (al-tasmiyah) at the time of slaughtering them. It is thus clear that they are the day of sacrifice and two days after it. Accordingly, neither the hadi nor the udhiyah is slaughtered on the last day of Mina, which is the thirteenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah.

Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: This view was explicitly stated by Ahmad, and he said: It is from more than one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Al-Athram narrated it from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas. Malik and al-Thawri also held it. It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: The days of sacrifice are the day of Eid al-Adha and three days after it. Al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and Ibn al-Mundhir also held this. The point of his statement ends here.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of this verse: They differed on how many days the days of sacrifice are. Malik said: three, the day of sacrifice and two days after it. Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri and Ahmad ibn Hanbal also held this. This was narrated from Abu Hurayrah and Anas ibn Malik without disagreement from either of them.

Al-Shafi'i said: four days, the day of sacrifice and three days after it. Al-Awza'i also held this. It was narrated from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them. It was also narrated from them the same as Malik's and Ahmad's view. The point of his statement ends here.

He also said: Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: The scholars agreed that the day of sacrifice is the day of Eid al-Adha (p-116). They agreed that there is no udhiyah after the end of Dhu al-Hijjah. In my view, only two opinions are sound on this: 
The first: the view of Malik and the Kufans. 
The second: the view of al-Shafi'i and the Syrians. These two views are narrated from the Companions, so there is no point in occupying oneself with what contradicts them, because what contradicts them has no basis in the Sunnah or in the statements of the Companions. Whatever departs from these two is abandoned in favour of them. End of quote.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: Regarding the time of slaughtering the hadi there are two methods. The more sound of them, and the one adopted by the Iraqis and others, is that it is specific to the day of sacrifice and the days of tashriq. The second: there are two views on it, the more sound of which is this, and the second is that it is not specific to any time, like the blood-offerings for compensation (dima' al-juban). According to the sound view, if one delays the slaughter until these days have passed, then if the hadi is obligatory, it is obligatory on him to slaughter it, and it becomes a make-up (qada'). If it is voluntary, the hadi has been missed. Al-Shafi'i and the companions said: If he slaughters it, it is a meat-sheep and not a rite (nusuk). The point of his statement ends here.

Al-Nawawi mentioned from al-Rafi'i that in some passages of his book, in the chapter on the description of Hajj, he definitively stated that it is not specific to the day of sacrifice and the days of tashriq, and that he mentioned the issue correctly in the chapter on the hadi.

The one who restricts this, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The view that it is not specific to the day of sacrifice and two or three days after it is clearly invalid, because non-specificity makes the time of sacrifice absolute, not restricted to a time. The explicit statement of His words is a refutation of this: ﴿And mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the livestock animals﴾. Placing the time-frame as known days refutes the absoluteness of time in a manner that should not be disputed, as you see.

Al-Nawawi also said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: The scholars agreed that the counted days (al-ayyam al-ma'dudat) are the days of tashriq, which are three days after the day of sacrifice. End of quote.

There is no basis for disagreement on this, especially since His statement connected to it indicates it: ﴿Then whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ and the rest of the verse. What is meant by that is the days of stoning, which are the days of tashriq, as you see.

Then al-Nawawi said: As for the known days, our school holds that they are the first ten of Dhu al-Hijjah until the last day of sacrifice. The point of his statement ends here. Ibn Kathir attributed this view to Ibn 'Abbas, saying: al-Bukhari reported it from him in definitive form. Ibn Kathir also narrated it from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, 'Ata' al-Khurasani and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i (p-117). He said: It is the school of al-Shafi'i, and the well-known view from Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Then he proceeded to mention the hadiths indicating the virtue of the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah.

The one who restricts this, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The interpretation of the known days in this verse of Hajj as the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah until the last day of sacrifice is without doubt not correct, even though it was held by some eminent scholars and some eminent Companions whom we have mentioned.

The clear proof of its invalidity is that Allah explained that they are the days of sacrifice by His saying: ﴿And mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the livestock animals﴾, which is mentioning His name over them at the time of slaughtering them, seeking nearness to Him, as is not hidden. The view that they are the ten mentioned implies that all ten are days of sacrifice, and that there is no sacrifice after them. Both of these matters are invalid, as you see, because sacrifice on the nine days before the day of sacrifice is not permitted, while sacrifice on the two days after it is permitted, and likewise the third day according to those we have mentioned. So the invalidity of this view is clear, as you see.

Then al-Nawawi, connecting to his first statement, said: Malik said: they are three days: the day of sacrifice and two days after it. The eleventh and twelfth are, according to him, among the known and the counted days.

Abu Hanifah said: the known days are three days: the day of 'Arafah, the day of sacrifice, and the eleventh. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the known days are four: the day of 'Arafah, the day of sacrifice, and two days after it.

The benefit of the disagreement is this: according to us, it is permitted to slaughter hadi and udhiyah animals on all the days of tashriq, while according to Malik it is not permitted on the third day. This is the statement of the author of al-Bayan, as reported by al-Nawawi. He remained silent on the statement of the author of al-Bayan, which is clearly invalid, because the view that the known days are the first ten does not indicate permission to slaughter after the day of sacrifice, since it is the last of them. It may indicate permission to slaughter before the day of sacrifice throughout all of the first nine days, because the Qur'an indicates that the known days are the time-frame for slaughter, as we have shown repeatedly. If they are the ten, then the ten are the time-frame for slaughter. It would not be permitted before them or after them, yet it would be permitted throughout all of them. The invalidity of this is clear, as you see. Then al-Nawawi, connecting to his earlier statement, said:

Al-'Abdari said: The benefit of describing it as known is the permissibility of sacrificing during it, and the benefit of describing it as counted is the cessation of stoning during it. He also said: Ahmad, Dawud and our school hold this. Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi said in his tafsir: Most of the exegetes said: the known days are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. He said: They were called known because of the eagerness to know them, since the time of Hajj is at their end.

He said: Muqatil said: the known days are the days of tashriq. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the known and the counted days are one and the same.

I say: Likewise Qadi Abu al-Tayyib and al-'Abdari, and many others, transmitted the consensus of the scholars that the counted days are the days of tashriq. As for what the author of al-Bayan transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, it contradicts what is well known from him.

The correct and known view from Ibn 'Abbas is that the known days are all ten days, as in our school, and this is among what our companions argued with, as I will mention shortly, if Allah wills. Those who side with Abu Hanifah and Malik argued that Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the livestock animals﴾. By mentioning the name of Allah on the known days, He meant the invocation of Allah over the slaughter. So the mention of Allah's name should be across all the known days, whereas according to al-Shafi'i it would only be on one of them, the day of sacrifice.

Our companions argued with what Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The known days are the days of the ten, and the counted days are the days of tashriq. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it with a sound chain.

They also used the argument employed by al-Muzani in his Mukhtasar: that difference in names indicates difference in what is named. Since the counted days and the known days were distinguished by name, this indicates that they are different. According to the view of the opponents, they overlap on some days. The answer to the verse is from two angles:

The first: the answer of al-Muzani: it does not follow from the context of the verse that slaughter exists throughout the known days. It suffices that it exists in the last of them, which is the day of sacrifice.

Al-Muzani and the companions said: A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nuh: 16], and it is not a light throughout all of them, but in some of them.

The second: that the mention intended in the verse is mentioning the name over the offerings, and we recommend that whoever sees a hadi or any livestock animal during the ten days say the takbir. And Allah knows best. End of al-Nawawi's statement.

The one who restricts this, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears to me, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that the Shafi'i position on the known days is contrary to what is correct, even though some eminent scholars held it (p-119). The answers they gave to the objections raised against it do not stand, because of what we previously set out: that Allah explained in His Book that the known days are the time-frame for slaughter and sacrifice. Therefore, interpreting them as the first ten entails permissibility of slaughter throughout all of them, and its impermissibility after sunset of the tenth day. All of this is invalid, as you see.

As for al-Muzani's claim, may Allah have mercy on him, that the verse is like His saying: ﴿And made the moon therein a light﴾, it is clearly untenable, because the moon being one star while the heavens are seven layers is a clear indicator that it is in one of them and not the other six.

As for His saying: ﴿And mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the livestock animals﴾, its apparent and immediate meaning is that all the known days are a time-frame for mentioning Allah's name over the slaughtered animals, and there is no indicator here restricting it to some of them over others. So restriction to some of them is not permitted except by an evidence that must be relied upon, and none exists here. Their interpretation of mentioning Allah's name over them as meaning that whoever sees a hadi or any livestock animal during the ten is recommended to say the takbir, and that this takbir is the mention of Allah over what He has provided of livestock animals, is clearly untenable, as you see, because it contradicts the interpretation of the majority of exegetes of this noble verse. The correct interpretation of it is what is well known among the people of tafsir in general: mentioning Allah's name over them at the time of slaughter, as indicated by His saying after it, joined to it: ﴿So eat from them and feed the miserable poor﴾ [al-Hajj: 28] and His saying: ﴿And do not eat from that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 121], and His saying: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat from that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 119]. The overlap of the days does not prevent their being different, because two things that are general in one respect and specific in another are different by consensus, even though they overlap in some cases.

The fact that they are the ten days mentioned refutes the view that the known days are those ten: if they were the ten mentioned, it would follow that slaughter is not permitted after sunset on the tenth day, and that is contrary to reality, since slaughter is permitted on the eleventh and twelfth days, and even on the thirteenth according to the Shafi'is. The verified position, God willing, on this matter is that the counted days (al-ayyam al-ma'dudat) are the days of tashriq (ayyam al-tashriq), which are the days of stoning the jamarat. Many scholars have related consensus (ijma') on this, and the proof for it is His saying, exalted be He, immediately connected to it: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203], and that the known days are the days of sacrifice (ayyam al-nahr), which include the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) and the two days after it. The disagreement concerns the thirteenth day: is it among them, as its detail has passed? Some people of knowledge have preferred that the thirteenth day is among them, and others have preferred that it is not.

Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni, in preferring the view that it is not among them, the following text: Our proof is that the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade eating from the sacrificial animals (nusuk) beyond three days. And it is not permissible that slaughter should be legislated at a time when eating is forbidden, and then the prohibition of eating be abrogated while the time of slaughter remains as it was. Also, the fourth day does not require stoning, so slaughter is not permitted on it, like the day after it.

Among what some have used to prefer that the fourth day is among them: that on it one performs some of the rites, namely stoning, if one has not hastened; so it is like its predecessors among the days of tashriq. And Allah knows best.

Among what clarifies that the known days are the days of sacrifice, whether we say they are three or four: that Allah explicitly stated that they are the days in which the name of Allah is mentioned, i.e., at the time of slaughter, over what He has provided for them of the cattle (bahimat al-an'am), as we have previously explained.

* *

Having known the words of the people of knowledge concerning the known days, which are the time of slaughter:

Know that the scholars differed regarding their nights, whether slaughter is permitted in them. Malik and his companions held that slaughtering the sacrificial animal (nusuk) at night is not permitted; if one slaughters it at night, it is not valid, and it becomes a sheep for meat, not a sacrifice. This is also a narration from Ahmad, and it is the apparent meaning of al-Kharaqi's words. Al-Shafi'i and his companions held that slaughter at night is permitted. Al-Nawawi said: This is also the view of Abu Hanifah, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and the majority, and it is the more correct position from Ahmad.

The argument of those who say slaughter is not permitted at night is that Allah specified it by the term "days" in His saying: ﴿in known days﴾. They said: Mentioning the day indicates that the night is not like that.

The argument of those who permitted it is that "days" in the language is applied to what includes the nights, and specifying it as days is more cautious, for conformity with the wording of the Qur'an. And Allah knows best.

* *

Having known the time of slaughtering the offering (al-hady), and that the offering is of two kinds: obligatory, and non-obligatory, which is the voluntary offering (hady al-tatawwu'), here are the details of the rulings of each of them.

As for the obligatory offering: by the first division it is of two kinds:

One of them: an obligatory offering by vow (nadhr), and discussion of it will come, God willing, in the commentary on His saying: ﴿and let them fulfill their vows﴾ [al-Hajj: 29]. And an obligatory offering other than by vow, which also divides into two parts:

One of them: the offering that is explicitly stated.

The second: the offering that is not explicitly stated, but the scholars analogized it to the explicitly stated offering.

As for the explicitly stated one, it is four kinds:

The first: the offering of tamattu' (hady al-tamattu'), which includes qiran, because the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, explicitly stated that the term tamattu' in the verse is applicable to qiran, as we previously set out clearly from Ibn 'Umar, 'Imran ibn Husayn, and others. And the Companions are the people most knowledgeable of the Arabic language and of the indications of the Qur'an.

The offering of tamattu' mentioned is explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿So whoever enjoys [tamattu'] the 'umrah until the hajj, then what is easy of the offering﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

The second: the offering of restriction (dam al-ihsar), explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿But if you are prevented, then what is easy of the offering﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

The third: the expiation offering for hunting game (dam jaza' al-sayd), explicitly stated in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And whoever of you kills it intentionally, then a penalty equivalent to what he killed of the livestock, as judged by two just men among you, as an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95].

The fourth: the expiation offering of ransom for harm (dam fidyat al-adha) mentioned in His saying: ﴿then a ransom of fasting or charity or sacrifice﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. These four offerings: two of them are optional (ala al-takhyir), namely: the offering of ransom in His saying: ﴿then a ransom of fasting or charity or sacrifice﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], as we previously clarified. And the second: the penalty for hunting game, which is also optional, as we previously clarified in full in the discussion of His saying: ﴿as judged by two just men among you, as an offering reaching the Ka'bah, or expiation: food for the needy, or the equivalent of that in fasting﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95].

We have fully clarified the discussion of the option in these two, enough to not repeat it here. One of the four mentioned offerings is in sequence (ala al-tartib) by consensus, namely the offering of tamattu', which includes qiran, because Allah made clear that it is in sequence by His saying: ﴿So whoever enjoys the 'umrah until the hajj, then what is easy of the offering﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], then He said, explaining the sequence: ﴿But whoever does not find, then fasting three days during the hajj and seven when you return﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

The fourth of the mentioned offerings is one about which there is disagreement. Whoever says it has a substitute when unable to perform it holds that it is in sequence; whoever says it has no substitute, the matter is clear according to his view, because there is no multiplicity there requiring sequence or its absence. This kind is the offering of restriction, and we previously discussed it fully in Surat al-Baqarah in the commentary on His saying: ﴿But if you are prevented, then what is easy of the offering﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

In summary: three of the four mentioned offerings, we have previously discussed each of them with complete clarity and thoroughness. The offering of ransom was discussed in the topics of the verse of hajj: ﴿And proclaim to the people the hajj﴾ [al-Hajj: 27], among the set of hajj issues we mentioned in discussing them. The expiation offering for hunting game we discussed fully in Surat al-Ma'idah in the commentary on His saying: ﴿an offering reaching the Ka'bah, or expiation: food for the needy, or the equivalent of that in fasting﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. The offering of restriction we discussed fully in Surat al-Baqarah in the commentary on His saying: ﴿But if you are prevented, then what is easy of the offering﴾.

As for the offering of tamattu', no clarification of it has preceded for us, and we will explain it now.

Regarding tamattu' with 'umrah: it is known that everyone who performs 'umrah in the months of hajj, then exits from his 'umrah, then performs hajj in the same year, and whose family were not present at the Sacred Mosque, is a mutamatti'.

We have explained that the Companions made clear that it includes qiran, in that each of them is an 'umrah in the months of hajj together with hajj, although between their realities there is a difference, as is clear.

Know first: the scholars stipulated conditions for the obligation of the offering of tamattu', some of which are agreed upon and some of which are disputed.

The first: that he performs 'umrah in the months of hajj. If he performs 'umrah outside the months of hajj, no offering is obligatory on him, because he did not combine the two rites in the months of hajj, so no offering is obligatory on him, like the one performing hajj alone (mufrid). The weakness of Tawus's view that he is a mutamatti' is not hidden, nor the weakness of al-Hasan's view that whoever performs 'umrah after the sacrifice is a mutamatti'.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: We do not know of anyone who said either of these two views, as stated in al-Mughni. If he entered ihram for it outside the months of hajj, but performed its acts within the months of hajj, then the scholars have two views:

One of them: an offering is obligatory on him, looking to the acts of 'umrah which occurred in the months of hajj.

The second: no offering is obligatory on him, looking to the fact that the ihram occurred before the months of hajj, and it is a rite without which 'umrah is not complete. Both have a basis in reasoning, and there is no explicit text on either. Among those who said there is no offering on him and that he is not a mutamatti' is Imam Ahmad.

In al-Mughni: The meaning of that is also reported from Jabir and Abu 'Iyad. It is the view of Ishaq and one of al-Shafi'i's two views. Tawus said: his 'umrah is in the month in which he enters the Sanctuary. al-Hasan, al-Hakam, Ibn Shubrumah, al-Thawri, and al-Shafi'i in one of his two views said: his 'umrah is in the month in which he circumambulates. 'Ata' said: his 'umrah is in the month in which he exits (ihlal), and this is the view of Malik. Abu Hanifah said: If he circumambulated four rounds for the 'umrah before the months of hajj, he is not a mutamatti'; and if he circumambulated the four in the months of hajj, he is a mutamatti', because the 'umrah was valid in the months of hajj, as evidenced by the fact that if he had intercourse, he would invalidate it, so it is like when he enters ihram for it in the months of hajj. Thus said al-Mughni. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The second condition: that he performs hajj in that same year in which he performed 'umrah in the months of hajj. If his hajj is in another year, then no offering is obligatory on him.

The author of al-Muhadhdhab said: This is because of what Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab related, saying: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to perform 'umrah in the months of hajj, and if they did not perform hajj in that same year, they did not offer a sacrifice. He said: And because the offering is only obligatory for abandoning ihram for hajj from the miqat, and this one did not abandon ihram for hajj from the miqat, for if he stays in Makkah, Makkah becomes his miqat, and if he returns to his land and comes back, then he has entered ihram from the miqat. Al-Nawawi said regarding the report mentioned: the narration from Ibn al-Musayyab is hasan; al-Bayhaqi related it with a hasan chain. And the weakness of al-Hasan's view that he is a mutamatti' even if he does not perform hajj in that same year is not hidden.

The third condition: that he does not return to his land, or to something comparable to it in distance. Some said: it suffices for this condition that he return to his miqat and enter ihram for hajj from it; others suffice with the distance of qasr (shortening prayer) after the 'umrah, then he enters ihram for hajj from the distance of qasr.

In summary: the four Imams agree that travel after the 'umrah, and entering ihram for hajj from the end of that journey, removes the obligation of the offering of tamattu', but they differ on the measure of the distance. Some of them say: he must, after the 'umrah in the months of hajj, return to the place from which he came, then set out on a journey for hajj and enter ihram from the miqat. Others say: it suffices for him to return to his land, or to travel a distance equal to the distance of his land. Others say: for them, the journey of the distance of qasr suffices. Others say: it suffices for him to return for the ihram of hajj to his miqat. We have previously set out their views in detail. Their proof is what they understood from His saying: ﴿That is for whoever whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. They said: there is no difference between the people present at the Sacred Mosque and others, except that others have eased things by dropping one of the two journeys, which is the journey for hajj after the journey for 'umrah; and if he travels for hajj after the 'umrah, the cause ceases, so the offering falls away with its cessation. They reinforced this with reports they related from 'Umar and his son, may Allah be pleased with them both. We have previously set out the two positions of the scholars regarding what the reference of the demonstrative in His saying: ﴿That is for whoever whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196] points to, and we discussed their proofs. We showed that according to the view held by al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, and those who agree with him, that the demonstrative refers to tamattu' itself, and that the people of Makkah have no tamattu' at all, there is no proof in the verse for the views of the Imams that we mentioned. And according to the other view, that the demonstrative refers to the ruling of tamattu', which is the obligation of what is easy of the offering and fasting when unable to do it, not tamattu' itself, then the Imams' use of it for the views mentioned has a basis in reasoning, as you see.

The essence is that their use of this verse as evidence is valid only on one of the two interpretations of what the demonstrative refers to in the verse, and we have already discussed this at length.

In my view, the more cautious position is that the sacrifice for tamattu' (the combined pilgrimage, *tamattu'*) is required even if the pilgrim travelled, because the verse is not explicit in exempting him, and because of the other possibility relied upon by al-Bukhari and the Hanafis, as already clarified. Among those who held this view is al-Hasan. Ibn al-Mundhir chose it because of the general wording of the verse, as reported in *al-Mughni*. And Allah knows best.

The fourth condition: that he is not one of the residents of al-Masjid al-Haram (the Sacred Mosque). As for one who is a resident of al-Masjid al-Haram, there is no sacrifice upon him, because of the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque.﴾

The most apparent of the scholars' opinions in my view regarding the meaning of "residents of al-Masjid al-Haram" is that they are the people of the Haram and those whose distance from it is less than the distance in which prayer is shortened (qasr). This is because al-Masjid al-Haram is often used to mean the entire Haram. Whoever is at a distance less than the distance of shortening is like a resident, and for this reason, if he travels from the Haram to that distance, his prayer is called the prayer of a resident, so he does not shorten it, and it is not the prayer of a traveller for which shortening is prescribed. Thus it is clear that he falls under the term "residents of al-Masjid al-Haram," on the basis that the intended meaning is the entire Haram. This is the most apparent view, contrary to those who restricted it to Makkah, those who restricted it to the Haram, and those who generalised it to everything within the miqat (the boundary point for entering ihram). (p-125) You know that this condition holds only on one of the two views regarding the verse.

The fifth condition: what some scholars said, namely that it is required that one intends the tamattu' (combining Hajj with 'Umrah) at the time of entering ihram for 'Umrah. They said: because he combined two acts of worship within the time of one of them, he needs an intention of combining, like combining two prayers. Based on this condition, the place of the intention of tamattu' is the time of entering ihram for 'Umrah.

Some said: he may form the intention of tamattu' as long as he has not finished the acts of 'Umrah, just as there is disagreement about the time of the intention to combine two prayers. Some said he must intend it at the start of the first of the two, and some said he may form his intention as long as he has not finished the first prayer. This is what some scholars have said. On this view, if he performed 'Umrah in the months of Hajj without intending Hajj in that year, and then after finishing 'Umrah it became apparent to him that he would perform Hajj that year, then there is no tamattu' sacrifice upon him. The condition of intention mentioned was attributed by the author of *al-Insaf* to al-Qadi and most of the Hanbalis, and he related the opposite, that it is not required, by "it is said" (qila), then said: this was chosen by "the author" (al-Musannif) and "the commentator" (al-Shariḥ), and it was given precedence in *al-Muharrar* and *al-Fa'iq*. The apparent view is that this condition falls away, and that whenever he performs Hajj after having performed 'Umrah in the months of Hajj of that same year, he must offer the sacrifice, because of the apparent generality of the noble verse. Restricting it by intention is therefore a restriction of the Qur'an, indeed a proof which must be returned to. What supports this is that they say the reason for the obligation of the sacrifice is that he enjoyed relief by dropping one journey of Hajj, and that reason exists in this case. And Allah, Exalted, knows best.

The sixth condition: what some scholars required, namely that the Hajj and 'Umrah mentioned must be on behalf of one person, such as performing 'Umrah on one's own behalf and Hajj on one's own behalf, all of it on one's own behalf and not on behalf of another; or that one person performs Hajj and performs 'Umrah on behalf of one person. As for when he performs Hajj on behalf of one person and 'Umrah on behalf of another, or performs 'Umrah on behalf of one person and Hajj on his own behalf, or performs 'Umrah on his own behalf and Hajj on behalf of another person, then is the sacrifice of tamattu' obligatory, in view of the fact that the one performing the two rites is one person, or is it not obligatory, in view of the fact that Hajj was performed on behalf of one person and 'Umrah on behalf of another, so it is as if two persons had done it, one performing Hajj and the other performing 'Umrah, and therefore there is no tamattu' upon either of them? Both have a basis in reasoning. The view of al-Shafi'i, which is the view of the majority of the Shafi'is, is that this condition is not required, in view of the unity of the one performing the rite. Its opposing view, which is weaker, is that the sacrifice is not obligatory, in view of the fact that Hajj was for one person and 'Umrah for another. The view of Malik on this is close to the view of al-Shafi'i in that there is disagreement and the preference is for not requiring the condition.

Shaykh al-Mawwaq said in his commentary on the words of Khalil in his *Mukhtasar*, in the list of conditions for the obligation of the tamattu' sacrifice, and regarding the condition that the two rites be on behalf of one person there is hesitation, the following: Ibn Shas mentioned among the conditions by which one becomes a tamattu' pilgrim: that the two rites be performed on behalf of one person. Ibn 'Arafa said: I do not know this; rather, in the book of Muhammad: whoever performs 'Umrah on his own behalf and then performs Hajj in the same year on behalf of another, that is tamattu'. Shaykh al-Hattab said in his commentary on the words of Khalil mentioned, the following: He indicated the hesitation because of the hesitation of later scholars in transmission. What was transmitted by the author of *al-Nawadir*, Ibn Yunus and al-Lakhmi is that this condition is not required. Ibn al-Hajib said: the more well-known view is that the two must be on behalf of one person, and Ibn Shas related two views on this. In *al-Tawdih* he said: he did not attribute either of them and did not specify which was the more famous. The author of *al-Nawadir* and Ibn Yunus did not relate anything except what occurred in *al-Muwaziyya*, that it is tamattu'. End of quotation. And in his rites (*manasik*), after mentioning the words of Ibn al-Hajib, Khalil said: I have not found in Ibn Yunus and others anything except the view of the obligation of the sacrifice.

Ibn 'Arafa said: Ibn Shas's condition is that the two rites be on behalf of one person, and Ibn al-Hajib related: I do not know it; rather, in the book of Muhammad, whoever performs 'Umrah on his own behalf and then performs Hajj in the same year on behalf of another is a tamattu' pilgrim. So what the author mentioned of hesitation is correct. But the known position is that this is not required, and his habit is to indicate hesitation regarding what has no preference in it.

Ibn Jama'a al-Shafi'i said in his large book on rites: it is not required that the two rites be on behalf of one person according to the majority of the Shafi'is. This is the view of the Hanafis and a narration of Ibn al-Mawwaz from Malik, and on this course several leading Maliki imams went, among them al-Baji and al-Tartushi. Among the Shafi'is some did require it. Ibn al-Hajib said: it is the more well-known view of the school of Malik, and the author of *al-Jawahir* followed Ibn al-Hajib in requiring it. His statement that it is the more well-known is not accepted, for al-Qarafi in *al-Dhakhira* mentioned the other conditions apart from this one, and said: the author of *al-Jawahir* added this condition and did not attribute it to anyone else. End of al-Hattab's words. The apparent conclusion from the transmissions he quoted is that the view that the two rites need not be on behalf of one person is the known position in the school of Malik, and this is so. The school of Ahmad is close to the school of Malik and al-Shafi'i, so there is also disagreement in it as to whether it is required that the two rites be on behalf of one person or not. Most of the Hanbalis hold that it is not required, and *al-Insaf* attributed this to some companions. The author of *al-Insaf* said: among them al-Munsif and al-Majd, as stated by al-Zarkashi, and it was confined to by *al-Furu'*, and he attributed the opposing view to the author of *al-Talkhis*. We have already mentioned in the words of Ibn Jama'a al-Shafi'i that the view that the two rites need not be on behalf of one person is also the view of the Hanafis. So it is clear that the well-known view in the four schools is that this condition is not required, and the view of those who required it has a basis in reasoning. And Allah, Exalted, knows best.

The seventh condition: that he exits from the state of 'Umrah (by shortening/completing it) before entering ihram for Hajj. If he enters ihram for Hajj before exiting from 'Umrah, he becomes a qarin (combining pilgrim), as happened to 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, in the Farewell Pilgrimage according to the more accurate view, as already clarified.

* *

The eighth condition: what some scholars required, namely that he is not counted as a tamattu' pilgrim unless he enters ihram for 'Umrah from the miqat. If he enters ihram for it from a point before the miqat, he ceases to be a tamattu' pilgrim, because he is then as though he were one of the residents of al-Masjid al-Haram. The falling away of this condition is not hidden.

The author of *al-Insaf* said: When this condition was mentioned, Abu al-Faraj and al-Hulwani mentioned it, and Ibn 'Aqil decisively affirmed it in *al-Tadhkira*, and it was given precedence in *al-Furu'*. The Qadi and Ibn 'Aqil said, and it was decisively affirmed in *al-Mustau'ab*, *al-Talkhis*, *al-Ri'aya*, and others: if the distance between him and Makkah is a distance of shortening, and he enters ihram from it, he is not obliged to the sacrifice of tamattu', because he is a resident of al-Masjid al-Haram, but rather the sacrifice for passing the miqat without ihram. The author (al-Musannif) and the commentator (al-Shariḥ) and others chose that if he enters ihram for 'Umrah from a point before the miqat, he is obliged to two sacrifices: the sacrifice of tamattu' and the sacrifice for entering ihram from before the miqat, because he did not reside there and did not intend to stay there, and he is not a permanent resident. They rejected what the Qadi said. End of his words. This latter is the apparent view. And Allah, Exalted, knows best.

The author of *al-Insaf* said after these words, connected to them: The author (al-Musannif) and the commentator (al-Shariḥ) said: If an outsider (*afaqi*) enters ihram for 'Umrah outside the months of Hajj, then stays in Makkah and performs 'Umrah from al-Tan'im, he is a tamattu' pilgrim. This is explicitly stated, and in its explicit statement of this case there is an indication that the sacrifice is obligatory in the first case by a fortiori reasoning. End of his words. One should not disagree about either of the two, since both are explicitly included in the general wording of the verse on tamattu', as you see. And Allah, Exalted, knows best.

Know that those among the scholars whose view is considered agree that the qarin is obliged to what the tamattu' pilgrim is obliged to of the offering (*hady*), and of fasting when unable to offer the sacrifice. We have already mentioned the sound and established reports from some eminent Companions that qiran falls under the name of tamattu'. On this basis it falls under the general wording of the verse. Both rites in it are tamattu' linguistically, because tamattu' derives from *mata'* or *muti'a*, which means enjoyment or benefit. From this is the poet's saying:

*I stood at the grave of a stranger in a desert,*
*a little enjoyment from a beloved who has departed.*

He made his companionship at the grave a "enjoyment" for his benefiting from that companionship. Each of the qarin and the tamattu' pilgrim benefited by dropping one of the two journeys, and the qarin, according to the majority, also benefited by the merging of the acts of 'Umrah into Hajj.

A group of scholars said: qiran does not fall under the general wording of the verse according to the literal meaning of its wording, and this is the more apparent view, because the limit in His words: ﴿So whoever enjoys tamattu' with 'Umrah until Hajj﴾ indicates (p-128) this. Those who said this said: it is attached to it in its ruling, because it has the same meaning. The general view of scholars, including the four Imams, is that the qarin is obliged to what the tamattu' pilgrim is obliged to, except for one who deviated into an opinion not worthy of consideration. Not every disagreement is considered valid, except a disagreement that has a basis in reasoning.

The author of *al-Insaf* said: Ibn Mushaysh asked him, meaning Imam Ahmad: Is the sacrifice obligatory upon the qarin as an obligation? He said: How could it be obligatory upon him as an obligation, when they only likened him to the tamattu' pilgrim? He said, in *al-Furu'*: so a narration may be inferred from this that there is no sacrifice upon him. End of his words.

It is not hidden that the school of Ahmad contradicts what they claimed as a narration, and that the qarin is like the tamattu' pilgrim in ruling. Ibn Qudama said in *al-Mughni*: We know of no disagreement regarding the obligation of the sacrifice upon the qarin except what is reported from Dawud that there is no sacrifice upon him, and this was also reported from Tawus. Ibn al-Mundhir related that when Ibn Dawud entered Makkah he was asked about the qarin, whether a sacrifice is obligatory upon him, and he said: No, so he was dragged by his leg. This indicates how well-known the matter was among them. End of his words. Al-Nawawi mentioned that al-Abdari related this view from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Surayj. The verified view is the opposite of this, and that the qarin is obliged to what the tamattu' pilgrim is obliged to.

Among the texts that indicate this is the hadith of 'A'isha, agreed upon, in which: "He entered upon us on the day of sacrifice with beef, and I said: What is this? It was said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sacrificed on behalf of his wives." Agreed upon.

Al-Majd said in *al-Muntaqa*: In it is evidence for eating from the blood-offering of qiran, because 'A'isha was a qarin. End of his words. And this indicates that the qarin is obliged to a sacrifice. And Allah knows best.

Among the most explicit evidences for this is what Muslim related in his Sahih from Jabir, in the wording: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sacrificed a cow on behalf of 'Aishah on the Day of Sacrifice." It is known that she was a qarin (one performing Qiran, combining Hajj and 'Umrah), according to the verified view, so that cow was a blood sacrifice of Qiran, and this is evidence for its obligation. As for what Ibn Qudamah mentioned in al-Mughni, that it was narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever combines his Hajj and 'Umrah, let him shed blood (sacrifice an animal)," I do not know of any basis for it, and the apparent view is that it is not authentically traced to the Prophet ﷺ as a marfu' (attributed) report. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Most scholars hold that if the qarin's family are present at the Sacred Mosque (ahl al-masjid al-haram, i.e., residents of its vicinity), then there is no sacrifice upon him, because he is a mutamatti' (one performing Tamattu') or in the ruling of a mutamatti', and Allah says: ﴿That is for one whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾.

Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni, and it is the view of the majority of scholars. Ibn al-Majishun said: he must offer a sacrifice, because Allah the Exalted removed the sacrifice from the mutamatti', and this one is not a mutamatti'. This is not correct, because we have mentioned that he is a mutamatti'; and even if he were not a mutamatti', he is subsidiary to it (the ruling is derived from it), and the obligation of the sacrifice upon the qarin was only by way of the meaning of the text on Tamattu'; so the branch may not contradict its root. End of quote from him.

The compiler of these notes (may Allah pardon him and forgive him) says: The summary of this discussion is that the qarin is like the mutamatti' in that each of them, if he is from the residents of the Sacred Mosque, has no sacrifice upon him. The author of al-Mughni mentioned that Ibn al-Majishun disagreed on this and said: he must sacrifice; and he has a strong point of view based on reasoning against the view of the majority: that one tawaf and one sa'y suffice for his Hajj and 'Umrah together. Thus he has benefited by the dropping of the work of one of the two rites, and the obligation of a sacrifice in exchange for that has a point of view, as you see.

An-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: Our companions said: the sacrifice of Qiran is not obligatory upon the residents of the Sacred Mosque, just as it is not obligatory upon the mutamatti'; this is the school's position, and the majority have decided on it. Al-Hannati and al-Rafi'i related a view that it is obligatory upon him. End of the relevant portion from him. This view among the Shafi'is is the view of Ibn al-Majishun from the Malikis, as mentioned by the author of al-Mughni, and the school of Malik and his companions, like the school of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, holds that if the qarin is from the residents of the Sacred Mosque, there is no sacrifice upon him. The residents of the Mosque, according to Malik and his companions, are the people of Makkah and Dhi Tuwa.

Shaykh al-Hattab said in his commentary on the words of Khalil in his Mukhtasar: "The condition for the sacrifice of both (Tamattu' and Qiran) is that he does not reside in Makkah or Dhi Tuwa..." etc., whose text is: Dhu Tuwa is the area between the pass descending from which one goes to the cemetery of Makkah called al-Ma'lah, and the other pass leading towards al-Zahir, which the people of Makkah call "between the two Hujuns." End of the relevant portion from him.

We have already mentioned that the school of Abu Hanifah and his companions holds that the people of Makkah and those similar to them who are inside the miqat (boundary) are not prescribed 'Umrah at all, so there is no Tamattu' or Qiran for them, based on the reference in His words: ﴿That is for one whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾ returning to Tamattu' itself, as was previously clarified; although they say that if they perform Tamattu' or Qiran they have done wrong and their ihram is valid, and they are obliged to offer a compensatory sacrifice (dam al-jabr). This sacrifice, in their view, is a sacrifice of transgression from which its owner may not eat, unlike the sacrifice of Tamattu' and Qiran for those who are not residents of the Sacred Mosque, which in their view is a sacrifice of worship, from which its owner may eat. Some Hanafis related from Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr that the people of Makkah have no Tamattu'. We have already mentioned that this is the opinion of al-Bukhari.

Know that we have mentioned that among the conditions for the obligation of the sacrifice of Tamattu' is that he does not return after the 'Umrah to his country or a distance equal to it, or travel a distance of qasr (shortening prayer), as we explained there from the sayings of the imams on this. We wish to mention here the ruling on the qarin who performed the acts of 'Umrah, then returned to his country, then performed Hajj in the same year, or traveled a distance of qasr, then entered ihram for Hajj from the miqat: does the sacrifice fall from him by that, as with Tamattu', or not? The school of Abu Hanifah holds that the sacrifice does not fall from him by his returning to his country after performing the acts of 'Umrah, if he returns and performs Hajj, because he has remained a qarin.

The author of al-Insaf said in discussing the qarin: the sacrifice is not obligatory upon the residents of the Sacred Mosque, as the author (al-Muqni') said; and this is stated in al-Furu' and elsewhere. He said: By analogy, it is not obligatory upon one who travels a journey of qasr or to the miqat, if we say so, as is the apparent school of al-Shafi'i; but their statements imply that it is obligatory, because the name of Qiran remains after the journey, unlike Tamattu'. End of his words.

The summary of his statement is that the apparent view of the Hanbalis is that travel after reaching Makkah does not drop the sacrifice of Qiran, and that the analogy requires that it drops it, by linking it to Tamattu'. An-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: If the qarin enters Makkah before the day of 'Arafah, then returns to the miqat, the school's position in al-Imla' is that there is no sacrifice upon him; many or most have decided on this, and al-Hannati and others declared it sound. Imam al-Haramayn said: If we say that the mutamatti' who entered ihram for Hajj then returned to it does not have the sacrifice dropped, then here it is more so; otherwise there are two views. The difference is that the name of Qiran does not cease by returning, unlike Tamattu'. If he entered ihram for 'Umrah from the miqat, entered Makkah, then returned to the miqat before his tawaf and entered ihram for Hajj, he is a qarin.

Al-Darimi said at the end of the chapter on missing Hajj (al-Fawat): If we say that when he enters ihram for both together, then returns, the sacrifice falls, then here it is more so; otherwise there are two views. End of his words.

The apparent statement of Khalil in his Maliki Mukhtasar is that travel does not drop the sacrifice of Qiran. The conclusion: we have clarified the disagreement of scholars regarding travel after the acts of 'Umrah or after entering Makkah, whether it drops the sacrifice of Qiran or not; and we have clarified the view of the author of al-Insaf that its dropping by travel is the requirement of analogy with Tamattu'.

The closest of the views to correctness in my opinion is that the sacrifice of Qiran is not dropped by travel. We have clarified that the more cautious view for us is that the sacrifice of Tamattu' is not dropped by travel, because the Qur'an explicitly mandates the offering upon the mutamatti', and the verse is not explicit about its dropping by travel. We have also mentioned that the obligation of the sacrifice upon the qarin who is from the residents of the Sacred Mosque has a point of view by reasoning, because he has sufficed with the work of one of the two rites for both, according to the view of the majority, as previously mentioned.

The more apparent of the two views of the scholars in our opinion is that if the Makkan wishes to enter ihram for Qiran, he enters ihram for it from Makkah, because he goes out in his Hajj to 'Arafah, thus combining the Hill and the Haram; contrary to the one who said: the Makkan must initiate his ihram from the nearest part of the Hill (al-Hill), and likewise the outsider (afaqi) who is in Makkah and wishes to enter ihram as a qarin; the more apparent view is that he enters ihram for Qiran from Makkah, contrary to the one who said he enters ihram for it from the nearest part of the Hill, for what we have explained. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

* *

Having known the conditions by which the sacrifice of Tamattu' and Qiran becomes obligatory, know that we wish here to clarify what suffices in it. The verified view is that it is whatever is easily available of the offering (al-hady): the least of it is a sheep that suffices for a sacrifice (udhiyyah), the highest is a camel (badanah), and the middle is a cow. The verified view is that one-seventh of a camel or cow suffices. So if seven of the mutamatti'in share in a camel or cow and slaughter it, it suffices for them, due to the sound texts indicating this, such as the hadith of Jabir, established in the Sahih, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded us to share in camels and cows, each seven of us in one badanah." And in a wording of Muslim, he said: "We shared with the Prophet ﷺ in Hajj and 'Umrah, each seven of us in one badanah." A man said to Jabir: Is what is shared in a camel the same as what is shared in a cow? He said: It is nothing but of the badanat (camels).

Muslim said in his Sahih: Qutaybah ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Malik related to us (h), and Yahya ibn Yahya related to us, and the wording is his, saying: I read to Malik from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "We sacrificed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the year of al-Hudaybiyah the camel on behalf of seven and the cow on behalf of seven." In a wording of Muslim from Jabir, he said: "We set out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entering ihram for Hajj, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded us to share in camels and cows, each seven of us in one badanah." In another wording of his from him, he said: "We performed Hajj with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and we slaughtered the camel for seven and the cow for seven." In another wording of his from him also, he said: "We shared with the Prophet ﷺ in Hajj and 'Umrah, each seven in one badanah." A man said to Jabir: Is what is shared in the badanah the same as what is shared in the camel? He said: It is nothing but of the badanat. Jabir attended al-Hudaybiyah and said: "We sacrificed that day seventy badanat, sharing each seven in one badanah." In another wording of his from him, while he was narrating about the Hajj of the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "He commanded us that when we exit ihram, we should offer the gift, and the group of us would join in the offering;" this was when he commanded them to exit from their Hajj in this hadith. In another wording of his from him also, he said: "We used to perform Tamattu' with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and we would slaughter the cow on behalf of seven among whom we share." End of the relevant portion from Sahih Muslim.

These sound narrations indicate that the sacrifice of Tamattu' is sufficed by sharing among seven in a camel or cow, and it indicates that this falls within "whatever is easily available of the offering." As for the sheep and the whole camel, the sufficiency of each of them is not problematic. Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: Ishaq ibn Mansur related to us, al-Nadr informed us, Shu'bah informed us, Abu Jamrah related to us, who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, about Tamattu'? He commanded me to do it. I asked him about the offering, and he said: In it is a camel, or a cow, or a sheep, or sharing in a blood sacrifice. The hadith... So his statement "or sharing in a blood sacrifice" means what the aforementioned sound narrations from Jabir clarified: that the camel and the cow both suffice for seven of the mutamatti'in. Ibn Hajar said in explaining this hadith: This agrees with what Muslim related from Jabir, who said: "We set out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entering ihram for Hajj, and he commanded us to share in camels and cows, each seven of us in one badanah." Then he said: On this view are al-Shafi'i and the majority, whether the offering is voluntary or obligatory, and whether they all intend nearness to Allah by it, or some of them intend nearness and some intend meat. From Abu Hanifah: sharing requires that they all intend nearness through the offering; and from Zufar the same, with the addition: that their causes must be one. From Dawud and some Malikis: it is permitted in voluntary offerings but not obligatory ones. From Malik: it is not permitted absolutely. End of his words.

The verification of the matter is that a seventh of a camel (badanah) and a seventh of a cow each substitutes for a sheep and falls under the general wording of ﴿whatever offering is feasible﴾. The sound narrations we have mentioned are a proof against everyone who opposes this, such as Malik and whoever agrees with him. As for what Isma'il al-Qadi argued in support of Malik, that joint sacrifice in the offering is not valid, the reply is that the hadith of Jabir was only at al-Hudaybiyah, where they were prevented from completing their rites. And that the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas was contradicted by Abu Jamrah, who narrated from him against the reliable transmitters among his companions, who related from him that "whatever offering is feasible" means a sheep. Then he cited that from them through sound but rejected chains. As for the claim that the hadith of Jabir was only at al-Hudaybiyah, where they were prevented, it is rejected by what is established in the sound narrations in Muslim, which we have cited in their wording: that they shared in that joint sacrifice together with him (ﷺ) too, in his Hajj. There is no doubt that his Hajj means the Farewell Pilgrimage, because he did not perform any Hajj after the Hijrah other than it. In some sound narrations in Muslim, which we have cited in their wording just above, there is an explicit statement that the sharing occurred in that Hajj, as is clear from the wording of Muslim that we have mentioned. As for the claim that Abu Jamrah opposed the reliable companions of Ibn 'Abbas by mentioning that joint sacrifice, it is also rejected by what Ibn Hajar mentioned in al-Fath (Fath al-Bari), where he said: "There is no conflict between the narration of Abu Jamrah and the narration of others, because he added to them the mention of sharing, and agreed with them on the mention of the sheep. Ibn 'Abbas only intended, by limiting it to the sheep, to refute those who claim that the offering is restricted to camels and cows. This is clear in what we will mention after this," up to his saying: "By this the reports are reconciled, and this is better than casting doubt on the narration of one whom the scholars unanimously deemed trustworthy, namely Abu Jamrah al-Duba'i." It has been narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he did not hold the view of sharing, then he retracted it when the Sunnah reached him. Ibn Hajar mentioned Ibn 'Umar's retraction from that, from Ahmad with his chain, through al-Sha'bi, from Ibn 'Umar.

The more apparent of the two opinions of the people of knowledge in my view is that a camel does not suffice for more than seven. Ibn Hajar mentioned in al-Fath, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, in one of the two narrations from him, that it suffices for ten. He said: "Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and Ibn Khuzaymah of the Shafi'is also held this." Ibn Khuzaymah argued for that in his Sahih and strengthened it, and he cited in its support the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij: "that he (ﷺ) divided and equalized ten sheep with one camel," the hadith. It is in the two Sahihs.

And they agreed that a sheep does not validly take a share in joint sacrifice, and his saying "or a sheep" is the saying of the majority of scholars. Al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it with sound chains from them. And it was narrated with a strong chain from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from 'A'ishah and Ibn 'Umar, that they did not see "whatever offering is feasible" as applying except to camels and cows. Al-Qasim and a group agreed with them. Isma'il al-Qadi said in his al-Ahkam: "I think they went to that because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have made the camels for you among the symbols of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]. So they went to restrict what the name 'badan' applies to." He said: "What refutes this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], and the Muslims agreed that for a gazelle a sheep is required, so the name 'offering' applies to it."

I say: Ibn 'Abbas himself argued with this. Al-Tabari narrated with a sound chain, to 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The offering is a sheep." It was said to him about that, and he said: "I will recite to you from the Book of Allah what you acknowledge: what is required for the gazelle?" They said: "A sheep." He said: "Allah says: ﴿as an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾." End of quotation from Fath al-Bari.

We have already mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah that it is established in the two Sahihs, from 'A'ishah, that she said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) once sent a gift of sheep as an offering," and this is a sound and explicit text from her in naming sheep as an offering, as you see.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him and forgive him) says: What appears to me to be correct regarding the offering of tamattu', which Allah has stated in His Book is whatever is feasible of the offering, is that it is a sheep, or a camel, or a cow. A seventh of a camel and a seventh of a cow suffice for one person performing tamattu'. A camel suffices for seven performers of tamattu', because the sound narrations establish this, and there has not arisen from the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ) any explicit text on the point of dispute that stands against them. The narration of Jabir that a camel suffices for seven in the offering is more specific to the point of dispute than the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij: "that he (ﷺ) made the camel in the division equal ten sheep," because that is about division, while the hadith of Jabir is about the offering specifically. And the more specific in the point of dispute takes precedence over the more general. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Among what clarifies this is what Ibn Hajar mentioned in al-Fath when explaining the hadith of Rafi' mentioned above. Al-Bukhari included it in the Book of Slaughtered Animals, from Rafi' ibn Khadij, with the wording: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) at Dhu al-Hulayfah, and we captured camels and sheep. The Prophet (ﷺ) was at the back of the people, so they hastened, set up the cooking pots, and the Prophet (ﷺ) came to them, ordered the pots to be overturned, then divided and equalized ten sheep with one camel, and a camel bolted from it," the hadith.

The wording of Ibn Hajar's statement on this hadith is: "This is to be understood as meaning that this was the value of sheep at that time. Perhaps camels were few or precious, and sheep were many or lean, such that the value of a camel was ten sheep. This does not contradict the rule regarding sacrificial animals, that a camel suffices for seven sheep, because that is the usual value of a sheep and a camel when they are moderate. As for this division, it was a specific event, so it is possible that the equalization was due to the mentioned preciousness of camels, not sheep."

The hadith of Jabir in Muslim is explicit in the ruling, where he said in it: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered us to share in camels and cows, each seven of us in one badanah," and the badanah is applied to the she-camel and to the cow.

As for the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey, and Eid al-Adha came, so we shared in a cow for seven, and in a camel for ten," Al-Tirmidhi graded it as hasan, Ibn Hibban authenticated it, and it is supported by this hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij. What is settled in this matter is that the original rule is that a camel is for seven, unless some intervening factor arises, such as preciousness or the like, in which case the ruling changes according to that. By this the reports on this matter are reconciled. Then what appears from the mentioned division is that it occurred regarding what remained after what was cooked and spilled from the camels and sheep they had taken as booty. It is possible, if the event occurred more than once, that the story mentioned by Ibn 'Abbas is one in which the meat was destroyed because it had been cut up for cooking, and the story in the hadith of Rafi' is one in which the sheep were cooked whole, for example, and when their broth was spilled, they were added to the sheep to be divided, and then whoever received them in his share cooked them. Perhaps this is the point behind the decline in the value of sheep from the usual, and Allah knows best. End of Ibn Hajar's statement.

(p-135) That the meat was returned so that the one who received it in his share could cook it a second time is not apparent to me, and Allah knows best.

The hadith of Rafi' mentioned was also reported by Muslim in the Book of Hunting and Slaughtered Animals, and the wording relevant to it, from Rafi', is: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Dhu al-Hulayfah of Tihamah, and we captured sheep and camels. The people hastened, boiled them in the pots, and he ordered them overturned, then he equalized ten sheep with one camel."

The summary is that the most specific and most explicit and clearest text in the point of dispute is the hadith of Jabir, whose narration we have mentioned in Muslim. As for the hadith of Rafi', it concerns the division of spoils, not the offering. As for the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, its apparent sense is that it concerns sacrificial animals. In any case, the hadith of Jabir is more authentic than it. So what appears is that the one performing tamattu' is sufficed by a seventh of a camel, and that the explicit text stated about this should be given precedence, over the view that a tenth of a camel suffices. I have seen the evidences of both opinions. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Topics related to this question

First branch: Know that there is no disagreement among the scholars that all of the year is a time for ʿUmrah, except the days of tashriq (ayyam al-tashriq, the days of sacrifice's aftermath). It is therefore not appropriate to perform ʿUmrah during them until the sun sets on the fourteenth day, according to what a group of the scholars have said.

(p-233) Second branch: Know that it has been authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "an ʿUmrah in Ramadan equals a Hajj." In some narrations of the hadith in the Sahih, the wording is: "equal to a Hajj with me."
