Third branch: Know that the verified position is that the Prophet (ﷺ) certainly did not perform ʿUmrah in Rajab after the Hijrah, and that he performed only four ʿUmrahs after the Hijrah. The first: the ʿUmrah of al-Hudaybiyah in Dhu al-Qaʿdah of the sixth year, when the polytheists prevented him; he exited the state of ihram, and slaughtered, without tawaf or sa'y, as is well known.

The second: the ʿUmrah of al-Qada' in Dhu al-Qaʿdah of the seventh year, which was the one agreed upon in the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah.

We have already mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah the reason it is named ʿUmrat al-Qada' and explained it. The third: the ʿUmrah of al-Jiʿranah in Dhu al-Qaʿdah of the eighth year, after the conquest of Makkah in Ramadan of the eighth year. The fourth: the ʿUmrah which he combined with the Farewell Hajj. This is the verified position.

We have already indicated this, and we will suffice here with what we have mentioned of the rulings of ʿUmrah, because most of its rulings we mentioned in the course of our discussion of the issues of Hajj. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾ [al-Hajj: 29]. The imperative form in this noble verse indicates the obligation of fulfilling the vow, as we have mentioned many times before that the imperative form demands obligation, according to the more correct view, unless there is a diverting proof.

Among what indicates from the Qur'an the binding nature of fulfilling vows is that He, the Exalted, pointed out that the cause of drinking from the cup mixed with camphor, in the context of the dread of the horrors of the Day of Resurrection, is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor, a spring from which the servants of Allah drink, making it gush forth in abundance﴾ [al-Insan: 5-6]. Then He pointed to some of the causes of that, saying: ﴿They fulfil [their] vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread﴾ [al-Insan: 7]. So fulfilling a vow is praiseworthy in every case, although the verse of al-Insan is not explicit about its obligation. Likewise His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And whatever expense you spend or vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 270], and so on.

We have explained in the introduction to this blessed book that clarification by the Qur'an, if it is not sufficient for the intended meaning, is completed by clarification from the Sunnah. Therefore we will explain here what the Sunnah requires regarding the vow that must be fulfilled and the vow that need not be fulfilled.

Know first that the vowed matter, in general, has two states:

First: that it contains obedience to Allah.

(p-234) Second: that it does not contain obedience to Allah. This latter is divided into two categories:

One: that which is disobedience to Allah.

The second: that which contains no disobedience in itself, but is not of the kind of obedience, such as a permissible matter that one has not been commanded to do.

What must be relied upon, by evidence, in the three categories mentioned is that if the vowed matter is obedience to Allah, fulfilling it is obligatory, whether it is in the category of recommended acts, such as one who vows to give charity in dirhams to the poor, or vows to slaughter a voluntary sacrifice, or to fast voluntary days, and the like. Such things become obligatory by the vow, and fulfilling them is binding. Likewise, if the vow is tied to an attribute of an obligatory act, such as one who vows to perform the prayer at its earliest time, it is obligatory upon him to fulfil that.

As for one who vows an obligatory act, such as the five daily prayers or the fasting of Ramadan, his vow has no effect, because Allah's obligation of that is greater than an obligation through a vow. If the vowed matter is disobedience to Allah, then it is not permissible to fulfil it. If it is permissible, with no prohibition or command concerning it, then fulfilling it is not binding.

As for the evidence for the obligation of fulfilling a vow of obedience and its prohibition in a vow of disobedience, it is that this has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: Abu Nuʿaym narrated to us, Malik narrated to us, from Talhah ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, from al-Qasim, from ʿAishah, may Allah be pleased with her, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him, and whoever vows to disobey Him, let him not disobey Him." End quote. It is clear regarding the obligation of fulfilling a vow of obedience and the prohibition of fulfilling a vow of disobedience.

Al-Bukhari also said: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, from Malik, from Talhah ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, up to the end of the isnad and text mentioned just above.

Since you know that this authentic hadith indicates the obligation of fulfilling a vow of obedience and its prohibition in a vow of disobedience,

know that the evidence for not fulfilling a vow concerning a permissible matter is that this too has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us, Wuhayb narrated to us, Ayyub narrated to us, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "While the Prophet (ﷺ) was delivering a sermon, he saw a man standing, so he asked about him. They said: Abu Isra'il vowed to stand and not sit, not to seek shade, not to speak, and to fast. (p-235) The Prophet (ﷺ) said: Command him to speak, to seek shade, to sit, and to complete his fast." End of the relevant point from Sahih al-Bukhari. In it is explicit statement that what was of his vow of the kind of obedience, namely fasting, he was commanded to complete it, fulfilling his vow; and what was of his vow permissible and not obedience, such as abstaining from speech, not sitting, and not seeking shade, he was commanded not to fulfil it, and this is explicit that fulfilling it is not obligatory.

Know that we have not mentioned the statements of the scholars here for brevity, and because of the existence of the sound evidence from the Sunnah for what we have mentioned.

* *

Topics related to this question

First branch: Know that there is no vow for a person regarding drawing near (to Allah) by something he does not own, and this has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: Zuhayr ibn Harb and ʿAli ibn Hujr al-Saʿdi narrated to me, and the wording is Zuhayr's, both said: Isma'il ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, Ayyub narrated to us, from Abu Qilabah, from Abu al-Muhallab, from ʿImran ibn Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Thaqif were allies of Banu ʿUqayl, and Thaqif captured two men from the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The hadith in full.

In it is the following text: "A woman of the Ansar was captured, and al-ʿAdba' was seized, and the woman was in bonds, and the people would let their camels rest before their houses. One night she escaped from the bonds, came to the camels, and whenever she approached a camel it groaned, so she left it, until she reached al-ʿAdba', and it did not groan. He said: It was a trained she-camel, so she sat on its hump, then drove it on, and it set off. They noticed her absence and pursued them, but she eluded them. He said: She vowed to Allah that if Allah delivered her upon it, she would slaughter it. When she reached Madinah, the people saw it and said: This is al-ʿAdba', the she-camel of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). She said: It was that she vowed that if Allah delivered her upon it, she would slaughter it. So they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him. He said: 'Subhan Allah, how evil is her recompense! She vowed to Allah that if Allah delivered her upon it she would slaughter it. There is no fulfilment of a vow in disobedience, nor in what the servant does not own.'" The hadith in full. The point of evidence in it is his saying (ﷺ): "nor in what the servant does not own." This is an authentic, explicit text for what we have mentioned, and it is corroborated by the hadith of Thabit ibn al-Dahhak: that he (ﷺ) said: "There is no fulfilment of a vow in disobedience to Allah, nor in severing ties of kinship, nor in what the son of Adam does not own." End quote.

The Hafiz said in Bulugh al-Maram: Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Tabarani, and the wording is his; it is of sound chain, and it has a supporting report from the hadith of Kardam in Ahmad.

* *

(p-236) Second branch: Know that scholars differed concerning one who makes a vow that it is not binding to fulfil, whether there is an obligation of expiation for an oath upon him, or nothing is obligatory upon him. The argument of those who said nothing is obligatory upon him is the hadith of Abu Isra'il's vow, that he would not sit, speak, or seek shade, and the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded him in the authentic hadith mentioned just above not to fulfil this vow, and did not tell him that he owes an expiation for an oath. We have already explained this clearly in Surat Maryam. We have already mentioned that al-Qurtubi said regarding the story of Abu Isra'il: this is the clearest proof for the majority in the non-obligation of expiation upon one who vows disobedience or what contains no obedience. Malik said when he mentioned it: I did not hear that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded him with expiation.

As for those who said that for a vow that need not be fulfilled an expiation for an oath is obligatory, they argued by what Muslim narrated in his Sahih: Harun ibn Sa'id al-Ayli, Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Ala, and Ahmad ibn ʿIsa narrated to me; Yunus said: "Akhbarana," and the other two said: Ibn Wahb narrated to us, informed me ʿAmr ibn al-Harith, from Kaʿb ibn ʿAlqamah, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Shimasah, from Abu al-Khayr, from ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who said: "The expiation for a vow is the expiation for an oath." End quote. Its apparent meaning includes the vow that need not be fulfilled.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh Muslim: The scholars differed about the intended meaning of it. The majority of our companions understood it as the vow of contention (nadhr al-lajaj), which is that a person who wishes to refrain from speaking to Zayd, for example, says: If I speak to Zayd, for example, then it is incumbent upon me for Allah to perform Hajj or something else. Then he speaks to him; he is then given the choice between an expiation for an oath and what he committed himself to. This is the correct position in our school. Malik and many, or most, understood it as the unrestricted vow, like the saying: "It is upon me to vow." Ahmad and some of our companions understood it as the vow of disobedience, like one who vows to drink wine. A group of jurists of the people of hadith understood it as covering all kinds of vows, and said: he has the choice in all vowed matters between fulfilling what he committed himself to and an expiation for an oath. And Allah knows best. End of al-Nawawi's words.

It is not hidden that after the last opinion, because of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾, this is a definitive command that precludes giving a choice between fulfilling it and something else.

The more apparent meaning of the hadith in my view is that one who makes an unrestricted vow, such as saying: "It is upon me for Allah to vow," an expiation for an oath is obligatory upon him, due to what Ibn Majah and al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound) narrated from ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The expiation for a vow, when it is not specified, is the expiation for an oath." Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah narrated something similar from Ibn ʿAbbas. In the two hadiths is an explanation of the intended meaning of the hadith of Muslim: that the intended meaning is the unrestricted vow (p-237) in which its maker did not specify what he vowed but left it unrestricted. Clarification may be by anything that removes ambiguity, as we have mentioned many times, and the unrestricted is to be understood in light of the restricted.

And among the evidence supporting the view that expiation is required for the vow of heated argument (nadhr al-lajaj) is that when the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade himself honey, in the matter of his wives conspiring against him, Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [at-Tahrim: 1]. Then Allah said after that: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ [at-Tahrim: 2]. This indicates that the expiation of an oath is required. Likewise Ibn 'Abbas and others said that the expiation of an oath is required, according to the view that he forbade his slave-girl (to himself). The opinions concerning one who forbids his wife, or his slave-girl, or some other lawful thing are well known among the scholars. Forbidding a thing other than a wife or a slave-girl does not make it unlawful, by unanimous opinion. The disagreement concerns whether the expiation of an oath is required or not, and the apparent meaning of the verse is that it is required. Some scholars say that nothing is required in this, and this is the position of Malik and his companions. As for a man forbidding his wife or his slave-girl, there are more than thirteen well-known positions among the scholars on it, in their proper places. Among those who apply analogy (qiyas) to forbidding a wife is the requirement of the expiation of zihar (the pre-Islamic divorce formula of likening a wife to one's mother), because whoever says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother," is in the same position as one who says to her, "You are unlawful (to me)." Allah has stated in His Book that zihar has its expiation, which is prescribed in the surah "al-Mujadilah."

As for the vow of heated argument, we have already presented the view that it carries the expiation of an oath. What is meant by the vow of heated argument is a vow intended to restrain oneself from a matter, not to draw near to Allah.

Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: The general principle is that if one puts a vow in the form of an oath, by restraining himself or another from something, or by urging someone toward something, such as saying, "If you speak to Zayd, then it is incumbent upon me for Allah to perform Hajj, or to give my wealth in charity, or to fast a year," then this is an oath. Its ruling is that he has the choice between fulfilling what he swore to, in which case nothing is required of him, or breaking the oath, in which case he may choose between doing what he vowed and the expiation of an oath. It is called the vow of heated argument and of anger, and its fulfilment is not obligatory. Then he said: This is the view of 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, 'A'ishah, Hafsah, and Zaynab bint Abi Salamah, and it was held by 'Ata', Tawus, 'Ikrimah, al-Qasim, al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, 'Abd Allah ibn Shuraik, al-Shafi'i, al-'Anbari, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: There is nothing (required) in swearing by the Hajj. And from al-Sha'bi, al-Harith al-'Ukli, Hammad, and al-Hakam: There is nothing (required) in swearing by giving away one's wealth, because expiation is only required when one swears by Allah, out of reverence for the Name; this one did not swear by the Name of Allah, and what he named is not obligatory, because he did not put it in the form of an act of devotion, but imposed it as a kind of punishment, so it is not binding on him. Abu Hanifah and Malik said: He must fulfil his vow, because it is a vow, and so its fulfilment is obligatory, like a vow of righteousness. Something similar is also narrated from al-Sha'bi.

Our evidence is what 'Imran ibn Husayn narrated, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "There is no vow in anger, and its expiation is the expiation of an oath." Narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Jawzajani in his al-Mutarjim. And from 'A'ishah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears by walking (to Makkah), or by offering a sacrificial animal, or makes his wealth (dedicated) in the way of Allah, or for the poor, or for the door of the Ka'bah, its expiation is the expiation of an oath." (Ibn Qudamah) continued: And there is a second narration from Ahmad: that the expiation is specifically required, and fulfilling the vow does not suffice for him. This is also the view of some of al-Shafi'i's companions, because it is an oath. End of the relevant portion from al-Mughni.

Abu Dawud narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that two brothers from the Ansar had an inheritance between them. One of them asked the other for its division, and he said: "If you ask me again for the division, then all my wealth is for the door of the Ka'bah." 'Umar said to him: "The Ka'bah is independent of your wealth; make expiation for your oath, and speak to your brother. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'There is no oath upon you, nor any vow in disobedience to the Lord, nor in severing kinship, nor concerning what you do not possess.'" Narrated by Abu Dawud. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab's hearing from 'Umar is not established. Some have said this, and according to this it is a mursal (a report in which a Successor omits the Companion from the chain). Several scholars mentioned that he was born two years into the caliphate of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. From Ahmad there is something indicating Sa'id's hearing from 'Umar, and he said: "If we do not accept Sa'id from 'Umar, then who will be accepted?" The apparent position is that he did hear from 'Umar, as the author of Tahdhib al-Tahdhib introduced it with what indicates this. From Malik and others it is reported that he did not meet 'Umar. The hadith of Sa'id mentioned from 'Umar is either muttasil (continuous), or mursal from Sa'id's mursal reports, and we have already presented the scholars' statements on these.

Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar: But Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab did not hear from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, so it is munqati' (broken in its chain). Something similar is narrated from 'A'ishah: she was asked about a man who made his wealth (dedicated) to the door of the Ka'bah if he spoke to a relative. She said: "He makes expiation for the oath." Reported by Malik and al-Bayhaqi with a sahih chain, and Ibn al-Sakan authenticated it. End quote. The wording of Malik in al-Muwatta' is: 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Its expiation is what expiates the oath." There is nothing in al-Muwatta' indicating that this fatwa of hers concerns a vow of heated argument; rather what is in it is that she was asked about a man who said: "My wealth is at the rita (door) of the Ka'bah," and rita is pronounced with a kasra on the ra' (رِتاجِ), then a tā' with two dots above, followed by an alif and a jīm.

This is the substance of the argument of those who said that the vow of heated argument carries the expiation of an oath, and it is the closer view in my opinion for what we have mentioned, against those who said there is nothing required in it. As for the vow of disobedience, there is no disagreement (p-239) that it is unlawful, and that fulfilling it is forbidden. The disagreement concerns only whether expiation is required for it. The majority of scholars held that there is no expiation for it. Expiation for it is reported from Ahmad, al-Thawri, Ishaq, some Shafi'is, and some Hanafis. al-Tirmidhi mentioned the disagreement of the Companions on this. Those who said there is no expiation for it argued from the authentic hadiths that state: "There is no vow in disobedience." The negation of a vow of disobedience absolutely indicates the negation of its effect, and when the vow is negated from its root, its expiation is negated, because the dependent falls away when the principal falls away. And if we say that the form in his saying "There is no vow in disobedience" is a report used to mean a directive, namely a prohibition against vowing disobedience, then the prohibition entails invalidity, and when the vowed act is invalidated by the prohibition, its effect on the expiation is nullified along with it. They said: The original state is the freedom of the obligation from expiation. They also said: What supports this are the hadiths stating: "There is no vow except that by which the Face of Allah is sought." Al-Majd said in al-Muntaqa: Narrated by Ahmad and Abu Dawud. In a wording with Ahmad: "The vow is only that by which the Face of Allah is sought," and it is from the narration of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather. There are objections to its chain which we have omitted for brevity. Those who said there is expiation for a vow of disobedience argued with some hadiths reported on this:

Among them: what is reported from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no vow in disobedience, and its expiation is the expiation of an oath." Al-Majd said in al-Muntaqa: Narrated by the Five, and Ahmad and Ishaq argued with it. It is known that by "the Five" he means Imam Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan. The wording of Abu Dawud in this hadith is:

Ishaq ibn Ibrahim Abu Ma'mar narrated to us: 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Yunus, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah, from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no vow in disobedience, and its expiation is the expiation of an oath."

Ibn al-Sarh narrated to us, saying: Wahb narrated to us, from Yunus, from Ibn Shihab, with a similar meaning. Its chain. Abu Dawud said: I heard Ahmad ibn Shabbawayh say: Ibn al-Mubarak said: meaning in this hadith: "Abu Salamah narrated," which indicates that al-Zuhri did not hear it from Abu Salamah. Ahmad ibn Muhammad said: And the confirmation of this is what Ayyub narrated to us, meaning Ibn Sulayman. Abu Dawud said: I heard Ahmad ibn Hanbal say: "They have corrupted this hadith for us." It was said to him: "And is its corruption established for you? Did anyone narrate it other than Ibn Abi Uways?" He said: "Ayyub was more reliable than him," meaning Ayyub ibn Sulayman ibn Bilal, and Ayyub had narrated it.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Marwazi narrated to us: Ayyub ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Uways, from Sulayman ibn Bilal, from Ibn Abi 'Atiq and Musa ibn 'Uqbah, from Ibn Shihab, from Sulayman ibn Arqam, that Yahya ibn Abi Kathir informed him, from Abu Salamah, from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no vow in disobedience, and its expiation is the expiation of an oath." Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Marwazi said: The hadith is really the hadith of 'Ali ibn al-Mubarak, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from Muhammad ibn al-Zubayr, from his father, from 'Imran ibn Husayn, from the Prophet (ﷺ). He meant that Sulayman ibn Arqam erred in it, and al-Zuhri took it from him and sent it (without the intermediaries) from Abu Salamah, from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her. Abu Dawud said: Baqiyyah narrated from al-Awza'i, from Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Zubayr, with the chain of 'Ali ibn al-Mubarak, the same. End quote from Sunan Abi Dawud in its wording. In this there is considerable ill opinion of al-Zuhri, namely that he omitted two intermediaries from the chain of the hadith: Sulayman ibn Arqam and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, and sent it from Abu Salamah. Likewise al-Tirmidhi said after transmitting the hadith of 'A'ishah: It is not authentic, because al-Zuhri did not hear this hadith from Abu Salamah. What further strengthens this ill opinion about al-Zuhri is that Sulayman ibn Arqam, whom he omitted from the chain, is abandoned (matruk) and his hadith is not used as evidence, so he omitted an abandoned narrator. Narrating his hadith from one above him among the reliable transmitters is a form of tadlis al-taswiyah (concealment by leveling the chain), which is the worst and most objectionable kind of tadlis. There is no doubt that this type of tadlis is damaging to one who does it deliberately. As for what some have mentioned, that al-Thawri and al-A'mash used to practise this type of tadlis, it is answered that they only practised tadlis on one who was reliable in their estimation, even if he was weak in the estimation of others. And it is far-fetched that al-Zuhri would hold a good opinion of Sulayman ibn Arqam, given the agreement of the memorizers (huffaz) that he is not to be used as evidence.

The conclusion is that the requirement of expiation for a vow of disobedience has come with multiple hadiths, none of which is free from criticism, and some of them strengthen one another.

Al-Shawkani said: Al-Nawawi said in al-Rawdah: The hadith "There is no vow in disobedience, and its expiation is the expiation of an oath" is weak by the consensus of the hadith scholars. The Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) said: I say: al-Tahawi and Abu 'Ali ibn al-Sakan have authenticated it, so where is the consensus? End quote. We have omitted tracing all the hadiths reported on this and discussing them, for brevity. The more cautious position is that expiation is required, because the command takes precedence over permissibility, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence, for the sake of caution in clearing oneself of the obligation of the demand. Whoever gives expiation for a vow of disobedience has, by the agreement of all, been freed from the demand for it. Whoever does not give it remains liable for it according to the view of Ahmad and those mentioned with him.

* *

The third branch: Know that whoever vows some act of obedience that he is not able to perform, the fulfilment of it is not obligatory upon him, because of his inability to do it.

(p-241) There is disagreement about what is required of him concerning that which he is unable to do. So if, for example, he vows to perform Hajj or 'Umrah on foot, while he is unable to walk, then it is permissible for him to ride, because he is unable to walk. And if he is able to walk, then it is obligatory on him.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 29 (part 3 of 5):

In the case where he rides when he is unable to walk, the scholars differed over what he is obligated to do. Some said: "Nothing is required of him, because he is incapable, and Allah says: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. He has become unable to do what he vowed, and nothing is obligatory on him beyond what he vowed." Some said: "He must pay the expiation for an oath (kaffarat yamin)." Some said: "He must fast three days." Some said: "He must sacrifice a badanah (a camel)." Some said: "He must offer a hady (a sacrificial animal)."

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: The gist is that whoever vows to walk to the Sacred House of Allah is bound to fulfil his vow. This is the view of Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir, and we know of no dissent on it. This is because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Journeys are not to be undertaken except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, this my mosque, and al-Masjid al-Aqsa." Walking does not suffice him except in Hajj or 'Umrah. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i, and I know of no dissent on it, because the walking known in the Shari'ah is walking in Hajj or 'Umrah, so when the one who vows does not specify, his vow is understood in terms of the known Shari'i meaning. He is obliged to walk in it because of his vow. If he is unable to walk, he rides, and he must pay the expiation for an oath. A second narration from Ahmad says that he must offer a dam (a blood sacrifice), and this is also the view of al-Shafi'i. 'Ata' issued this ruling, on the basis of what Ibn 'Abbas transmitted: "The sister of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir vowed to walk to the Sacred House of Allah, so the Prophet ﷺ commanded her to ride and to offer a hady (sacrifice)." Abu Dawud narrated it, and it contains weakness. Also, he has neglected an obligation of the ihram, so a hady is required of him, like one who abandons ihram from the miqat (the prescribed station). From Ibn 'Umar and Ibn al-Zubayr it is reported that they said: "He performs Hajj the following year, and he rides for the distance he walked and walks for the distance he rode, and the like." Ibn 'Abbas said, adding: "And he offers a hady." From al-Hasan there is the same as the three views mentioned. From al-Nakha'i there are two narrations: one is like the view of Ibn 'Umar, and the second is like the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and this is the view of Malik. Abu Hanifah said: "He must offer a hady whether he is unable to walk or able to." The least hady is a sheep. Al-Shafi'i said: "When he is unable, no expiation is required of him in any case, except if the vow was to walk to the Sacred House of Allah, in which case is a hady required of him? On this there are two opinions." As for others, nothing is required of him when he is unable. End of the relevant part from *al-Mughni*.

Now, when you know the views of the scholars on what is required of one who vows something and is unable to do it, these are the evidences for their views. We have quoted them in summary through al-Majd's transmission in *al-Muntaqa*, because he gathered them in one place.

As for the one who said that he must pay the expiation for an oath, he relied on what Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Whoever vows a vow and does not name it, his expiation is the expiation for an oath. And whoever vows a vow he is unable to fulfil, his expiation is the expiation for an oath." End of quotation.

Al-Hafiz said in *Bulugh al-Maram*: Regarding the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: its isnad (chain of transmission) is sound, but the hadith memorisers (huffaz) preferred that it is stopped at Ibn 'Abbas (mawquf), as has already been indicated.

Among the evidences of the proponents of this view is what Kurayb narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A woman came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my sister vowed to perform Hajj on foot.' He said: 'Allah does not gain anything from the hardship of your sister. Let her go out riding, and let her pay the expiation for her oath.'" Ahmad and Abu Dawud narrated it. In *Nayl al-Awtar* he said: Abu Dawud and al-Mundhiri were silent about this hadith, and its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih. The apparent and obvious meaning is that what is meant by atonement for the oath is the well-known expiation for an oath. Al-Shawkani was right that the narrators of the hadith of Abu Dawud mentioned are the narrators of the Sahih, because Abu Dawud said: "Hajjaj ibn Abi Ya'qub narrated to us, Abu al-Nadr narrated to us, Shurayk narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, mawla of the family of Talhah, from Kurayb, from Ibn 'Abbas," up to the end of the hadith with its text. The first tabaqah (tier) of its isnad is Hajjaj ibn Abi Ya'qub, who is Hajjaj ibn al-Sha'ir, whom Muslim cited extensively in his Sahih. He is trustworthy (thiqah) and a memoriser (hafiz). The second tabaqah is Abu al-Nadr, who is Hashim ibn al-Qasim ibn Miqsam al-Laythi al-Baghdadi, of Khurasani origin, whose nickname is Qaysar, and he is trustworthy and firm, and all of them cited him. The third tabaqah is Shurayk, who is Ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Shurayk al-Nakha'i, Abu 'Abd Allah al-Kufi, the judge. al-Bukhari cited him in ta'liq (suspended narrations), and he is among the narrators of Muslim. The apparent sense of Ibn Hajar's words in *Tahdhib al-Tahdhib* is that Muslim only cited him in the supporting narrations (mutaba'at), and the statements of the scholars about him vary considerably between those who praised him and those who mentioned other things. The fourth tabaqah is Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, mawla of the family of Talhah, who is among the narrators of Muslim, and he is trustworthy. The fifth tabaqah is Kurayb ibn Abi Muslim al-Hashimi, mawla of Ibn 'Abbas, and it is well known that he is trustworthy, and all of them cited him.

This is the essence of the argument of the one who said that whoever vows a vow and is unable to fulfil it owes an expiation for an oath.

As for those who said that he must fast three days, they relied on what Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, may Allah be pleased with him: "His sister vowed to walk barefoot and without covering her head, so he asked the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: 'Allah does not gain anything from the hardship of your sister. Command her to cover her head, and let her ride, and let her fast three days.'" End of quotation through al-Majd's *al-Muntaqa*. Al-Shawkani said about this hadith: al-Tirmidhi graded it hasan, but its isnad contains 'Ubayd Allah ibn Zahr, about whom more than one of the imams has spoken. End of the relevant point from him.

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The apparent sense of Abu Dawud's words about the aforementioned 'Ubayd Allah ibn Zahr is that he is trustworthy in his view, because he mentioned his praise from Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Ansari, and he did not object to that with anything.

Abu Dawud said in this hadith: "Musaddad narrated to us, Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan narrated to us, who said: Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Ansari informed me, 'Ubayd Allah ibn Zahr informed me that Abu Sa'id informed him that 'Abd Allah ibn Malik informed him that 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir informed him: that he asked the Prophet ﷺ about a sister of his who vowed to perform Hajj barefoot and without covering her head, so he said: 'Command her to cover her head, and let her ride, and let her fast three days.'"

"Makhlad ibn Khalid narrated to us, 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ibn Jurayj narrated to us, who said: I wrote to Yahya ibn Sa'id, [saying]: 'Ubayd Allah ibn Zahr, mawla of Banu Damrah, informed me, and he was a most excellent man, that Abu Sa'id al-Ru'ayni informed him with the isnad of Yahya, and its meaning.'" End of quotation from the Sunan of Abu Dawud. So the writing of Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Ansari to Ibn Jurayj about Ibn Zahr, the aforementioned, and "he was a most excellent man," contains the greatest praise, because the phrase "he was an excellent man" indicates that he is among the distinguished men, and the superlative in this context refers only to trustworthiness and integrity, as you see. From this same category is the saying of the shepherd poet:

*So I gestured to Habtar with a subtle sign, and by Allah, what excellent eyes Habtar has, what a youth!*

Ibn Hajar said in *al-Taqrib* about the aforementioned Ibn Zahr: "Truthful, but he makes mistakes." The statements of the imams of hadith about him are many, among them those who praised him and among them those who criticised him.

As for the argument of the one who said that he must sacrifice a badanah, it is what 'Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "'Uqbah ibn 'Amir asked the Prophet ﷺ, and said: 'His sister vowed to walk to the House,' and he complained to him of her weakness. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Allah is not in need of your sister's vow. Let her ride, and let her offer a badanah.'" Ahmad and Abu Dawud narrated it. Al-Shawkani said about this hadith: Abu Dawud and al-Mundhiri were silent about it, and its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih. al-Hafiz said in *al-Talkhis*: its isnad is sound.

As for the argument of the one who said that he must offer a hady, it is what Abu Dawud narrated: "Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, Abu al-Walid narrated to us, Hammam narrated to us, from Qatadah, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: that the sister of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir vowed to walk to the House, so the Prophet ﷺ commanded her to ride and to offer a hady." Al-Shawkani said about this hadith: Abu Dawud and al-Mundhiri were silent about it, and the obligation of the aforementioned hady is narrated from Malik in *al-Muwatta'*, and he interpreted the hady as a camel (badanah), or a cow, or a sheep, if she does not find other than these.

This is the essence of the evidences of the views of the scholars regarding what is required of one who vows something and is unable to do it. The view of the hady and the view of the badanah can be reconciled, because the badanah is a hady, and the specific (khass) takes precedence over the general ('amm).

We have mentioned the statements of people about the chains of the hadiths related on this matter, and the most cautious view regarding one who is unable to walk, when he vowed it in Hajj, is the badanah, because it is the greatest of what has been said on this matter. It is not improbable that the badanah is obligatory, and that a hady, fasting and the expiation for an oath would also suffice, because none of the hadiths on this matter explicitly denies the sufficiency of anything else. The hadith on the obligation of the expiation for an oath does not explicitly state that the badanah is not sufficient, and the hadith on the hady does not explicitly state that fasting, for example, is not sufficient, and so on.

You have learned the views of the scholars on this matter, although none of the hadiths is free from some criticism. The apparent sense of the general texts is that nothing is required of him, because Allah says: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and He says: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16], and the Prophet ﷺ says: "When I command you with something, do of it what you are able." It is established in Sahih Muslim that when the Prophet ﷺ recited: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame on us if we forget or make mistakes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], Allah said: "I have done so." In another narration: "Yes." And within the ruling of this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with that which we have no ability to bear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286].

* *

The fourth branch: On the ruling on undertaking a vow, together with its definition linguistically and in the Shari'ah.

Know that the sound hadiths indicate that a vow is not commendable, and that it is forbidden, but if it occurs, fulfilling it is obligatory, provided it is an act of worship (qurbah), as has already been mentioned.

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: "Yahya ibn Salih narrated to us, Fulayh ibn Sulayman narrated to us, Sa'id ibn al-Harith narrated to us: that he heard Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, saying: 'Were they not forbidden from vows? The Prophet ﷺ said: "A vow does not bring forward anything or delay anything, and it is only by a vow that something is extracted from the miser."'" And in al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ forbade vows and said: 'It does not turn away anything, but by it something is extracted from the miser.'" And in a wording of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The son of Adam does not bring by a vow anything that I had not decreed, but the vow leads him to the decree that has been decreed for him; so Allah extracts by it from the miser, and he gives that which he had not been giving before." End of quotation from the Sahih of al-Bukhari. It is explicit in forbidding vows, and that initiating it is not among the acts of obedience that are encouraged.

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: "And Zuhayr ibn Harb and Ishaq ibn Ibrahim narrated to me. Ishaq said: 'He informed us', and Zuhayr said: 'Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from 'Abd Allah ibn Murrah, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ once took hold of [the matter] and forbade us from vows and said: 'It does not turn away anything, but by it something is extracted from the stingy.'"" In a wording of Muslim, from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "The vow does not bring forward anything or delay it, but by it something is extracted from the miser." In another wording of Muslim, from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ: "He forbade vows and said: 'It does not bring any good, but by it something is extracted from the miser.'"

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 29 (part 4 of 5):

Muslim also said in his Sahih: Qutaybah ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-'Aziz, meaning al-Darawardi, narrated to us, from al-'Ala', from his father, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not make vows, for a vow does not avail anything against divine decree; it is only by it that something is extracted from the miser." And in another wording of Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that "he forbade vowing and said: 'It does not turn back anything from the decree; it is only by it that something is extracted from the miser.'" And in another wording of Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A vow does not bring to the son of Adam anything that Allah had not decreed for him, but the vow coincides with the decree, and so by it something is extracted from the miser that the miser did not intend to give." End of quotation from the Sahih of Muslim.

What we have mentioned from the hadiths of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), from Ibn 'Umar and Abu Hurayrah, contains clear evidence for the prohibition of undertaking a vow, and that it brings no good, but only something is extracted by it from the miser. In the aforementioned hadiths there is a well-known difficulty, because the Qur'an has indicated praise for those who fulfil their vows, and that it is among the causes of entering Paradise, as in the saying of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor﴾ ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah will drink, making it gush forth in abundance﴾ ﴿They fulfil [their] vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread﴾ [al-Insan: 5-7], and the saying of the Most High: ﴿And whatever you spend or whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 270]. The Book and the Sunnah have also indicated the obligation of fulfilling a vow of obedience, as in the saying of the Most High in this verse with which we are concerned: ﴿Then let them end their state of disarray and fulfil their vows﴾ [al-Hajj: 29], and in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him." This is further supported by what is established in the Sahih concerning the censure of those who did not fulfil their vows.

(p-246) Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: Musaddad narrated to us, from Yahya, from Shu'bah: Abu Jamrah narrated to me, Zahdam ibn Mudarrib narrated to us, saying: I heard 'Imran ibn Husayn (may Allah be pleased with them both) narrate from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The best of you is my generation, then those who follow them" ["'Imran said: I do not know whether he mentioned two or three after his generation"], "then there will come a people who make vows but do not fulfil them, who betray and are not trusted, who bear witness but are not asked to testify, and in whom corpulence appears." End of quotation from the Sahih of al-Bukhari. This is very clear regarding the sin of those who do not fulfil their vows, and that they are like those who betray and are not trusted. This hadith was also recorded by Muslim in his Sahih, from 'Imran ibn Husayn. And al-Nawawi said in his commentary on this hadith of 'Imran: It contains the obligation of fulfilling a vow, and it is obligatory without disagreement, even though the initiation of a vow is forbidden, as has preceded in its chapter. End of the relevant point.

Because of this difficulty, the scholars differed regarding the ruling on undertaking a vow. The Malikis held that vowing recommended acts is permissible, except for one that is repeated constantly, such as fasting one day every week, which is disliked according to them. Most of the Shafi'is held that it is disliked, and some of them reported this from the explicit text of al-Shafi'i, citing the hadiths indicating its prohibition. Something similar has also been reported from the Malikis, and Ibn Daqiq al-'Id stated it definitively on their behalf. Ibn al-'Arabi pointed to the difference of opinion among them and to the Shafi'is' definitive view of disliking it. The Hanbalis definitively held that it is disliked, and among them there is a narration that it is makruh tahrim (disliked to the degree of prohibition), though some of them questioned its authenticity; and its being disliked is also reported from some of the Companions. End of quotation via Ibn Hajar's transmission in al-Fath. The author of al-Mughni definitively stated that the prohibition concerning it is a prohibition of disliking (karahah).

The author of these lines, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The apparent resolution to this difficulty, from which one should not深 depart, is that the vow of devotion is of two types.

The first: one that is conditional upon the attainment of a benefit, such as saying: "If Allah cures my sick person, then upon me for Allah is a vow of such-and-such," or "If Allah rescues me from such-and-such feared matter, then upon me for Allah is a vow of such-and-such," and similar.

The second: one that is not conditional upon a benefit to the one vowing, such as drawing near to Allah in pure devotion by vowing such-and-such from kinds of obedience. The prohibition applies only to the first type, because the vow in it was not made purely for drawing near to Allah, but on condition that the vower obtain a benefit; and that benefit which the vower seeks is the very thing concerning which the hadiths indicate that decree prevails over the vow, and that the vow does not turn back anything of the decree.

As for the second type, the pure vow of devotion without conditioning a benefit upon it, it is the one in which there is encouragement and praise for those who fulfil it, implying that it is among the good deeds. This distinction has been adopted by a group of the people of knowledge.

We said that one should not depart from it for two reasons:

The first: the hadiths reported on this matter themselves contain a clear indication pointing to it, namely what is repeated in them: that a vow does not turn back anything of the decree, nor advances anything, nor delays anything, and the like. So the statement that it does not turn back anything of the decree is a clear indication that the vower intended by the vow to bring about an immediate benefit or to avert an immediate harm. The Prophet (ﷺ) then explained that what Allah has decreed in this regard will certainly occur, and that the vow of the vower does not turn back anything Allah has written for him; but if Allah decrees what the vower wished by his vow, then by it something is extracted from the miser, namely the thing he vowed. This is very clear, as we have mentioned.

The second: reconciling the evidences is obligatory when it is possible, and this is a possible reconciliation among the evidences, clear, by which the evidences are harmonized and there is no contradiction between them. It is also supported by the fact that the ignorant vower may think that a vow can turn back from him what Allah has written for him. This is the apparent resolution of this difficulty, and many have said so. And Allah knows best.

Note:
If it is said: the conditional vow, such as saying "If Allah cures my sick person or rescues me from such-and-such, then for Allah upon me is a vow of such-and-such," you have stated that it is the one prohibited; and once it is established that it is prohibited, it is not of the category of devotion, so how can fulfilling a prohibited thing be obligatory?

The answer: the sound text indicates this, so it indicates the prohibition of it at the outset, as we mentioned in the hadiths that indicate this, and it indicates the obligation of fulfilling it after it has occurred. The Prophet's (ﷺ) saying "it is only by it that something is extracted from the miser" is an explicit text that the miser is bound to pay what he vowed to pay, and this is the very thing explicitly prohibited at the outset. There is nothing strange in this, for one and the same thing may have two aspects. The vowed act has one aspect for which it is prohibited from the outset, namely that the attainment of a benefit is made a condition for it; and it has another aspect in which it is an act of devotion, namely paying what was vowed in order to draw near to Allah and spending it in obedience to Allah. And Allah knows best.

Know that the vow (nadhr) in the lexicon means the obligation (nahb), which is what a person makes an obligatory debt upon himself to discharge, and from it is the saying of Labid:

Do you not ask a man what he is striving for: is it a debt to be discharged, or error and falsehood?

Its essence is that a person binds himself to something that was not binding upon him, making it obligatory upon himself; and in the technical usage of the Shari'ah it is the commitment of a responsible person to an act of devotion that was not obligatory upon him. Ibn al-Athir said in al-Nihayah: It is said: "I vowed (nadhartu), I vow (andhiru and anduru), a vow (nadhr)," when one makes obligatory upon oneself something voluntarily, of worship, charity, or otherwise. The mention of prohibiting it has been repeated in his hadiths, and this is an emphasis of its matter and a warning against neglecting it after making it obligatory. Had its meaning been the deterrence from it so that it is not done, that would nullify its ruling and drop the obligation to fulfil it, since by the prohibition it would become sinful, and so it would not be binding. Rather, the meaning of the hadith is that he informed them that this is a matter that brings them no benefit in the immediate and does not avert from them any harm nor turn back any decree. So he said: "Do not make vows," on the basis that you may obtain by the vow something Allah has not decreed for you, or turn away by it what the decree has passed upon you. So when you vow without believing this, then discharge it by fulfilment, for what you have vowed is binding upon you. End of the point from Ibn al-Athir's words. Others have also said this, but the apparent meaning of the hadiths does not support it.

So the apparent conclusion, the stronger view from which one should not depart, is what we have put forward of reconciliation. And Allah knows best.

Know that the Malikis' definition of vow in the Shari'ah, as "the commitment of a Muslim responsible person, even if angry, to the end," contains two points:

The first: the condition of Islam in the vow is open to question, because what a disbeliever vows of acts of obedience may be validly vowed, as evidenced by his performing it after he embraces Islam; and if it were void and not valid, it would have no effect after Islam.

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: 'Abd Allah narrated to us, 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Umar informed us, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, that 'Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, I vowed in the Jahiliyyah to perform i'tikaf for a night in the Masjid al-Haram." He said: "Fulfil your vow." End of quotation. So the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to 'Umar in this sound hadith, "Fulfil your vow," although he vowed it in the Jahiliyyah, is explicit in this, as you see; and there is no regard for what some of the Malikis and others have interpreted it to mean. As for the Malikis' definition of the vow, "even if angry," it is not hidden that the scholars differ concerning the vow of one who is angry: whether it is binding as he vowed, or whether it is of the nature of contentious oath-taking, in which an expiation for an oath is binding, as we have explained its ruling earlier.

The Fifth Branch: Know that the hadith indicates that whoever vows to slaughter an animal as an act of devotion to Allah at a specific place, there is no harm in fulfilling his vow by slaughtering at that specific place, provided that it was not previously the case that there was an idol worshipped there, or a festival of the festivals of the Jahiliyyah. Its implication is that if it was previously the case that there was an idol worshipped there, or a festival of the festivals of the Jahiliyyah, then slaughter there is not permissible.

Abu Dawud said in his Sunan: Dawud ibn Rashid narrated to us, Shu'ayb ibn Ishaq narrated to us, from al-Awza'i, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, who said: Abu Qilabah narrated to me, who said: Thabit ibn al-Dahhak narrated to me, who said: "A man vowed during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to slaughter camels at Buwanah. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I vowed to slaughter camels at Buwanah.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Was there in it an idol of the idols of the Jahiliyyah that was worshipped?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'Was there in it a festival of their festivals?' They said: 'No.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Fulfil your vow, for there is no fulfilment of a vow in disobedience, nor in what the son of Adam does not possess.'" End of quotation.

In it is clear indication that slaughtering in a place where an idol was worshipped or a festival of the Jahiliyyah was held is disobedience to Allah the Most High, and that it is not permissible in any circumstance. And Allah knows best. The chain of this hadith is sound.

* *

The Sixth Branch: Know that the sound hadiths indicate that whoever dies with an unfulfilled vow, it is to be fulfilled on his behalf. We will confine ourselves here to a few of them, for brevity, given their soundness and establishment.

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: Abu al-Yaman narrated to us, Shu'ayb informed us, from al-Zuhri, who said: 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah informed me that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas informed him: "Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah al-Ansari asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for a ruling concerning a vow that was upon his mother, and she died before fulfilling it, so he ruled that he should fulfil it on her behalf, and it thereafter became a sunnah." End of quotation from the Sahih of al-Bukhari.

We have already mentioned some of the hadiths indicating this concerning one who dies with an unfulfilled vow of Hajj, that it is to be fulfilled on his behalf, as previously clarified; and the hadiths on this subject are numerous and well known.

Note:

Know that Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas issued a ruling that a vowed prayer is to be performed on behalf of a deceased person who died without having performed what he vowed. Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "Chapter: Whoever dies with a vow owed upon him." Ibn 'Umar ordered a woman whose mother had vowed a prayer at Quba' to pray on her behalf. Ibn 'Abbas said something similar. End of quotation from al-Bukhari.

In the Muwatta', from Malik, from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr, from his paternal aunt, that she told him, from his grandmother, that she had vowed to walk to the Mosque of Quba', but she died without fulfilling it, so 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas ruled that her daughter should walk on her behalf. (p-250) Yahya said: I heard Malik say: No one walks on behalf of anyone else. End of quotation from the Muwatta'.

Al-Zurqani said in his commentary: Ibn al-Qasim said: Malik rejected the reports about walking to Quba', and he did not recognise walking except to Makkah specifically. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said, meaning: he did not recognise that walking is obligatory for one who swears an oath or makes a vow. As for the voluntary act, Malik has narrated, as passed earlier, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to come to Quba' riding and walking, and that coming to it is encouraged. End of quotation.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What the majority of scholars hold, and Ibn Battal related the consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) on it, is that no one prays on behalf of anyone else. As for fasting and Hajj on behalf of the deceased, we have already mentioned their legislated status. Although most scholars differ regarding fasting on behalf of the deceased, and Allah knows best. In the Muwatta', from Malik, after he mentioned the hadith: "Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him, and whoever vows to disobey Allah, let him not disobey Him," Yahya said: I heard Malik say: The meaning of the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "and whoever vows to disobey Allah, let him not disobey Him," is that a man vows to walk to Syria, or to Egypt, or to al-Rabadhah, or something similar that is not an act of obedience to Allah, [such as vowing] if he speaks to so-and-so or the like. There is nothing upon him in any of that if he speaks to him, or breaks what he swore to, because in these matters there is no obedience to Allah. Rather, what is fulfilled for Allah is that in which there is obedience to Him. End of quotation from the Muwatta'.

* *

Seventh branch: In my view, the most apparent position is that whoever vows all his wealth for Allah, to be spent in the way of Allah, it suffices for him to give a third and he is not obliged to give all of it. This is the view of Malik and his companions, Ahmad and his companions, and al-Zuhri. On this question the scholars have ten positions, the most apparent of which to us is what we have mentioned. Next in apparentness to us is the view of those who said: he must give all of it. This is narrated from al-Shafi'i and al-Nakha'i. There is another narration from Ahmad that he must pay an expiation for an oath (kaffarat yamin). From Rabi'ah: he must give charity equal to zakat. From Jabir ibn Zayd and Qatadah: if the wealth is large, meaning two thousand, he gives a tenth of it; if it is moderate, meaning one thousand, he gives a seventh of it; if it is small, meaning five hundred, he gives a fifth of it. From Abu Hanifah: he gives away all zakatable wealth. From him there are two narrations regarding other than that:

One: he gives it in charity.

The second: nothing is obligatory upon him.

From al-Nakha'i, al-Batti and al-Shafi'i: he gives away all his wealth. From al-Layth: if he is well-off, it is obligatory on him; if he is poor, he must pay an expiation for an oath. Ibn Wahb agreed with him and added: if he is of moderate means, he gives out an amount equal to the zakat on his wealth. This is also narrated from Abu Hanifah, and it is the view of Rabi'ah as mentioned earlier. From al-Sha'bi: nothing is obligatory at all. It has been said: everything is obligatory except in a vow of obstinacy (nadhr al-lajaj), in which case there is an expiation for an oath. From Sahnun: he must give out what does not harm him. From al-Thawri, al-Awza'i and a group: he must pay an expiation for an oath, without distinction.

Now that you know the views of the scholars on this question:

Know that most of them are not supported by evidence, and of those that are supported by evidence there are three positions:

The first: the one we previously stated is the most apparent to us, which is sufficing with a third.

The second: the obligation to give charity with all the wealth.

The third: the view of Sahnun, that he must give out what does not harm him.

As for sufficing with a third, which is closest to us, it may be supported by some authentic hadiths which forbid giving away all one's wealth and state that a third is much.

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: "Chapter: When one gives his wealth as a gift in the form of a vow and repentance." Ahmad ibn Salih narrated to us, Ibn Wahb narrated to us, Yunus informed me, from Ibn Shihab, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah informed me, from 'Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, who was the guide of Ka'b among his sons when he went blind, who said: I heard Ka'b ibn Malik say in his hadith: "And [He also turned in mercy] to the three who were left behind" [al-Tawbah: 118]. At the end of his hadith he said: "Part of my repentance is that I should withdraw from my wealth as a charity to Allah and His Messenger." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Keep some of your wealth for yourself, for it is better for you." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning of this authentic hadith is that Ka'b did not seek advice, but rather intended to strip himself of all his wealth as a vow and an act of repentance, as the chapter heading indicates. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded him to keep some of his wealth and declared explicitly that this was better for him. It has also come in some narrations that he explained that portion he should keep as two-thirds, and that he should give a third in charity. Ibn Hajar said in his commentary on this hadith, regarding the words "Keep some of your wealth for yourself, for it is better for you": Abu Dawud added, from Ahmad ibn Salih, with this same chain: "I said: I will keep my share which is at Khaybar." This is in the work of the author (al-Bukhari) through another route from Ibn Shihab. And in the narration of Ibn Ishaq from al-Zuhri with this same chain, in Abu Dawud: "Part of my repentance is that I should leave all my wealth for Allah and His Messenger as charity." He said: "No." I said: "Half of it?" He said: "No." I said: "A third of it?" He said: "Yes." I said: "Then I will keep my share at Khaybar." End of the relevant point from Fath al-Bari.

Know that Ibn Ishaq, in this hadith in Abu Dawud, explicitly stated that he heard it from al-Zuhri, so his tadlis (concealment of sources) is ruled out. Ibn Hajar then said: He also narrated through the route of Ibn 'Uyaynah, from al-Zuhri, from the son of Ka'b ibn Malik, from his father, that he said to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned the hadith, in which: "I will withdraw from all my wealth as a charity." He said: "A third suffices for you." And in the hadith of Abu Lubabah, in Ahmad and Abu Dawud, there is something similar. End of quotation.

I have seen the narrations explicitly stating that a third suffices for the whole of the wealth. The apparent meaning of the hadith is that the speaker was resolute and not seeking advice. Whoever among the scholars claims that he was seeking advice is contradicting the apparent wording, because the wording begins with a declarative sentence emphasised by the particle of emphasis, which is the kasra-vowelled inna in his words: "Part of my repentance is that I should withdraw from my wealth." A wording of this kind cannot be read as hesitation or seeking counsel, as you can see. So his words, peace be upon him, to Ka'b ibn Malik and Abu Lubabah, that a third suffices in place of giving charity with all the wealth, is the evidence we cited for our view that the closest position to us is sufficing with a third.

As for the view of the one who said that he must give charity with all of it, he cites the authentic hadith: "Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him." This indicates fulfilling his vow even if it encompasses all the wealth. However, the evidence for the previous position is more specific to the point of dispute, and the more specific takes precedence over the more general.

As for Sahnun's view, that he must give charity with what does not harm him, he cites the words of Allah, the Exalted: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: 'The surplus.'" [al-Baqarah: 219], the verse. Because al-'afw (the surplus), according to the more correct of the two interpretations, is what its spending does not harm the spender, and does not impoverish him by keeping what covers his necessary needs. This may return to the first view, because a third is part of the surplus whose spending does not impoverish him. So the first view is the most apparent, as we have mentioned. As for the remaining positions, I know of no evidence for them that is convincing from the Book or the Sunnah, and what some scholars have offered in justifying those positions does not appear sound to me. And Allah knows best.

* *

Eighth branch: Know that the authentic text has indicated that whoever vows to travel to a mosque in order to pray there, such as the Mosque of Basra or Kufa, or the like, is not obliged to travel to any of those mosques. He should perform the prayer he vowed in the place where he is. The authentic text mentioned is the hadith: "Journeys should not be undertaken except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), this mosque of mine, and the Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem)." According to the principles, nothing is excluded from this restriction which the Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly stated in this authentic hadith, except what is excluded by an authentic text to which one must refer, from the Book or the Sunnah. The more apparent view is that whoever vows to travel for a prayer in the Mosque of Ilya' (Jerusalem) and prays it in the Mosque of Makkah or Madinah has fulfilled it, because those two are superior to it.

Abu Dawud said: Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us, Hammad narrated to us, Habib al-Mu'allim informed us, from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: "A man stood up on the day of the Conquest and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I vowed that if Allah granted you Makkah, I would pray two rak'ahs in Bayt al-Maqdis.' He said: 'Pray here.' He repeated it to him; he said: 'Pray here.' He repeated it to him; he said: 'Then it is up to you.'" Abu Dawud said: Something similar has been narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, from the Prophet (ﷺ). In a wording of Abu Dawud, from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, from men among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), he (ﷺ) said: "By Him who sent Muhammad with the truth, if you had prayed here, it would have sufficed for you in place of a prayer in Bayt al-Maqdis." End of quotation. And Allah knows best.

We will suffice with what has been mentioned here of the issues of vows, given how much we have written in the verses of Surat al-Hajj of the legal rulings and the views of scholars on them. Vows are a topic mentioned in the books of furu' (derivative jurisprudence). Whoever wishes to comprehensively cover all its issues should consult the books of furu' of the four schools. We have here mentioned the essential and important points of its issues. And Allah knows best.

* *

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾.

Regarding the meaning of "ancient" (al-'atiq) here, the scholars have three views:

The first: that it means the old, because it is the oldest place of worship.

The second: that Allah freed it from tyrants (al-jababirah).

The third: that the meaning of freedom (al-'itq) in it is nobility (karam). The Arabs call the old 'atiq and 'ati, and from this is the saying of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

"Like musk you mix it with rainwater or with an old wine, blood-red of a slaughtered beast, pure."

Because what he means by 'ati is old wine that has remained in its jar for a long time. They also call the noble 'itq, and from this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

"A she-camel with a prominent hump, for one who sees her there is clear 'itq, and in her cheeks there is smoothness."

So his words, "clear 'itq," mean clear nobility. From this is the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

"The 'itq of horses is made clear in their neighing,"

meaning their nobility. And:

"Freedom from tyrants is like freedom from slavery,"

and this is well known.

Knowing this, know that a verse of the Book of Allah has indicated that the 'atiq in the verse (p-254) means the first, ancient one, and it is His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96], the verse. Although both other meanings are true, the Qur'an has indicated what we have mentioned, and the best way to interpret the Qur'an is by the Qur'an.

Two admonitions:

The first: this noble verse indicates the obligation of the Tawaf al-Ifadah (the circumambulation of return), and that Hajj is not valid without it.

The second: this verse also indicates the obligation of circumambulating from behind the Hijr, which has a short wall on the north side of the House, because its origin is from the House, so it is included in the name "the Ancient House," as its explanation has already been given.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the cattle have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you﴾. He did not specify here what is recited to them, the exception from the lawfulness of the cattle. However, He clarified it in His saying in Surat al-An'am: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is impure, or a deviant offering over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. This that we have mentioned is the correct view. As for what a number of the people of tafsir (exegesis) have said, that the verse which clarified the generality (ijmal, i.e. a general statement needing specification) in His saying here, ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ [22], is His saying in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that over which other than Allah has been invoked, the strangled, the beaten to death﴾, and so on [al-Ma'idah: 3], then this is an error. This is because al-Ma'idah is among the last of what was revealed of the Qur'an, whereas this verse of al-Hajj was revealed long before the revelation of al-Ma'idah. Therefore it is not valid to refer the clarification, in His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾, to that verse. Rather, the one that clarifies that generality is the verse of al-An'am which we have mentioned, because it was revealed in Makkah. So it is valid for it to be the clarifier of the verse of al-Hajj mentioned, as more than one scholar has pointed out.

As for His saying in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1], its clarification is valid by His saying in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion and blood﴾, and so on [al-Ma'idah: 3], as we explained at the beginning of al-Ma'idah. And Allah knows best.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So shun the impurity of the idols﴾. The "min" (from) in this verse is explanatory (bayaniyyah).

The meaning: shun the impurity which is the idols, that is, (p-255) their worship. And "rijs" (impurity) is filth which souls loathe. In this noble verse is the command to avoid the worship of idols, and included in its ruling and meaning is the worship of every object of worship other than Allah, whoever it may be. This command to avoid the worship of other than Allah mentioned here has been explained in verses such as His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying]: Worship Allah and avoid al-Taghut (every false object of worship)﴾ [al-Nahl: 36]. And He, exalted is He, made clear that this is a condition for the validity of one's faith in Allah, in His saying: ﴿So whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut and believes in Allah has grasped the most reliable handhold﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256]. Allah praised those who avoid the worship of al-Taghut and turn in repentance to Allah, and He made clear that for them is good news, which is what gladdens them with their Lord, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who avoid al-Taghut from worshipping it and turn back to Allah – for them is good news﴾ [al-Zumar: 17]. Ibrahim also asked his Lord to grant him the avoidance of the worship of al-Taghut, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35]. And idols enter into al-Taghut by primary inclusion.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And avoid the word of falsehood, being people of pure faith (hunafa') devoted to Allah, not associating anything with Him﴾. In this noble verse He commanded the avoidance of the word of falsehood (qawl al-zur), which is lying and falsehood, such as their saying that Allah prohibited the bahirah and the sa'ibah, and similar things, and their claim that He has children and partners. Every saying that deviates from the truth is zur (falsehood), because the root of the word zur is from izwirar, meaning inclination and crookedness, as we explained in the discussion of His saying: ﴿...inclining away from their cave on the right...﴾ [al-Kahf: 17].

Know that we have already mentioned, in the introduction to this blessed book, that among the types of clarification it contains is that a general term is mentioned, then in some places it is explicitly stated that some individual members of that general term are included in it. Examples of this have preceded, and some of its examples will come in the verses close to this surah of al-Hajj.

Knowing this, understand that here He said: ﴿And avoid the word of falsehood﴾ in a general form, then He clarified in some places some individual instances of the forbidden word of falsehood, such as His saying, exalted is He, concerning the disbelievers who denied him (ﷺ): ﴿And those who disbelieve say: This is nothing but a lie which he has fabricated, and other people have helped him with it. Indeed, they have produced injustice and falsehood﴾ [al-Furqan: 4]. So He explicitly stated that their saying is of injustice and falsehood. And He said concerning those who make their wives unlawful by zihar, when one of them says to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother": ﴿And indeed, they say an objectionable word and falsehood﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 2]. So He explicitly stated that their saying is objectionable and falsehood. It has been established in the Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Bakrah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins?" We said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Associating partners with Allah, and disobedience to one's parents." He was reclining, then he sat up and said: "Beware, and the word of falsehood. Beware, and the testimony of falsehood." He kept repeating it until we said: "I wish he would be silent." End quote. Here He has combined the word of falsehood and associating partners with Him, exalted is He, in His saying: ﴿And avoid the word of falsehood﴾, ﴿being people of pure faith devoted to Allah, not associating anything with Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 30–31]. Just as He combined the two here, He also combined them in other places, such as His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden immoral deeds, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, sin, unjust transgression, associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah that which you do not know﴾ [al-A'raf: 33]. This is because His saying ﴿and saying about Allah that which you do not know﴾ is the word of falsehood. And it came accompanied by His saying ﴿and associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority﴾. This indicates the greatness of the word of falsehood, because associating partners with Allah may enter into the word of falsehood, such as their claim of partners and children for Allah, and such as their denial of him (ﷺ). All of that falsehood contains the greatest disbelief and association of partners with Allah. We seek refuge in Allah from every evil.

As for the meaning of hunafa': we have mentioned it repeatedly before, together with some Arabic evidence, so there is no need to repeat it here.

The Most High said: ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind carried him off to a distant place.﴾ In this noble verse, the Most High explains that whoever associates a partner with Allah, meaning he dies without repenting of that, has fallen into a destruction from which there is no escape in any way and no salvation with it in any condition. This is because He likened him to one who fell (*kharra*), that is, dropped from the sky to the earth, so that his joints were torn apart, and the birds began snatching at them, and the wind carried them and cast them into a *sahīq* (distant) place, that is, a far-off location, because of the violence of its blowing with his torn joints. Whoever has this description has no hope of escape and no expectation of salvation, so he is certainly destroyed. For one who falls from the sky to the earth does not ordinarily reach the earth except with his joints torn apart. When the birds snatch his limbs and they are scattered in their crops, or the wind throws him in a distant place, this is a certain destruction from which there is no escape. What this noble verse contains regarding the destruction of one who associates others with Allah, and that no escape is hoped for him, is clarified in other places, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah, Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 72], and His saying: ﴿They said, "Indeed, Allah has forbidden them both to the disbelievers"﴾ [al-A'raf: 50], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [an-Nisa': 48], in both places in Surat an-Nisa'. *Al-khatf* means taking swiftly, and *al-sahīq* means distant. From it is His saying: ﴿So away with the companions of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 11], that is, far away with them.

Other verses show that the place of this destruction, from which there is no escape in any condition, applies only to one who dies upon that association and does not repent of it before the arrival of death. As for one who repents of his shirk before the arrival of death, Allah forgives him, because Islam erases what came before it.

The verses indicating this are numerous, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, what has passed will be forgiven for them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38].

• His saying: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right … except one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds; for those, Allah will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Furqan: 68–70].

• His saying concerning: ﴿those who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73], ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 74].

• His saying: ﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving toward whoever repents, believes, and does righteous deeds﴾ to the end of the verse [Ta-Ha: 82].

And besides that, there are other verses. As for one whose repentance from his shirk occurs at the arrival of death, it does not benefit him.

This is indicated by verses of the Book of Allah, such as the saying of the Most High: ﴿And repentance is not for those who keep committing evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ [an-Nisa': 18]. The verse indicates equating death upon disbelief with repentance from it at the arrival of death. And His saying: ﴿So when they saw Our punishment, they said, "We believe in Allah alone and reject what we used to associate with Him." But their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 84–85]. And His saying about Pharaoh: ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe that there is no deity except the One in whom the Children of Israel have believed, and I am of the Muslims." "Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters"﴾ [Yunus: 90–91].

Nafi' read this word as ﴿fa-takhatafahu﴾ with a fatha on the *kha'* and a shadda on the *ta'*, its original form being *fa-tatakhatafahu* (with two *ta'*s), one of which was dropped. The rest of the seven readers read ﴿fa-takhtafahu﴾ with a sukun on the *kha'* and a light *ta'*, the present tense of *khatifahu* (with a kasra).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 32:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That [is so]. And whoever honors the symbols of Allah – indeed, it is from the piety of hearts﴾.
