We have mentioned shortly before that we mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book that among the types of clarification (bayan) it contains is that a general term (lafz 'amm) is mentioned, and then in some places it is explicitly stated that some individual members of that general term are included in it, so that individual is definitively included and cannot be excluded by a specifier (mukhassis). We promised to mention some examples of this in these verses, and our intention by this is this noble verse, because His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That [is so]. And whoever honors the symbols of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 32] is general over all the symbols of Allah. Allah, may He be exalted, has explicitly stated that the camels (al-budn) are an individual member (p-258) of this generality, definitively included in it, in His saying: ﴿And the camels – We have made them for you among the symbols of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]. Therefore, the honoring of camels, fattening them and choosing them well enters into the verse, as we previously cited from al-Bukhari: that they used to fatten the sacrificial animals, and they considered that to be honoring the symbols of Allah. We have also previously mentioned that Allah explicitly stated that al-Safa and al-Marwa are included in this generality by His saying: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158], and that the honoring of them mentioned in this verse indicates not neglecting the sa'y (running) between al-Safa and al-Marwa, as was previously explained in the discussion of the sa'y. His saying in this verse, "that," has three grammatical possibilities (wujuh min al-i'rab).

The first: that it is in a position of nominative (raf') as the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate (khabar) omitted, i.e., "that is the ruling and command of Allah."

The second: that it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, i.e., "the obligatory is that" or "the required is that."

The third: that it is in a position of accusative (nasb) by an omitted verb, i.e., "follow that" or "comply with that." Similar to this demonstrative usage in Arabic speech is the saying of Zuhayr:

"This, but he is not like one who, in his arrangement, is among the generous when a speaker speaks."

This was said by al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan. As for the feminine pronoun in His saying: ﴿indeed, it is from the piety of hearts﴾, al-Qurtubi said: it refers to the act implied by the speech. Then he said: It was also said that it refers back to the symbols, by omitting a modifier (mudaf), i.e., "indeed, the honoring of them," meaning of the symbols; the modifier was omitted because the context indicates it, so the pronoun returned to the symbols. End of quote. And al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: ﴿indeed, it is from the piety of hearts﴾, i.e., indeed, honoring them is from the actions of those possessing piety of hearts; these modifiers were omitted, and the meaning cannot be sound except by estimating them, because there must be a returning pronoun from the conditional (jaza') to "man" (min) to link it. End of his words.

The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 22, verse 33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And give good tidings to the humble (al-mukhbitin)﴾ ﴿Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and the patient over what befalls them﴾. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to give good tidings to the humble, that is, those who are humble before Allah and at peace, whose attribute is that when they hear the mention of Allah, their hearts tremble, that is, they fear Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and to give good tidings to the patient over the harm that befalls them. The object of the good tidings is omitted because the context indicates it, meaning: give them good tidings of Allah's reward and His Garden. He has explained in another place that those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned are truly the believers, and their being truly believers makes them worthy of the good tidings mentioned here (p-259). This is in His saying: ﴿The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾ [al-Anfal: 2], and so on. In another place He commanded him to give good tidings to the patient over what befalls them, along with an explanation of some of what they are given good tidings of. This is in His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ ﴿Who, when a calamity afflicts them, say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return"﴾ ﴿Those are the ones upon whom are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and those are the rightly guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155–157].

Know that the trembling of hearts at the mention of Allah, that is, their fear of Allah when they hear His mention, does not contradict what He, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned, that the hearts of the believers find rest in the remembrance of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28]. The way to reconcile praising them for trembling, which is fear, when He is mentioned, with praising them for being at rest through His remembrance, while fear and rest are contrary, is what we have clarified in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book). It is that the rest through the remembrance of Allah comes through the expansion of the breast by knowledge of monotheism and the truthfulness of what the Messenger ﷺ brought. Their rest in this is strong, because doubts and confusions have not reached it. The trembling at the mention of Allah, Exalted, occurs out of fear of swerving from guidance and of their deeds not being accepted, as He, Exalted, said of those firm in knowledge: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8]. He, Exalted, also said: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful, because they will return to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60]. He, Exalted, also said: ﴿The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. For this reason, the Prophet ﷺ used to say in his supplication: "O Turner of the hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion."

﴿So eat from them and feed the contented one and the beggar.﴾ We have already noted that God commanded eating from the livestock (*bahimat al-an'am*), namely camels, cattle, and sheep and goats of their eight kinds. He commanded feeding the wretched poor from them, and He commanded eating from the *budn* (sacrificial camels, singular *badanah*) and feeding the contented one and the beggar from them. Whatever is a camel is, without disagreement, one of the *budn*.

The scholars differed over the cow: whether it is a *badanah*. We have already cited the sound hadith that the cow is among the *budn*, and we have also cited what indicates that it is not a *badanah*. The more evident of the two views is that it is among the *budn*.

The scholars gave several closely related interpretations of "the contented one" (*al-qani'*) and "the beggar" (*al-mu'tarr*). The most evident of these, in my view, is that *al-qani'* is the one who is greedy, who asks to be given some of the meat. From this is the verse of al-Shammakh:

*Wealth sets right the man's condition, enriching his poverty,*
*and it is more chaste than the begging of the contented.*

That is, more chaste than asking people and being greedy toward them. And *al-mu'tarr* is the one who comes to them, presenting himself for giving without asking or requesting. God knows best. We have already set out the ruling on eating from the types of gifts and sacrifices, and the statements of the people of knowledge on that, in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary.

* *

﴿Thus We have subjected them to you that you may be grateful.﴾ The word *kadhalika* is an adjectival modifier of a verbal noun: that is, the *budn* subjected to you with a subjection like that, the subjection you witness. We made them tractable for you and made them submissive to you, so that you do with them what you wish: slaughtering, riding, milking, and other benefits. Had God not made them tractable for you, you would not have been able to control them, because they are stronger than you. Do you not see that a camel, when it becomes wild, its owner cannot control it and cannot benefit from it?

As for His words here, ﴿that you may be grateful﴾: we have already stated several times that *la'alla* (perhaps) occurs in the Qur'an with several meanings, the two closest of which are these:

The first: it retains its original meaning, which is expectation and anticipation. On this view, the intended reference is specifically to the creatures, because they are the ones from whom gratitude for blessings is hoped for, without certainty, that they will be thankful for them or not deny them, since they do not know what matters will come to. This meaning does not apply to God, exalted is He, because He knows what will occur, so it is not permissible concerning Him, exalted and majestic is He, to use the sense of hoping and anticipating, in order to declare Him free of that, given the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of what the unseen will reveal. God said to Moses and Aaron: ﴿Speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:44]. That is, according to your hope and expectation that he will be reminded or will fear, even though God, in His eternal prior knowledge, knows that Pharaoh will not be reminded and will not fear. So the meaning of *la'alla* is relative to the creatures, not to the Creator, exalted and majestic is He.

The second meaning: some of the scholars said that every *la'alla* in the Qur'an denotes causation (*ta'lil*), except the one in Surat ash-Shu'ara: ﴿And you take for yourselves fortresses, perhaps you will abide forever﴾ [ash-Shu'ara 26:129]. He said that it there means "as if you will abide forever." The use of the word *la'alla* to express causation is well known in the speech of the Arabs, and we have explained it clearly several times. Among its Arabic witnesses we have already cited the poet's words:

*You said to us: "Cease the wars, so that we may cease,"*
*and you pledged to us every pledge.*

That is, "cease the wars in order that we may cease."

Now, when you know that in this noble verse God makes clear that His subjecting the livestock to the children of Adam is one of His blessings, which requires gratitude, as His words show: ﴿perhaps you will be grateful﴾.

Understand, then, that He explained this in other places, such as His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We created for them, from what Our hands have made, livestock of which they are the owners? And We have subjected them to them, so some of them they ride and some of them they eat. And for them in them are benefits and drinks; will they not then be grateful?﴾ [al-Hajj 22:36 / Ya-Sin 36:71–73, as cited]. His words in the verse of Ya-Sin, ﴿will they not be grateful?﴾, are like His words in the verse of al-Hajj, ﴿perhaps you will be grateful﴾. This meaning is also alluded to in His statement shortly after: ﴿Thus He has subjected them to you that you may glorify God for having guided you﴾ [al-Hajj 22:37]. We have already set out the meaning of the servant's gratitude to his Lord and the Lord's gratitude to His servant several times, in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary. And *at-taskhir* (subjugation) means making tractable.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed﴾. In this noble verse, He, glorified and exalted, makes clear that He repels evil from His servants who have believed in Him with true faith, and suffices them against the evil of the wicked. He has alluded to this meaning in other places,

• such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah – then He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 3], to the end of the verse,

• and His saying: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ [al-Zumar: 36],

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands and disgrace them and give you victory over them and heal the breasts of a believing people. And He will remove the rage of their hearts﴾ [al-Tawbah: 14–15],

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 51], to the end of the verse,

• and His saying: ﴿And it was incumbent upon Us to help the believers﴾ [al-Rum: 47],

• and His saying: ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers – they will be the victorious﴾ [al-Saffat: 173],

and other verses besides these. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited this letter as: ﴿Indeed, Allah defends (yudafi'u) those who have believed﴾, with a fatha on the yā' and the fā' with a silent dāl between them, the imperfect of the unaugmented verb dafa'a (to repel). According to this reading, the object is omitted, meaning: He repels from those who have believed the evil and harm, because faith in Allah is the greatest cause of repelling what is disliked. The rest of the readers recited yudafi'u with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatha on the dāl followed by an alif, and a kasra on the fā', the imperfect of the augmented verb dafa'a, which has an alif between the fā' and the ʿayn on the pattern of fā'il. In the reading of the majority there is a well-known difficulty: that the form of mufā'ala, by its Arabic convention, requires the sharing of two agents in the verbal noun, whereas Allah, glorified and exalted, repels whatever He wills without there being any opponent who repels anything.

The answer is what is known: that the form mufā'ala may come in the sense of the unaugmented, as in: jāwaztu al-makān (I passed the place), meaning jutuhu (I crossed it); 'āqabtu al-liṣṣ (I punished the thief); sāfartu (I travelled); ʿāfākā Allāh (may Allah grant you well-being), and similar. In all of these, fā'ala carries the sense of the unaugmented form. Accordingly, His saying yudafi'u means yadfa'u (He repels), as the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr indicates. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whoever recites yudafi'u, its meaning is: he exerts himself in repelling from them, just as one who contends with an opponent exerts himself in it, because the act of one who contends comes stronger and more emphatic." End of his words. In my view, it is not far-fetched that the reason for the mufā'ala is that the disbelievers employ every means within their power to harm and afflict the believers, while Allah, glorified and exalted, repels their scheming from the believers. His repelling, glorified and exalted is He, is thus against a great power whose people are in severe tyranny, seeking to inflict harm upon the believers. On this basis, the expression with mufā'ala in His saying yudafi'u is used, even though He, glorified and exalted, is able to destroy them and repel their evil from His believing servants. Among what clarifies this meaning we have alluded to is the verse of Ka'b ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him:

*They claimed that Sakhinah would overcome their Lord,*
*but the overcomer of the overcomers shall surely prevail.*

And Allah knows best. The object of yudafi'u is omitted. According to the view that it means yadfa'u, we have already mentioned its estimated object. According to what we have pointed to last, the estimated object is: yudafi'u 'anhum a'da'ahum wa khusumahum (He defends them against their enemies and adversaries), so He turns their scheming back upon their own necks.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ungrateful one﴾. In this noble verse He, glorified and exalted, has stated explicitly that He does not love every treacherous ungrateful one. Both khawwān (treacherous) and kafūr (ungrateful) are intensive forms, since fa'ʿāl with gemination and fa'ūl with a fatha on the fā' are among the forms of intensification. It is established in the science of Arabic grammar that negating the intensity of an act does not entail negating the act itself. So if you say: Zayd is not a killer of men (laysa bi-qattālin li-l-rijāl), you have negated his intensity in killing them, and that does not entail that no killing at all has come from him to some of them; rather, he has not exaggerated in killing. On this well-known Arabic principle, the verse explicitly states that Allah does not love those who exaggerate in disbelief and those who exaggerate in treachery, and it does not address one who is characterized by treachery in general or disbelief in general without intensity. There is no doubt that Allah hates the treacherous person absolutely and the disbeliever absolutely, and He, glorified and exalted, has clarified this in some places. He said regarding the treacherous: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms. Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous﴾ [al-Anfal: 58], and He said regarding the disbeliever: ﴿Say, "Obey Allah and the Messenger." But if they turn away, then indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 32].

The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 22, verse 39:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged. And indeed, Allah is able to give them victory.﴾ The object of "أُذِنَ" (permission was given) is omitted in this noble verse; the meaning is: permission was given to them to fight, as indicated by His saying "يُقاتَلُونَ" (who are being fought). He, exalted is He, has clearly stated in this noble verse that permission was given to "those who are being fought," and they are the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions. His saying "يُقاتَلُونَ" also indicates that what is meant is those among them who are fit for fighting, not those who are not fit for it, such as the blind, the lame, the sick, the weak, and those unable to travel for jihad due to poverty, as evidenced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Nur: 61].

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger. There is no cause [for blame] against the good-doers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91].

And His saying: ﴿because they have been wronged.﴾ The "bi" (ب) in "بِأنَّهم" is causal (sababiyyah), and it is one of the particles of causation (ḥurūf al-ta'līl (particles of causation)), as established in the method of the explicit text (maslak al-nass al-ẓāhir) among the methods of determining the cause (ʿillah). This verse is the first verse revealed concerning jihad, as many scholars have said. It contains no rulings of jihad beyond the bare permission to them to engage in it. However, other verses have come indicating additional rulings beyond mere permission, so they make clear that it is not limited to permission, as is apparent from this verse. A group of the people of knowledge have said: indeed Allah, blessed and exalted, because of the greatness of His wisdom in legislation, when He wishes to legislate something burdensome upon souls, His legislation proceeds by gradual steps (tadrīj), because imposing it suddenly, all at once, without gradation, would entail great hardship upon those who are obligated by it. They said: among that is jihad, for it is a matter burdensome upon souls, because it exposes them to the causes of death, since fighting against a strong disbelieving enemy is ordinarily among the greatest causes of death, even though the term is fixed with Allah, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿And it is not for a soul to die except by the permission of Allah, a decree with a specified term﴾ [Al 'Imran: 145]. Allah, exalted is He, has explained the hardship of making jihad obligatory upon them:

- By His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were told, "Restrain your hands, establish prayer, and give zakat"? But when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a faction of them fear men as they fear Allah or with greater fear, and they say, "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You would delay us to a near term."﴾ [al-Nisa': 77]. Along with exposing souls to the greatest causes of death, it also requires the spending of wealth, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives﴾ [al-Saff: 11]. They said: since jihad involves this degree of hardship, and Allah wished to legislate it, He legislated it gradually, so He first permitted it without making it obligatory.

- By His saying: ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Hajj: 39]. Then, when their souls became accustomed to it because of the permission, He made it obligatory, saying: "fight those who fight you, but do not transgress" — [i.e., obligatory against those who fight them, not against those who do not fight them]

- By His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, and do not transgress﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Baqarah: 190]. This is a gradation from permission to a specific kind of obligation. Then, when their souls had become accustomed to its obligation in general, He made it obligatory upon them as a general, definitive obligation in verses of His Book:

- such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, and capture them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5].

- And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36].

- And His saying: ﴿You will fight them, or they will submit﴾ [al-Fath: 16].

- And other verses besides these.

Know that some people of knowledge have views on some of the verses we have mentioned other than what we have mentioned. However, this gradation we have mentioned is indicated by inductive study (istiqra') of the Qur'an in the legislation of burdensome rulings. A parallel to this is the drinking of wine, for abandoning it is burdensome for one accustomed to it. When Allah wished to prohibit wine, He prohibited it gradually: first He mentioned some of its harms, as in His saying: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, "In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. Then, when their souls became accustomed to the idea that wine has more sin than benefit, He prohibited it for them during the times of prayer, by His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 43]. After its revelation, they would drink it only at a time when intoxication would wear off before the time of prayer, that is, after the 'Isha' prayer and after the Fajr prayer, because between 'Isha' and Fajr the drunkard ordinarily sobers up, and likewise between Fajr and Dhuhr. This is a gradation from criticism of it to its prohibition at certain times. Then, when their souls became accustomed to its prohibition, He prohibited it for them as a general, definitive prohibition by His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, indeed wine, gambling, stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful﴾ up to His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90-91].

Likewise fasting: since abstaining from the desires of the private parts and the stomach was burdensome upon souls, and Allah, exalted is He, wished to legislate it, He legislated it gradually. He first gave a choice between fasting a day and feeding a needy person, by His saying: ﴿And for those who are able to fast, there is a ransom: the feeding of a needy person﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. Then, when souls had become accustomed to it in general, He made it obligatory too, as a general, definitive obligation, by His saying: ﴿So whoever witnesses the month among you, let him fast it﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Baqarah: 185]. Some people of knowledge said: the gradation in legislating fasting was in three stages, as with what came before it. They said: He first made obligatory on them a light fast that involved no hardship, which is the fasting of the day of 'Ashura' and three days of every month. Then, when He wished to make the fasting of Ramadan obligatory, He legislated it gradually through the two stages we have just mentioned. This is what groups of the people of knowledge have said, and it has a basis, and Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And indeed, Allah is able to give them victory﴾ points to two meanings.

The first: that it contains an indication of His promise to the Prophet and his Companions of victory over their enemies, as He said just before it: ﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed﴾ [al-Hajj: 38].

The second meaning: that Allah is able to grant the Muslims victory over the disbelievers without fighting, by virtue of His power to destroy them however He wills, and grant the Muslims victory over them by His destroying them. But He legislated jihad for wisdoms, among them: testing the sincere in his faith from the one who is not sincere in it; and among them: facilitating the attainment of the virtue of martyrdom in the way of Allah through the killing of disbelievers by the martyrs of the Muslims, for had it not been for that, no one would have attained the virtue of martyrdom in the way of Allah. As He, exalted is He, indicated the wisdom of testing the sincere in faith and others through jihad in verses of His Book:

- such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is so; and if Allah had willed, He would have taken vengeance upon them, but He would test some of you by means of others﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

- And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the evil from the good. And Allah would not reveal to you the unseen﴾ up to the end of the verse [Al 'Imran: 179].

- And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do you think that you will be left alone while Allah has not yet made evident those among you who strove and did not take other than Allah and His Messenger and the believers as intimate friends? And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ [al-Tawbah: 16].

- And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strove and made evident the patient?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 142].

- And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely test you until We make evident those who strive among you and the patient, and We test your reports﴾ [Muhammad: 31], and other verses besides these.

- And His saying, exalted is He, regarding the wisdom of the mentioned trial and the facilitation of martyrdom in His way: ﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the other people. And We alternate these days among the people so that Allah may know those who believe and take from among you martyrs. And Allah does not like the wrongdoers﴾ and ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe and destroy the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140-141].

This letter (حرف) was read by Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim as "أُذِنَ" with a damma on the hamzah and a kasra on the dhal, in the passive form (mabni lil-maf'ul). The rest read it with a fatha on the hamzah, in the active form (mabni lil-fa'il), meaning: Allah gave permission to those who are being fought. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hafs, from 'Asim, read "يُقاتَلُونَ" with a fatha on the ta', in the passive form. The rest read it with a kasra on the ta', in the active form.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Hajj.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged.﴾

This noble verse indicates that fighting the disbelievers is permitted, not obligatory. Yet verses have come indicating its obligation, such as His saying: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Tawbah: 5].

And His saying: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Tawbah: 36], and other verses besides these.

The answer is evident: He first gave permission for it without making it obligatory, then made it obligatory afterward, as was mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah. This is supported by what was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Zayd ibn Aslam, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and others, as Ibn Kathir and others transmitted from them, that the verse "Permission is given to those who are being fought" is the first verse revealed concerning jihad. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who have been expelled from their homes without right, only because they say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾. What clarifies this verse has already passed, from the verses in Surah "Bara'ah" (al-Tawbah), in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And they resent only that Allah and His Messenger enriched them from His bounty﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will surely support whoever supports Him. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Exalted in Might﴾. In this noble verse, Allah, majestic and exalted, makes clear that He has sworn to surely support whoever supports Him. It is well known that the support of Allah is nothing other than following what He has legislated, carrying out His commands, avoiding His prohibitions, supporting His messengers and their followers, supporting His religion, and fighting His enemies and subduing them, until His word, majestic and exalted, is the highest, and the word of His enemies is the lowest. Then Allah, majestic and exalted, described the attributes of those whom He promised His support, to distinguish them from others, saying (p-266), explaining who it is that He swore He would support, because they support Allah, majestic and exalted: ﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakah, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong﴾ [al-Hajj: 41], and the verse. What this noble verse indicates, that whoever supports Allah, Allah supports him, has come explained in other places,

such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, if you support Allah, He will support you and plant firmly your feet﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve, for them is destruction, and He will waste their deeds﴾ [Muhammad: 7-8].

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And already has Our word preceded to Our servants, the messengers﴾ ﴿Indeed, they would be the ones given victory﴾ ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers will be the predominant﴾ [al-Saffat: 171-173].

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has decreed: "Indeed I will prevail, I and My messengers"﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 21].

And His saying: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe among you and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession upon the earth﴾, the verse [al-Nur: 55], along with other verses. And in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land﴾, the verse [al-Hajj: 41], is evidence that there is no promise from Allah of victory except with the establishment of prayer, giving of zakah, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong. Those whom Allah establishes in the land, making for them the word and authority therein, yet who do not establish prayer, nor give zakah, nor enjoin what is right, nor forbid what is wrong, have no promise from Allah of victory, because they are not of His party, nor among His allies whom He promised victory. Rather, they are the party of Satan and his allies. If they sought victory from Allah on the basis that He had promised it to them, their likeness is that of the hired worker who refrains from doing the work for which he was hired, then asks for the wage. One whose condition is this has no intellect. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Strong and Exalted in Might﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]: al-'Aziz (the Exalted in Might) is the Overpowering, whom nothing overpowers, as we have mentioned many times with its Arabic evidences. And these verses indicate the validity of the caliphate of the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, because Allah gave them victory over their enemies, since they supported Him: they established prayer, gave zakah, enjoined what is right, and forbade what is wrong. He established them and made them successors in the land, as He said: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe among you and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession upon the earth﴾, the verse [al-Nur: 55].

The truth is that the verses mentioned include the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and every one who stood to support the religion of Allah in the most complete manner. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 45 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How many a town have We destroyed while it was committing wrong, so it lies in ruins upon its roofs, and [how many] a deserted well and a lofty palace.﴾ In this noble verse, Allah, exalted is He, makes clear that He destroyed many towns while they were wrongdoing, meaning because of that wrong, which is disbelief in Allah and denial of His messengers. As a result of the destruction and annihilation, their dwellings became collapsed and their wells became disused, none of their water being drawn, because their people who used to draw water from them had been destroyed. (p-270) This meaning which Allah mentions in this verse is explained clearly in many other verses, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how many a town that defied the command of its Lord and His messengers, so We called it to a severe account and punished it with a terrible punishment. So it tasted the consequence of its affair, and the outcome of its affair was loss. Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment.﴾ [At-Talaq: 8–10] And His saying: ﴿And such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.﴾ [Hud: 102]. It is established in the two Sahihs (Sahihayn, the two authentic collections of Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah gives respite to the wrongdoer, until when He seizes him, He does not release him." Then he (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.﴾ [Hud: 102], along with other verses.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿so it lies in ruins upon its roofs﴾ [Al-Hajj: 45], "al-'urush" means the roofs, and "al-khawiyah" means the fallen. From this is the saying of al-Khansa':

"Abu Hassan was a roof that collapsed, [a thing] built by time, far-reaching and shady."

The meaning is that the roofs fell, and then their walls fell upon them, according to the most apparent of the explanations. "Al-qasr al-mashid" means the palace plastered with "al-shid," with a kasra on the shin, which is gypsum (plaster). It was also said that "al-mashid" means the high and fortified, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you should be in towers well-built﴾ [An-Nisa': 78], meaning strong, lofty fortresses. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿and a deserted well﴾ is coordinated with "town," meaning: "How many a town have We destroyed, and how many a well have We left disused by destroying its people, and how many a palace have We emptied of its residents, and We destroyed them when they disbelieved and denied the messengers." In this verse and similar ones there is a warning to the disbelievers of Quraysh who denied him (ﷺ), and a caution to them lest there befall them what befell those towns of punishment when they denied their messengers.

* *

Notice
A question appears to the seeker of knowledge in this verse: His saying ﴿so it lies in ruins upon its roofs﴾ indicates the collapse of their dwellings and their falling down, while His saying ﴿and a lofty palace﴾ indicates that their buildings remained standing and built up.

My commentator (may Allah pardon him and forgive him) says: The apparent answer to this question, in my view, is that the palaces of the towns which Allah destroyed, at the time of the revelation of this verse, were partly collapsed, as indicated by His saying ﴿so it lies in ruins upon its roofs﴾, and partly still standing and intact in their construction, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and a lofty palace﴾. I have only favored this combination because the Qur'an indicates it, and the best of what the Qur'an is explained by is the Qur'an itself (p-271). This is in His saying, Majestic and Exalted, in Surah Hud: ﴿That is from the news of the towns which We relate to you; of them some are standing and some are reaped﴾ [Hud: 100]. He here clearly stated that of them there is one standing and of them there is one reaped down.

The most apparent of the opinions, and the one most consistent with the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, is that "the standing" is that which has not collapsed, and "the reaped" is that which has collapsed and whose rubble has scattered. A parallel from the speech of the Arabs is the saying:

"Among people, in the division of death, are like crops: some standing and some reaped."

There are other opinions regarding the meaning of "the standing" and "the reaped" besides what we have mentioned, but what we have mentioned is the most apparent of them. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned something from which another interpretation of the combination may be understood, namely that the meaning of His saying "khawiyah" is "khaliyah" (empty) of its people, from the saying "khawa al-makan" when it became empty of its people, and that the meaning of "ala 'urushiha" is that the buildings remain, meaning: it is empty of its people while its roofs remain standing upon its walls. But what we mentioned first is the correct view, if Allah the Exalted wills.

This noble verse and its like in the Qur'an indicate that the word "qaryah" (town) is applied at times to the buildings themselves and at times to their inhabitants who dwell in them. So the destruction in His saying "We destroyed it" and the wrongdoing in His saying ﴿while it was wrongdoing﴾ refer to its inhabitants who dwell in it, while His saying ﴿so it lies in ruins upon its roofs﴾ refers to the buildings, as He said in the verse: ﴿And ask the town in which we were﴾ [Yusuf: 82], and He said in another: ﴿until, when they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food﴾ [Al-Kahf: 77].

In our treatise entitled "Man' jawaz al-majaz fi al-manzil lil-ta'abbud wa al-i'jaz" (Prohibiting the permissibility of metaphor in the revealed text for worship and inimitability), we have explained that what the rhetoricians call "the metaphor of deletion" (majaz al-naqs) and "the metaphor of addition" (majaz al-ziyadah) is not actually metaphor, even according to the majority of those among the jurists of legal theory (usuliyyun) who hold that metaphor exists. We established the proof for this.

Ibn Kathir recited this letter as "wa ka'in" with an alif after the kaf, and after the alif a kasra-marked hamza, then a sakin nun. The rest read "wa ka'ayyin" with a fathah-marked hamza after the kaf, followed by a kasra-marked and shaddah-marked ya, then a sakin nun. The meaning of both readings is one, and they are two eloquent dialects and two authentic Sab'i (canonical seven) readings.

Abu 'Amr pauses on the ya, while the rest pause on the nun. Abu 'Amr read "ahlaktuha" with the first-person-speaker ta with a damma after the kaf, without an alif, while the rest read with a fathah-marked nun after the kaf and an alif after the nun. The intended meaning of the plural form, according to the reading of the majority, is glorification, as is clear. Warsh and al-Susi, and Bir (a reading transmitted from the one called Bir), replaced the hamza with ya, while the rest keep the sakin hamza.

* *

(p-272) Issue
Know that "ka'ayyin" has many dialects. The two most eloquent are the two we have mentioned. "Ka'ayyin" with a fathah on the hamza and a kasra-marked shaddah ya is more common in the speech of the Arabs, and it is the reading of the majority, as we have shown. "Ka'in" with the alif and a kasra-marked hamza is more common in the poetry of the Arabs, and none of the Seven read it except Ibn Kathir, as we have shown. The meaning of "ka'ayyin" is like the meaning of "kam" in the informative sense (kam al-khabariyyah), so it indicates informing about a large number. Its specification (tamyiz, the noun that clarifies it) has two states:

The first: that it is put in the genitive with "min" (from), and this is the language of the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿And how many a town﴾ [At-Talaq: 8], and His saying ﴿And how many a prophet﴾, the verse [Al 'Imran: 146], and ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth﴾, the verse [Yusuf: 105]. A parallel to this in the speech of the Arabs, in putting the specification of "ka'ayyin" in the genitive with "min," is the saying:

"And many a friend in the valleys, who would see me, if I were struck, would be struck himself."

The second state: that it is put in the accusative. From this is the saying:

"And many a favor and bounty of ours upon you, [given] of old, and you do not know what benefactor [it was]."

And the saying of another:

"Drive away despair with hope, for many a [one] afflicted, whose hardship was followed by ease after hardship."

In the Khulasah (the summary of Ibn Malik's grammar) he said:

"Like 'kam,' 'ka'ayyin,' and 'kadha,' and the specification of these two ends in the accusative, or join to it [the word] 'man tusib' (whoever is struck)."

As for interrogation with "ka'ayyin," it is rare, and only Ibn Malik, Ibn Qutayba and Ibn 'Usfur affirmed it. Ibn Malik argued for it with what is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, that he said to Ibn Mas'ud: "How many verses of Surah al-Ahzab do you recite?" He said: "Seventy-three." End of quotation.

It has been disputed whether "ka'ayyin" is simple (basitah) or compound (murakkabah). If it is compound, then it is composed of the kaf of comparison and "ayyin" with tanwin. Some said: because of its composition it is permissible to pause on it with the nun in the reading of the majority, since the tanwin, when it enters into the composition, resembles the original nun, and for this reason it is written with a nun in the Mushaf. The reading of Abu 'Amr pausing on the ya is based on considering the ruling of the tanwin in origin, which is to delete it in pausal form.

My commentator (may Allah pardon him and forgive him) says: What appears more correct to me is that "ka'ayyin" is simple, and that it is a word (p-273) which the Arabs coined to inform about a large number, like "kam." There is no proof requiring that one return to the claim that its origin is compound. Among the evidence that it is simple is the writing of its nun in script, since the original rule for the nun of tanwin is that it is not written. The claim that composition made it like an original nun is a bare claim without evidence. Abu Hayyan chose that it is not compound, and he argued for that by the Arabs' playing with it in multiple dialects, for there are five dialects, two of which we have already mentioned, and we showed that they are two Sab'i readings, since Ibn Kathir read with one and the majority read with the other. The third dialect is "ka’in" with a sakin hamza then a kasra ya; the fourth is "kay'in" with a sakin ya and a kasra hamza; the fifth is "ka'an" with a fathah hamza and a sakin nun. End of quotation. Abu Hayyan spoke truly that this play with the word's form into these dialects indicates that its origin is simple, not compound.

And Allah knows best.

Note: Concerning what many exegetes mention in explaining this noble verse, that the disused well and the lofty palace are well known, and that they are in Hadramawt, and that the palace overlooks the summit of a mountain that cannot be climbed in any way, and that the well at its base does not keep anything that falls into it, but the winds bring it back out; and what they also mention, that the well is "al-Rass," and that it was in Aden in Yemen, in Hadramawt, in a town called Hadur, and that four thousand of those who believed in Salih came down to it and were saved from the punishment, together with Salih; then Salih died, so the place was named Hadramawt, because when Salih was present there (hadarahu) he died; so they built Hadur and settled by this well, and appointed over them a man called al-'Alas ibn Julas ibn Suwayd, or Jalhas ibn Julas, who was of good conduct among them as their governor, and they made his vizier Sanjarib ibn Sawada. They remained for a long time and multiplied until they became numerous, and the well used to water the whole city and its surroundings, and all that was in it of animals, sheep, cattle and other things; for it had many pulleys set over it, and many men appointed to tend it, and many basins around it, which were filled for the people, basins for the animals, basins for the sheep, and basins for the cattle; and they had no water other than it. Their affairs reached the point where their king died, and they smeared his body with oil to prevent its decay; and that Satan entered into his body and claimed to them that he was the king, and that he had not died, but had only gone out of their sight to see what they were doing; and he ordered them to put a screen between them and the body. Satan used to speak to them from the king's body from behind the screen, lest they discover the truth that he was dead. He continued with them until they disbelieved in Allah, exalted is He. Then Allah sent to them a prophet named Handhalah ibn Safwan, to whom revelation came in sleep and not in waking. He informed them that Satan had misled them, and told them that their king had died, and forbade them from associating partners with Allah, admonished and advised them, and warned them of the punishment of their Lord. But they killed their prophet mentioned above in the marketplace, and threw him into a well. At that moment the punishment of Allah came upon them. They woke up and the well's water had dried up, and its rope had gone slack, so they all cried out together, and women and children wailed, until all of them died of thirst. And that this well was the disused well in this verse: all of this is not to be relied upon, because it belongs to the category of Isra'iliyyat (narrations of Israelite origin), and the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates otherwise. For His saying ﴿and how many a town﴾ [Al-Hajj: 48] means the information that a great number of towns were destroyed by Allah for their wrongdoing, that many of their wells remained disused with the destruction of their people, and that many of the lofty palaces remained after the destruction of their people, without them; because the specification of "ka'ayyin," although its wording is singular, its meaning includes a large number, as is known in its proper place.

Abu Hayyan said in "al-Bahr al-Muhit," citing Imam Abu al-Qasim al-Ansari, who said: "I saw the grave of Salih in al-Sham, in a town called Akka, so how could it be in Hadramawt? It is well known that the dwellings of the people of Salih, among whom they were destroyed, are famous, and the one traveling from Medina to al-Sham passes by them. We have already mentioned in Surat al-Hijr that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by them on his way to Tabuk during the Battle of Tabuk. It is far-fetched that Salih and those among his people who believed would traverse this long, distant stretch from the land of al-Hijr to Hadramawt without any call or necessity compelling them to do so, as you see. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted."

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth, so that they might have hearts with which to understand, or ears with which to hear?﴾ In this noble verse, Allah, majestic and exalted, makes clear that the disbelievers of Makkah, who denied our Prophet (ﷺ), ought to travel through the earth so that they would have hearts with which to understand, or ears with which to hear. For when they travel, they pass by the dwellings of the people of Salih, the dwellings of the people of Lut, and the dwellings of the people of Hud. They find their lands empty and their traces effaced, with none left of them, neither caller nor responder, because of their denial of their messengers and their disbelief in their Lord. Thus they perceive with their minds that their denial of their Prophet is not safe from bringing upon them the wrath of Allah like that which befell those who passed by their dwellings, now empty, whose people were overtaken by destruction. And they would have ears with which to hear what Allah related in His Book to His Prophet of the reports of those nations, and of the complete annihilation and destruction that befell them, so that they would beware lest there descend upon them what descended upon those.

The verses indicating this meaning are many, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them.﴾ [Muhammad: 10]. Then He made clear His threat to the disbelievers of Makkah by what He did to the past nations, in His saying: ﴿And for the disbelievers is the like of them.﴾ [Muhammad: 10]. And like His saying about the people of Lut: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning﴾ ﴿and at night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [as-Saffat: 137-138] (p-275) And like His saying about them: ﴿And indeed, it is on a road that remains﴾ and the verse continues [al-Hijr: 76]. And like His saying about the people of Lut and the people of Shu'ayb: ﴿The companions of the thicket﴾ [Qaf: 14] ﴿And indeed, they were on a clear highway [imam mubin]﴾ [al-Hijr: 79]. This is because the meaning of the two verses is that their dwellings are upon the road which they pass along, which is expressed by the words sabil (road) and imam (highway). Verses of this kind are many, and we have already presented sufficient examples of them in the surah of al-Ma'idah and elsewhere.

The verse indicates that the seat of reason is in the heart, and the seat of hearing is in the ear. Therefore, what the philosophers claim, that the seat of reason is the brain, is false, as we have clarified in another place. Likewise, the saying of one who claims that reason has no place at all in the human being, because it is merely temporal and not spatial, is in the utmost degree of falsehood and invalidity, as you see.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but it is hearts that are blinded within the breasts.﴾ We have already presented the verses that clarify the meaning of this verse in the surah of "Bani Isra'il", in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world] will be blind in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Isra': 72], together with some Arabic evidences, so that this suffices and there is no need to repeat it here.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but it is hearts that are blinded within the breasts.﴾

The apparent meaning of this verse is that eyes are not blinded. But other verses have come indicating the blindness of eyes, such as His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, so He has deafened them and blinded their eyes﴾ [Muhammad: 23], and His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾ [an-Nur: 61].

The answer is that the distinguishing between truth and falsehood, between the harmful and the beneficial, and between the ugly and the good, since all of it is by insights and not by eyes, the true blindness becomes the blindness of insight and not the blindness of eyes. Do you not see that the soundness of the two eyes is of no benefit when there is no reason, as is self-evident? And His saying: ﴿So He has deafened them and blinded their eyes﴾ means their insights, or it means He blinded their eyes from the truth even if they see other than it.

(p-345) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.﴾

This noble verse indicates that the measure of a day with Allah is a thousand years. Likewise His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it will ascend to Him in a day, the measure of which is a thousand years of what you count.﴾ [as-Sajdah: 5].

But another verse has come indicating otherwise, namely His saying, may He be exalted, in the surah of "Sa'ala Sa'il": ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day, the measure of which is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4], and the verse continues.

Know first that Abu 'Ubaydah narrated from Isma'il ibn Ibrahim, from Ayyub, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, that he attended both Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib when they were asked about these verses, and he did not know what to say about them, and he would say: "I do not know."

There are two ways of reconciling them:

The first is what Ibn Abi Hatim brought out through the chain of Simak, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: that the day of the thousand years in the surah of "al-Hajj" is one of the six days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth; the day of the thousand years in the surah of "as-Sajdah" is the measure of the travel of the affair and its ascent to Him, may He be exalted; and the day of the fifty thousand years is the Day of Resurrection.

The second way: that all of them refer to the Day of Resurrection, and the difference is with regard to the state of the believer and the disbeliever. This is indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So that Day will be a difficult day﴾ ﴿for the disbelievers, not easy﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 9-10]. The author of al-Itqan mentioned these two ways. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 47 (part 1 of 2):**

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will never fail His promise﴾. In this noble verse, Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, mentions that the disbelievers ask the Prophet (ﷺ) to hasten the punishment with which he threatens them, out of rebellion and obstinacy.

The verses that indicate this meaning are many in the Qur'an, such as:

• His saying: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share [of punishment] before the Day of Account"﴾ [Sad: 16]

• His saying: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, but indeed Hell encompasses the disbelievers﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 54]

• His saying: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, and were it not for a specified term, the punishment would have come upon them﴾ to the end of the verse [al-'Ankabut: 53].

We have explained the verses indicating this meaning in several places in this blessed book: in surah "al-An'am," in the discussion of His saying: ﴿What you ask to hasten is not with me﴾ [al-An'am: 57], and in Yunus, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Only now, when it has befallen, do you believe in it?﴾ [Yunus: 51], in addition to other places.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿and Allah will never fail His promise﴾, the apparent meaning is that the "promise" here is what He promised them of punishment, which they seek to hasten.

(p-276) The meaning is: He will certainly fulfil what He promised them of punishment. When the appointed time for it comes, as He said: ﴿Were it not for a specified term, the punishment would have come upon them, and it will surely come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 53]. And His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the Day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them, and there will befall them what they used to mock﴾ [Hud: 8], and His saying: ﴿Only now, when it has befallen, do you believe in it, though you used to seek to hasten it?﴾ [Yunus: 51]. From this you know that "promise" is used in the Qur'an for a promise of evil.

Among the verses clarifying this is His saying: ﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire, which Allah has promised those who disbelieved; and wretched is the destination"﴾ [al-Hajj: 72]. In this verse, concerning the Fire, He said "wa'adaha Allah" (Allah promised it), using the triliteral form whose verbal noun is "al-wa'd," and He did not say "awada-ha" (He threatened it). What is mentioned in this verse, that what He promised the disbelievers of punishment is certainly going to happen, and that He does not fail His promise in this, has been explained in other places:

• Like His saying in surah "Qaf": ﴿He said, "Do not dispute before Me, for I had already presented to you the warning. The word is not changed with Me"﴾ to the end of the verse [Qaf: 28]. The correct view is that the meaning of ﴿The word is not changed with Me﴾ is that what He threatened the disbelievers with of punishment is not altered by Him; rather, it will certainly occur,

• And His saying: ﴿Each one denied the messengers, so My warning came true﴾ [Qaf: 14], meaning: it became binding and established, so it is impossible for it not to occur in any way,

• And His saying: ﴿Indeed, each one denied the messengers, so My punishment became due﴾ [Sad: 14]. As we explained in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" (Removing the Illusion of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), in surah "al-An'am," in the discussion of His saying: ﴿He said, "The Fire is your residence, wherein you will abide eternally, except as Allah wills"﴾ to the end of the verse [al-An'am: 128]. We explained that what the disbelievers are threatened with is never failed in any way, as the mentioned verses indicate. As for what the sinful Muslims are threatened with, it is what may be not carried out, and He may pardon it, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 48].

From the verification we have mentioned, you know that "promise" is used for both good and evil, as we have shown. What has spread on the tongues of many people of tafsir (exegesis), that "promise" is used only for good, and that this is what Allah does not fail, while if what is promised is evil, it is a "warning" (wa'id) and a "threat" (i'ad), is not correct. They said: The Arabs regard going back on a promise as baseness, and going back on a threat as generosity. It is related from al-Asma'i that he said: "I was with Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', when 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd came to him and said, 'O Abu 'Amr, does Allah fail the appointment (al-mi'ad)?' He said, 'No.' So he cited a verse of warning. He said to him, 'Are you from the non-Arabs? The Arabs regard going back on a promise as baseness and going back on a threat as generosity. Have you not heard the poet's saying:'" (p-277)

> "The cousin and the neighbour do not fear my wrath, nor does one who threatens turn back from my might;
> For though I threaten him or promise him, I will fail my threat and fulfil my promise."

In this there is an objection from two aspects.

The first: what we have explained earlier, that "promise" in the Qur'an is applied to the threat of the Fire and punishment, as in His saying: ﴿The Fire, which Allah has promised those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Hajj: 72], and His saying: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will never fail His promise﴾ [al-Hajj: 47]. This is because the apparent meaning of the verse, from which it is not permissible to deviate, is that "Allah will never fail His promise" concerns the descent of the punishment with which they ask you to hasten, since it is linked to His saying: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 47]. So its connection to it is the apparent meaning.

The second: what we have shown, that what Allah threatens the disbelievers with cannot in any way be failed. The claim that it is permissible to fail it, because it is a threat, and because the Arabs regard going back on a threat as generosity, is refuted by two matters:

The first: it necessarily entails that no disbeliever would enter the Fire at all, since their threat of putting them into the Fire is something which they claimed that going back on is generosity, and there is no doubt that this is false.

The second: what we have mentioned of the verses indicating that Allah does not fail what He threatened the disbelievers with of punishment:

• Like His saying: ﴿He said, "Do not dispute before Me, for I had already presented to you the warning. The word is not changed with Me"﴾ to the end of the verse [Qaf: 28–29],

• And His saying concerning them: ﴿so My warning came true﴾ [Qaf: 14],

• And His saying concerning them: ﴿so My punishment became due﴾ [Sad: 14].

The meaning of "haqqa" is: it became binding and established, so there is no way for it to be negated in any way, as we have explained here and in other places.

* *

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾. In this noble verse, Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, has explained that a day with Him is like a thousand years of what His creation reckons. What He mentioned here, that a day with Him is like a thousand years, He alluded to in surah "al-Sajdah" with His saying: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day, the extent of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Sajdah: 5]. And in surah "al-Ma'arij" He mentioned that the extent of a day is fifty thousand years, in His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a Day the extent of which is fifty thousand years﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Ma'arij: 4]. So the verse of al-Hajj and the verse of al-Sajdah are in agreement, each confirming the other and matching it in meaning, while the verse of al-Ma'arij differs from their apparent meaning by being fifty times more. We have mentioned the way of reconciling these verses in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab," and we will mention it here, if Allah wills, in summary and brevity, adding to it some of what the need calls for. (p-278)

We have mentioned in summary: Abu 'Ubaydah narrated from Isma'il ibn Ibrahim, from Ayyub, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, that he was present with Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab when they were asked about these verses. He did not know what to say about them and said, "I do not know." Then we mentioned that there are two ways of reconciling them. The first: what Ibn Abi Hatim related through the chain of Simak, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the day of a thousand years in surah al-Hajj is one of the six days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth; the day of a thousand years in surah al-Sajdah is the measure of the affair's ascent and its rising to Him, the Exalted; and the day of fifty thousand years is the Day of Resurrection.

The second way: that all of them refer to the Day of Resurrection, and that the difference in the length of the day is due to the condition of the believer and the condition of the disbeliever, because the Day of Resurrection is lighter upon the believer than upon the disbeliever, as He said: ﴿So that Day will be a difficult day, for the disbelievers, not easy﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 9–10]. End of quote. Sahib al-Itqan (al-Suyuti, author of "al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an") mentioned these two ways.

We have also mentioned in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab," in surah "al-Furqan," in the discussion of His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day will be better in residence and finer in resting place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], the following in summary: that this verse of al-Furqan indicates that the reckoning will be concluded at midday, because al-maqil is the qaylulah (the midday rest), or its place, which is the rest at midday in the heat. Among those who said that the reckoning will be concluded at midday were Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Jubayr, based on the indication of this verse, as Ibn Kathir and others related from them.

In the tafsir of al-Jalalayn is the following text: "And from this is derived that the reckoning will be concluded at midday, as is related in a hadith, the end of which [is quoted], although He, the Exalted, mentioned that the extent of the Day of Resurrection is fifty thousand years in His saying: ﴿in a Day the extent of which is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4], and it is the Day of Resurrection without any disagreement about that."

The apparent answer is that the Day of Resurrection is prolonged for the disbelievers and shortened for the believers. This is indicated by His saying shortly after this: ﴿The dominion on that Day will be true, for the Most Merciful; and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Furqan: 26]. His specifying the difficulty of that day for the disbelievers indicates that the believers are not like that. And His saying: ﴿So that Day will be a difficult day, for the disbelievers, not easy﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 9–10] indicates, by the implication of its opposite, that it is easy for the believers and not difficult, as His saying indicates: ﴿Hastening toward the caller. The disbelievers will say, "This is a difficult day."﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]. (p-279)

And Ibn Jarir said: Yunus narrated to me, Ibn Wahb informed us, 'Amr ibn al-Harith informed us, that Sa'id al-Saww'af narrated to him that it had reached him that the Day of Resurrection will be shortened for the believers, until it will be like the time between the afternoon prayer and the sunset, and that they will roam in the meadows of Paradise until people are finished with judgment. This is His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day will be better in residence and finer in resting place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24]. Ibn Kathir related this from him in his tafsir. As for the view of one who explains "al-maqil" in the verse as "the abode and dwelling," like Qatadah, may Allah have mercy on him, there is then no indication in the verse for any of what we have mentioned. It is well known that whoever is in joy and blessing will find long time shortened greatly for him, unlike whoever is in humiliating punishment, afflictions and distress, for short time will become very long for him. This is a well-known matter, and it is common in the speech of the Arabs. In our aforementioned book we have mentioned some of the evidences indicating it, such as the words of Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, may Allah be pleased with him, lamenting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):

> "I stayed awake, so my night remained without end, and the night of one afflicted by calamity is long in it."

And the saying of another:

> "Their short [nights] with sorrows are long, and their long [nights] with joy are short."

And the saying of another:

> "My night and Laylah's night, sleep denied to me the difference between them in length; and length is good for me, if they were equal:
> My night gives the length generously whenever Laylah's night withholds length, and if she gives length, it withholds."

Similar to this is very abundant in the speech of the Arabs. Among the most witty of what has been said about it is what is related from Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah, that he said:

> "I do not ask Allah to change what she has done; she slept, while her eyes had kept mine awake.
> So the night is longest of all things when I miss her, and the night is shortest of all things when I meet her."

Some hadiths have been narrated indicating the apparent meaning of the verse of al-Hajj and the verse of al-Sajdah. We will mention here a portion of them through the transmission of Ibn Kathir in his tafsir of this verse from surah al-Hajj. Ibn Kathir said: Ibn Abi Hatim said: al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah narrated to us: 'Abdah ibn Sulayman narrated to me, from (p-280) Muhammad ibn 'Amr, from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The poor among the Muslims will enter Paradise before the rich by half a day, five hundred years." It was related also by al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i through the hadith of al-Thawri from Muhammad ibn 'Amr with the same wording, and al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan sahih."

Ibn Jarir also narrated it from Abu Hurayrah as a statement of his own (mawquf). He said: Ya'qub related to me: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us: Sa'id al-Jurayri related to us, from Abu Nadrah, from Sumayr ibn Nahar, who said: Abu Hurayrah said: "The poor among the Muslims will enter Paradise before the rich, by a span of half a day." I said: "And what is the measure of half a day?" He said: "Do you not recite the Qur'an?" I said: "Yes." He said: ﴿And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Hajj: 47].

Abu Dawud said at the end of the Book of Battles (Kitab al-Malahim) in his Sunan: Amr ibn 'Uthman related to us, Abu al-Mughirah related to us, Safwan related to me, from Shurayh ibn 'Ubayd, from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I truly hope that my Ummah will not fall short before its Lord, that He will delay them by half a day." It was said to Sa'd: "And how much is half a day?" He said: "Five hundred years."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Ahmad ibn Sinan related to us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi related to us, from Isra'il, from Simak, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Hajj: 47], that he said: "It is of the days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth." Ibn Jarir also narrated it from Ibn Bashshar, from Ibn al-Mahdi. This view was also held by Mujahid and 'Ikrimah. Ahmad ibn Hanbal stated it explicitly in his book Al-Radd 'ala al-Jahmiyyah. Mujahid also said: this verse is like His saying: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day, the measure of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Sajdah: 5]. End of quotation from Ibn Kathir, which is the point of relevance.

The narrations he cited may be reconciled with what we have mentioned, namely that the original day is like a thousand years, but for the believers it becomes shorter and lighter, until it is like half a day. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read this letter as (كَألْفِ سَنَةٍ مِمّا يَعُدُّونَ) with the third-person yā' (ya' al-ghaybah, "they count"), while the rest read تَعُدُّونَ with the second-person tā' (tā' al-khitab, "you count"). The meaning of both readings is clear, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how many a town did I give respite while it was wrongdoing, then I seized it; and to Me is the final return.﴾ The verses that clarify the meaning of this verse have already been presented shortly before, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾, and up to His saying ﴿and a lofty palace﴾ [al-Hajj: 44–45].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 49:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O mankind, indeed I am to you a clear warner.﴾

(p. 281) Allah, Mighty and Exalted, commanded His Prophet ﷺ in this verse to say to the people: ﴿Indeed, I am to you a clear warner.﴾ That is: I am not your Lord, nor is your guidance in my hand, nor is your punishment on the Day of Resurrection upon me; rather, I am one who warns you of the punishment of Allah and His wrath.

Verses with this meaning are very numerous. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And upon you is only the conveyance [of the message], and upon Us is the account﴾ [al-Ra'd: 40]; His saying: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]; His saying: ﴿I am not but a clear warner﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 115]; His saying: ﴿So We did not send you over them as a guardian; your duty is only conveyance﴾ [al-Shura: 48]; His saying: ﴿He is not but a warner to you before a severe punishment﴾ [Saba': 46]; and His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]. The verses with this meaning are very numerous indeed.

As for His saying in this noble verse, "mubin" (clear), the apparent reading is that it is a descriptive form from abana (in the quadriliteral, intransitive form, meaning the same as bana, "to be clear/manifest"). The Arabs say abana, meaning the same as bana, so "mubin" is from the intransitive verb which does not take a direct object. From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

*A she-camel with a curved... in its two dark-red patches is, for the one who sees it, a clear noble lineage (itq mubin), and in its cheeks is softness.*

So his saying "itq mubin" means: manifest nobility. And from the intransitive abana is the saying of Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a al-Makhzumi:

*Were a single ant to crawl upon the surface of her skin, the traces of its movement would become manifest (la-abana) from her swellings.*

That is: it would become apparent and visible, with swelling appearing from their traces. From this is the saying of Jarir:

*When our fathers and your father outnumbered [others], the mixed-blood (muqrifat) ones became manifest (abana) among the purebred Arabian (ʿirab) horses.*

That is: it became apparent, and the mixed-breed ones appeared among the purebred. It is also possible that his saying in this verse, "mubin," is the active participle of the transitive abana, with the object omitted for generality. That is: clarifying to you in my warning everything that benefits you and everything that harms you, so that you may bring about benefit and avoid harm. The first is more apparent, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 50:

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and generous provision﴾ ﴿But those who strive against Our verses, seeking to frustrate them, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾. In this noble verse, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, makes clear that those who believe in Him, His messengers, and everything that must be believed in, and who do righteous deeds by carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions, will have forgiveness of their sins from Allah and generous provision, meaning good provision, which is the blessings He will grant them in His Gardens. And (p-282) those who acted contrary to that are the companions of the Fire, meaning the Fire whose heat is intense. This verse contains a promise for whoever obeys Him and a warning for whoever disobeys Him. Verses of this kind are numerous in the Qur'an,

such as His saying ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful. And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾ [al-Hijr: 49-50],

and His saying ﴿Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment, Possessor of bounty﴾ [Ghafir: 3], and others besides these verses. We have explained them in other places.

And His saying in this noble verse ﴿those who strive against Our verses, seeking to frustrate them﴾ [al-Hajj: 51].

Mujahid said: "mu'ajizin" means they discourage people from following the Prophet (ﷺ). Likewise 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said: "muthabbitin" (discouraging). Ibn 'Abbas said: "mu'ajizin" means overcoming and opposing. From al-Farra': "mu'ajizin" means "mu'anidin" (obstinate ones). From al-Akhfash: "mu'ajizin" means "musabiqin" (those who race ahead). From al-Zajjaj: "mu'ajizin" means those who think they can overpower us, because they thought there would be no resurrection and that Allah could not prevail over them.

Know that this word has two canonical readings. The majority read ﴿mu'ajizin﴾ with an alif between the 'ayn and the jim, in the form of the verbal noun of the pattern "mufa'alah" (the active participle of 'ajazahu). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿mu'ajjizin﴾ without an alif, with a shadda on the kasra-vowelled jim, in the form of the active participle of 'ajjazahu.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The apparent meaning, according to Arabic usage, in the majority's reading ﴿mu'ajizin﴾ is that it implies two parties, because the apparent meaning is not to be departed from except by a proof that must be returned to. The "mufa'alah" pattern implies two parties unless a proof diverts from that. The implication of two parties in the verse is by way of two paths.

The first: it is what Ibn 'Arafa said, that the meaning of ﴿mu'ajizin﴾ in the verse is that they try to outmaneuver the prophets and their followers, so each of the two sides tries to outmaneuver the other. The prophets and their followers try to outmaneuver the disbelievers and subdue them to accept what came from Allah, Exalted, and the disbelievers fight the prophets and their followers, resist them, to reduce them to incapacity in carrying out Allah's command. This aspect is evident, as Allah, Exalted, said ﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217]. Accordingly, the object of ﴿mu'ajizin﴾ is omitted, meaning: ﴿mu'ajizin﴾ the prophets and their followers, that is, overcoming them, so that they may render them incapable of establishing the truth.

The second path is the one we mentioned just above from al-Zajjaj, that the meaning of ﴿mu'ajizin﴾ is: thinking that they will render their Lord incapable, so that He cannot prevail over them, because they claim that He cannot resurrect them after death, as Allah, Exalted, said ﴿The disbelievers claim that they will never be resurrected﴾ [al-Taghabun: 7], and as Allah, Exalted, said ﴿And he presents to Us a parable and forgets his own creation; he says, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78], and Allah, Exalted, said about them that they said ﴿And we will not be resurrected﴾ [al-An'am: 29] ﴿And we will not be raised﴾ [al-Dukhan: 35]. According to this view, the disbelievers are ﴿mu'ajizin﴾ Allah in their false assumption. Allah, Exalted, has made clear in many verses that their assumption is false, and that they can by no means render their Lord incapable,

such as His saying ﴿And know that you will not escape Allah, and that Allah will disgrace the disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 2],

and His saying ﴿So know that you cannot escape Allah, and give the disbelievers tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Tawbah: 3],

and His saying ﴿And you cannot escape Him on earth or in heaven﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 22],

and His saying in "al-Jinn" ﴿And we thought that we would never cause Allah to fail on earth, nor could we escape Him by flight﴾ [al-Jinn: 12],

and others besides these verses.

We have already mentioned that what clarifies this last aspect is the saying of Ka'b ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him:

"Sakhina claimed that it would overcome its Lord,
but the most powerful of the overcomers will surely be overcome."

By "Sakhina" he means Quraysh, meaning that they try to overcome their Lord, while Allah is undoubtedly their Overcomer. The first aspect is more apparent.

As for the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, ﴿mu'jizin﴾ with a shadda on the kasra-vowelled jim, without an alif, the more apparent meaning is that it means ﴿mu'jizin﴾, that is, discouraging whoever wishes to enter faith from entering it.
